en: *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Bodhisattvas Dharmapāla and others;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
I prostrate to the nature of consciousness-only, the perfectly pure and purified one.
I now explain that teaching for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
I have composed this treatise so that those who are confused or mistaken regarding the two kinds of emptiness may give rise to correct understanding.

The generation of understanding is for the purpose of severing the two heavy obstacles; since the two obstacles arise together with the grasping at a self and at phenomena, once the two emptinesses are realized, those obstacles are accordingly severed.

The severance of obstacles is for the purpose of attaining the two supreme fruits: by severing the afflictive obstacles that cause rebirth, one realizes true liberation; by severing the cognitive obstacles that hinder comprehension, one attains great enlightenment.

Furthermore, this treatise was composed to reveal the errors of those who cling to a self and phenomena while being deluded regarding consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), so that they may realize the two kinds of emptiness and come to know the principle of consciousness-only as it truly is.

Moreover, there are those who are confused about the principle of consciousness-only: some maintain that external objects are not non-existent in the same way that consciousness is; some maintain that internal consciousness is non-existent in the same way that objects are; some maintain that the various consciousnesses have distinct functions but a single substance; and some maintain that there are no mental factors (*caitta*) distinct from the mind itself. To refute these various heterodox attachments and to enable them to attain a correct understanding of the profound and subtle principle of consciousness-only, this treatise was written.
If there is only consciousness, why do the world and the various sacred teachings speak of a self and phenomena?
The verse says:
1. Because of the conventional designation of "self" and "phenomena," Various appearances arise.
That [object] depends on what is transformed by consciousness; this transforming [consciousness] is of only three types:
namely, the ripening [consciousness], the deliberating [consciousness], and the consciousness that discriminates objects.
The treatise says:
The noble teachings of the world speak of a self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*), but these exist only as provisional designations and do not possess a real intrinsic nature.
"Self" refers to a sovereign controller, and "phenomena" refers to that which maintains its own characteristics; both of these manifest through various modes of appearance.
The various characteristics of the self refer to such things as sentient beings, living entities, and so forth; or stream-enterers, once-returners, and so forth.
The various characteristics of phenomena refer to such things as substance, qualities, and activities; or the aggregates, bases, and elements, and so forth.
"Transformation" refers to the appearance of difference as it is provisionally designated in accordance with conditions.
If these various characteristics are established through metaphorical designation (*prajñapti*), upon what basis are they accomplished?
Those characteristics are all provisionally designated based on the transformations of consciousness.
"Consciousness" (vijñāna) means "discernment" (vijñapti); here, the term "consciousness" also includes mental factors (caitta), because they are necessarily associated with it.

"Transformation" (pariṇāma) means that the substance of consciousness shifts to resemble two parts, for both the image-part (nimittabhāga) and the seeing-part (darśanabhāga) arise based upon self-cognition (svasaṃvitti).
Based on these two aspects, the designations of "self" and "phenomena" are established, for those two have no basis apart from them.

Alternatively, when internal consciousness transforms and appears as external objects, due to the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the discrimination of self and phenomena, the various consciousnesses, upon arising, manifest as if they were self and phenomena; although these appearances of self and phenomena exist within internal consciousness, they appear as if they were external objects due to such discrimination.

Since beginningless time, all classes of sentient beings have, conditioned by this [consciousness], grasped it as a real self and real dharmas. Just as one afflicted by a dream, due to the power of that affliction, perceives various external objects appearing within the mind and, conditioned by this, grasps them as truly existent external objects.
The real self and real dharmas imagined by the foolish do not exist at all; they are merely established in accordance with deluded sentiments, and are therefore said to be "provisional.

Although the semblances of self and dharmas manifested by internal consciousness exist, they lack the nature of a real self or real dharma; nevertheless, because they appear as those [semblances], they are said to be "provisional."
Because external objects are established in accordance with mental dispositions, they do not exist in the manner that consciousness does;

because internal consciousness necessarily arises in dependence upon causes and conditions, it is not non-existent in the manner that objects are. By this, the two types of clinging—namely, superimposition and denial—are refuted.
Because objects are provisionally established based upon internal consciousness, they exist only conventionally;
because consciousness is the substantial basis upon which these provisional objects depend, it also exists ultimately.
How should one understand that external objects do not truly exist and that there is only internal consciousness appearing as external objects?
Because a real self and real dharmas cannot be apprehended.
How is it that a real self cannot be apprehended?
Briefly, there are three types of selves that are clung to:

First, they cling to the notion that the self is eternal and all-pervasive, equal in extent to empty space, because it creates karma and experiences pleasure and pain in accordance with every location.
Second, they cling to the notion that although the essence of the self is eternal, its extent is not fixed, because it contracts and expands according to the size of the body.
Third, [the claim] that the essence of the self is eternal and as subtle as a single atom, moving secretly within the body to perform various activities:
first of all, this is irrational. Why is that?
If one clings to a self that is permanent, omnipresent, and equal in extent to space, it should not experience suffering, pleasure, and so forth in accordance with the body.
Furthermore, because it is permanent and omnipresent, it should be incapable of movement; how then could it follow the body to perform various karmic actions?
Furthermore, regarding the self that you postulate, are all sentient beings identical or distinct?

If you say they are identical, then when one performs an action, all should perform it; when one experiences a result, all should experience it; and when one attains liberation, all should be liberated—this would constitute a great error.
If one were to say they are different, then because the selves of all sentient beings would mutually pervade one another, their substances would necessarily be intermingled.

Furthermore, when one performs an action or experiences a result, since there would be no distinction between that self and the locus of all other selves, it would follow that everything performed and experienced by one must be attributed to all.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because the agent and the experiencer each have their own respective domains, this reasoning is also incorrect; for it is illogical that karma, its fruit, and the body would be conjoined with various selves such that they belong to one and not to another.
If liberation occurred for one, it would follow that all should be liberated, because the dharmas cultivated and realized would be conjoined with the self in every respect.
This middle position is also irrational. Why is this so?
If the essence of the self were eternally abiding, it should not expand or contract in accordance with the body.
Since there is indeed expansion and contraction—like the wind within a bellows—it should not be eternally abiding.
Furthermore, the self would have to be divisible in accordance with the body; how then can one maintain that the essence of the self is a single unity?
Therefore, what he has said is like the play of a child;
it is also unreasonable later on. Why is this so?
If my measure were as small as a single atom, how could I cause a large body to move throughout its entirety?

If you argue that although it is small, it moves rapidly through the body—like a whirling firebrand appearing to move everywhere—then the self you assert would be neither unitary nor permanent, for all things that involve coming and going are neither permanent nor unitary.
Furthermore, the self as it is conceived is of three kinds:
first, identical with the aggregates; second, distinct from the aggregates; and third, neither identical with nor distinct from the aggregates.
First, regarding the self identical with the aggregates, this is logically untenable, for the self would then be impermanent and non-unitary, just like the aggregates.
Furthermore, internal material forms (*rūpa*) are certainly not a real self, because they possess substantiality and resistance (*sapratigha*), just like external material forms.
Mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are also not a real self, because they do not continue in an unchanging succession and depend upon various conditions (*pratyaya*).
Other formations and other forms are likewise not the real self, because, like space and so forth, they lack the nature of cognition.
Furthermore, the notion of a self that exists apart from the aggregates is logically untenable, for it would follow that, like space, it would be devoid of both action and experience.

Furthermore, the subsequent claim that it is neither [conditioned nor unconditioned] is likewise unreasonable; for if one admits that the self is established in dependence upon the aggregates, yet is neither identical to nor distinct from them, it must follow that—like a jar or other such things—it is not a real self.

Moreover, since it cannot be described as either conditioned or unconditioned, it should likewise be impossible to describe it as either a self or a non-self; thus, the real self as they conceive it is not established.
Furthermore, regarding the substantially existent self-body that you all maintain: does it possess volition or is it devoid of volition?
If it possesses volition, it must be impermanent, because it does not possess volition at all times.
If it were devoid of volition, it would be like space, incapable of performing actions and unable to undergo results.
Therefore, the self as you conceive it is logically untenable in either case.
Furthermore, regarding the substantial self-entity you maintain, does it possess activity or is it devoid of activity?
If it possesses activity, such as that of the hands or feet, it must be impermanent.
If it lacks activity, such as that of a rabbit's horns, it cannot be a real self.
Therefore, the self as it is grasped is not established in either case.
Furthermore, regarding the substantial self-entity that you all grasp: is it the object-condition (*ālambana*) of the view of self?
If it is not the object-condition of the view of self, how do you know that a real self exists?

If the self-view were the object of its own focus, then the self-view would not be subsumed under the category of cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*), because it would be knowing [the object] as it truly is.

If that were so, how could all the authoritative scriptures (*āptāgama*) trusted by those who cling to a self denounce the self-view and praise non-self, stating that the view of non-self can realize *nirvāṇa*, while clinging to the self-view leads to sinking into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*)?
How could it be that false views can realize nirvāṇa, while right view, on the contrary, causes one to sink into the cycle of birth and death?
Furthermore, various forms of self-view do not take a real self as their object, because they possess an object of perception, just like other cognitions that take other things as their objects.
The object of the view of self is certainly not a real self, because it is an object of cognition, just like all other phenomena.

Therefore, the view of self does not take a real self as its object; rather, it takes the various aggregates manifested by the transformation of internal consciousness, subjecting them to various conceptual constructions according to one's own deluded sentiments.
However, there are briefly two types of self-grasping:
first, the innate (*sahaja*), and second, the conceptual (*vikalpita*).

Innate self-grasping has existed since beginningless time due to the internal causal force of false habitual tendencies; it is always coexistent with the body and operates spontaneously without depending on false teachings or false conceptualization, and is therefore called "innate."
This, moreover, is of two kinds:

first, that which is constantly continuous in the seventh consciousness, which, taking the eighth consciousness as its object, gives rise to the appearance of its own mind and clings to it as a real self;

second, that which is intermittent, residing in the sixth consciousness, which, taking the appearances of the five appropriated aggregates transformed by consciousness—either collectively or individually—as its object, gives rise to the appearance of its own mind and clings to it as a real self.

These two forms of self-grasping are subtle and therefore difficult to sever; they can only be eliminated by repeatedly cultivating the superior contemplation of the emptiness of persons during the subsequent path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Furthermore, the conceptually constructed self-grasping does not arise simultaneously with the body due to the power of present external conditions; rather, it must await false teachings and false conceptualization before it arises. Thus, it is called "conceptually constructed" and exists solely within the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
This also has two types:
first, taking as an object the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) as taught by false teachings, one gives rise to mental conceptualization and discrimination, grasping them as a real self;
second, taking as an object the characteristics of a self as taught by false teachings, one gives rise to mental conceptualization and discrimination, grasping them as a real self.
These two forms of self-clinging are coarse and thus easy to sever;
at the time of the initial path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one can eliminate them by contemplating the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of arising in all phenomena.

Regarding all such self-clinging as described: whether the aggregates (*skandha*) external to one's own mind exist or not, the aggregates within one's own mind are always present. Therefore, all instances of self-clinging falsely grasp the characteristics of the impermanent five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) as being a self.

However, because the various aggregates arise from conditions, they exist like illusions; whereas the self that is falsely grasped exists only as a result of arbitrary conceptual construction and is therefore definitively non-existent.
Thus, a sutra says:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that all views of a self held by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world arise in dependence upon the five aggregates of clinging."
If a real self did not exist, how could there be such things as recollection, cognition, study, or the recording of enmity and gratitude?

Since the real self you maintain is eternal and unchanging, these phenomena should either have existed previously just as they do now, or they should not have existed previously just as they do not now; for the essence of the self remains no different between the later and the earlier states.

If it is argued that the self is not the essence because its functions undergo change over time, this reasoning is also incorrect; for since function is not separate from essence, the self should be eternal, and since essence is not separate from function, the self should be non-eternal.

However, each sentient being possesses its own fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), which continues as a single stream, sustains seeds, and acts as a mutual cause for all phenomena; through the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), such functions as memory and cognition are thereby possible.
Therefore, the objections you have raised constitute a fault for you, not for our school.
If there were no real self, who could perform karma and who could experience its fruit?
Since the substantially existent self that is grasped is immutable, like space, how could it possibly create karma and experience its results?
If it were subject to change, it would necessarily be impermanent.

Nevertheless, because the minds and mental factors of sentient beings continue in an uninterrupted succession through the power of causes and conditions, there is no logical contradiction in their performing karma and experiencing its results.
If the self truly did not exist, who would transmigrate through the various realms of birth and death?
Furthermore, who would grow weary of suffering and seek to proceed toward Nirvana?
Since the "real self" you cling to is devoid of arising and ceasing, how can one speak of the cycle of birth and death?
Being eternally like space and not afflicted by suffering, for what reason would one grow weary of it and seek to proceed toward Nirvana?
Therefore, what they say always works to their own detriment.

Nevertheless, the continuum of body and mind among sentient beings revolves through the various realms of existence by the power of afflictions and karma; because they weary of suffering, they seek to proceed toward nirvana.
From this, it is known that there is certainly no real self;

there are only the various consciousnesses which, from beginningless time, arise in succession as cause and effect—the former perishing and the latter being born—wherein, due to the habitual perfuming of delusion, a semblance of a self appears, and the ignorant falsely grasp at this as a self.
How is it that external phenomena, which truly exist, cannot be apprehended?
It is because the external phenomena grasped by non-Buddhists and followers of other vehicles do not exist according to reason.
Why is that which is grasped by non-Buddhists non-existent?

Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the self (*ātman*) is consciousness (*cetanā*), which experiences the twenty-three principles, such as the Great One (*mahat*), which are composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

However, these principles, such as the Great One, are formed from the combination of the three *guṇas*; they are real and not merely conventional, being apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That position is irrational.

Why is this? Since the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and other such phenomena are produced by many causes, they must be conventional designations (*prajñapti*) rather than real entities—just like an army or a forest. How, then, can it be said that they are apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?
Furthermore, if the dharmas such as the "great elements" (mahābhūta) were substantially existent, they should not be composed of the three [qualities], just like their primary matter (prakṛti).
Since the three—sattva and the others—are identical to the great elements and so forth, the great elements and so forth should likewise be composed of the three [qualities].
Transformation is not permanent, and the same principle applies to the examples as well.
Furthermore, since each of the three fundamental entities possesses multiple capacities, their substance (*bhāva*) should also be manifold.

Because capacity and substance are one, if the substance of the three were all-pervasive, then when one undergoes transformation in a particular location, the others should likewise do so, for there would be no distinction between their substances.
If these three things are admitted to have distinct essential natures and characteristics, how can they combine to form a single characteristic?
It cannot be that they transform into a single characteristic at the time of combination, for their essence would be no different from what it was before they combined.
If one were to claim that the three factors differ in substance while being identical in characteristic, this would contradict one’s own tenet that substance and characteristic are one.

If substance were identical to characteristic, it should be indistinguishably one; if characteristic were identical to substance, it should be manifestly three. Therefore, one should not say that the three combine to form one.
Furthermore, the three [substances] are particulars, while "greatness" (*mahat*) and so forth are generalities. Since the general and the particular are one, they should not be both one and three.

If these three, when undergoing transformation, do not combine to form a single characteristic, they should remain as they were before transformation; how then is it that we currently perceive them as a single color and so forth?
If the three factors combined were to constitute a single characteristic, they would lose their original individual characteristics, and their substance would likewise be lost.

One cannot say that each of the three possesses two characteristics—one general and one particular—because if the general were identical to the particulars, then the general would also be three; how then could one perceive a single [characteristic]?
If you claim that each of the three entities possesses its own three characteristics and that they appear as one because their intermingling makes them difficult to discern:
since each already possesses three characteristics, how can they be seen as one?
Furthermore, how can it be known that these three things are distinct?

If each of those [entities] were to possess all three characteristics, then each individual thing should be able to constitute form and so forth; what would be lacking that would require the conjunction of the three?
Furthermore, the substance itself should also be threefold, because the substance is identical to the characteristics.

Furthermore, since all dharmas such as the great elements (mahābhūta) are composed of the three [qualities], they would have no mutual distinction when compared to one another; consequently, the distinctions between the causes and effects—the great elements and the sense faculties—would be mere designations and could not be established at all.
If that were so, a single sense organ would have to apprehend all objects, or else all objects would have to be apprehended by a single sense organ.

In that case, as we clearly perceive in the world that sentient and insentient things, pure and impure objects, and so forth, would—according to both direct perception and inference—be indistinguishable, which would constitute a great error.
Therefore, the "real dharmas" (dravya-dharma) they maintain are not established; they are merely imagined as existing through false conceptualization.
The categories (padārtha), such as substance (dravya) and so forth, maintained by the Vaiśeṣikas are for the most part real entities (dravya-sat), obtained through direct perception (pratyakṣa).
That position is irrational. Why is this so?

Among the categories of existence (*padārtha*), that which is eternal, if it were capable of producing an effect, would necessarily be impermanent because it possesses causal activity, just like the effect produced.
If it does not produce an effect, it must not possess a real intrinsic nature apart from consciousness, like a rabbit's horn and so forth.

Furthermore, among all impermanent things, those that possess material obstruction must have spatial dimensions and can therefore be analyzed, like an army or a forest; thus, they do not possess a truly existent nature.
If they were devoid of resistance, like the mind and mental factors, they would not possess a real intrinsic nature apart from these [elements].

Furthermore, the earth, water, fire, and wind as conceived by them should not be resistant; yet they are subsumed under the category of "real entities" (dravyapadārtha) because they are touched by the body faculty.

Just as hardness, moisture, heat, and motion are not included within the category of "quality" (guṇa-padārtha) as being unobstructed, so too those very things grasped as hardness, moisture, heat, and so forth, should not be categorized as qualities because they are objects of touch by the body-faculty (kāyendriya), just like earth, water, fire, and wind.
The triad of earth, water, and fire, along with blue and other colors, are all equally objects seen by the eye.

By this analogy, one should raise the following objection: therefore, we know that there are no real earth, water, fire, or wind that possess distinct intrinsic natures such as solidity or moisture; nor is it the case that real earth, water, or fire are seen by the eye.

Furthermore, regarding those "real categories" (*padārtha*) they maintain that are both resistant and eternal: because they all possess resistance, they should be impermanent, just like coarse earth and so forth.

Among all categories, those phenomena perceived by the sensory faculties that lack physical resistance should nonetheless possess resistance, because you admit they are apprehended by the sensory faculties, just like earth, water, fire, and wind.

Furthermore, those things they grasp as "non-real qualities" and so forth should not possess a distinct self-nature apart from consciousness, because they are subsumed under the category of "non-real," like the son of a barren woman.

Likewise, those things they grasp as "non-existent" and so forth should not possess a distinct self-nature apart from consciousness, because they are subsumed under the category of "non-existent," like flowers in the sky.

That which they maintain to exist must lack a distinct intrinsic nature apart from substance (*dravya*) and the rest, because it is admitted not to be non-existent, just like substance, qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth.

Alternatively, if it were separate from substance and the rest, it would follow that it does not possess the nature of existence, because it is admitted to be different from substance and the rest, just like absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
If existence is not non-existence, yet there is no separate nature of existence, how can existence truly have a separate nature of existence?
If there were a separate nature of existence apart from existent phenomena, there should likewise be a separate nature of non-existence apart from non-existent phenomena.
Since that is not the case, how could this be so? Therefore, the existence of intrinsic nature is merely a false conceptual construction.
Furthermore, it is logically impossible for the nature of real qualities and actions as they are grasped by them to be distinct from those actual qualities and actions.
Nor should it be claimed that this [entity] is not of the nature of substance, quality, or action, because it is distinct from substance and so forth, just like qualities, actions, and the like.

Furthermore, substance and so forth would have to be included within what is not substance and so forth, because they are distinct from the nature of substance and so forth, just like qualities, actions, substance, and the like.
The mutual interrogation regarding the nature of earth and so forth in relation to the substance of earth and so forth should be understood according to this principle.
Just as there is no distinct reality in the nature of reality and so forth, there should likewise be no distinct reality in the substance of reality and so forth.
If there were the nature of being real apart from what is real, then there should likewise be the nature of being unreal apart from what is unreal.
Since that is not the case, how could this be so?
Therefore, the nature of identity and difference is merely a conventional designation.

Furthermore, the category of "conjunction" (saṃyoga) as they conceive it cannot possibly be a real entity, because it is not subsumed under any of the categories such as "existence" (sat), and is thus like an absolute non-entity.

Even that which they admit to be obtained through direct perception, such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, is not truly existent when subjected to logical analysis; how much less could their own admitted category of "inherence" (*samavāya*), which is not obtained through direct perception, be truly existent?
Even if one maintains that the composite (*saṃghāta*) is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is nonetheless not substantially real (*dravyasat*) for the reasons stated above.

Furthermore, those [categories] such as "substance" (*dravya*) and so forth are not objects of direct perception obtained through a cognition that apprehends a self-nature (*svabhāva*) existing independently of consciousness; this is because they are admitted to be objects of knowledge, like the hair of a tortoise and similar [non-existent] things.

Furthermore, cognition that takes reality as its object is not subsumed under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the self-nature of reality apart from consciousness, because it arises through conceptual synthesis, like the cognition of virtue and so forth.

To speak at length, up to: cognition that takes a composite as its object is not subsumed under direct perception of the self-nature of the composite apart from consciousness, because it arises through conceptual synthesis, like the cognition of reality and so forth.
Therefore, the categories such as "substance" (dravya) posited by the Vaiśeṣikas are likewise merely conceptual constructs devised according to their own inclinations.
Some maintain that there exists a single Great Lord (Maheśvara), whose essence is real, all-pervading, and eternal, and who is capable of producing all phenomena.
That position is irrational. Why is this so?
Because any phenomenon that is capable of arising must necessarily be impermanent; whatever is impermanent must necessarily be non-pervasive; and whatever is non-pervasive cannot be ultimately real.
Since its essence is eternal, omnipresent, and endowed with all functional capacities, it should produce all phenomena simultaneously at all places and times.
To claim that it can only produce them by depending on desire or conditions contradicts the doctrine of a single cause.
Alternatively, desire and its objects should also arise simultaneously, because their cause is ever-present.

Other assertions—that there exists a single Great Brahmā, time, space, the primal limit (*ādi*), nature (*svabhāva*), emptiness, or a self (*ātman*) that are eternally real and possess all functional capacities to produce all phenomena—are all refuted in the same manner.
There are others who hold the biased view that the sounds of the *vidyā* treatises are eternal and can serve as valid means of cognition to express all phenomena.
Others maintain that all sounds are eternally existent, and only become manifest with expressive power when conditions await their revelation.
Both of these positions are unreasonable. Why is this so?
First, since the sound of the *Veda* is admitted to be expressive, it should not be eternal, just like all other sounds.
Other sounds should likewise not have sound as their permanent essence, because they depend upon various conditions, just like jars, garments, and so forth.
There are non-Buddhists who maintain that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of earth, water, fire, and wind are substantially permanent and are capable of producing coarse matter.
The coarse matter that is produced does not exceed the dimensions of its cause; although it is impermanent, its substance is substantially existent.
That too is unreasonable. Why is this so?
If the atoms (paramāṇu) that are apprehended possess spatial dimensions, as in the case of ants marching in a line, their substance would necessarily be unreal.
If they lack spatial dimensions, like the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta), they should not be able to aggregate together to produce gross derivative matter (upādāya-rūpa).
Since they can produce effects just as those produced by them do, how can you say that atoms are permanent?

Furthermore, since the produced effect does not exceed the magnitude of its cause, it should—like the atom—not be called a coarse form (*audārika-rūpa*); thus, this resultant form would not be perceivable by the sense organs such as the eye, which contradicts your own tenets.
If it is argued that the resultant matter (phala-rūpa) is perceived by the sense organs as coarse because it is conjoined with the quality of coarseness due to its magnitude, [we reply:
since the magnitude of the asserted resultant matter is identical to that of its causes, it should—like an atom—lack any conjunction with the quality of coarseness.
Alternatively, atoms should also be conjoined with coarse qualities, just like coarse derivative matter (*bhautika-rūpa*), because there is no difference in their location.

If it is argued that derivative matter pervades its own causes and may thus be called "coarse" because those causes are not unitary, then the substance of this derivative matter must itself not be unitary, because the locations of the causes where it resides are each distinct.
If that were so, this effect would likewise not be coarse; consequently, it could not be apprehended by the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).

If the effect is considered coarse because it is a conglomeration of many [parts], then a multitude of causal atoms (*paramāṇu*) in conjunction should likewise not be subtle, as they would suffice to constitute the object of the senses (*indriyaviṣaya*); what need then is there for a "resultant" entity?
Since it is divided into many parts, it cannot be substantially existent; thus, what you maintain is internally contradictory.
Furthermore, if the effect and the cause both possess material obstruction, they should not occupy the same location, just as two atoms do not.
If you claim that the essence and characteristics of cause and effect undergo mutual assimilation— just as sand receives water or medicinal herbs enter molten copper—
who would grant that the essences of sand or copper assimilate water or medicine?
Alternatively, they must be distinct and subject to transformation, being neither unitary nor permanent.

Furthermore, if the substance of the coarse material fruit were a single entity, then when one part is apprehended, the whole should be apprehended, because this and that are one; thus, "that" should be just like "this.

To deny this would contradict reason, yet to accept it would contradict empirical fact. Therefore, what they maintain fails from every perspective and is merely a false conceptualization following their own whims.
However, although the various classes of non-Buddhists are numerous, the entities they grasp as existing do not exceed four types:
first, those who grasp that the entity of an existent phenomenon and its nature of existence are definitely identical in essence, such as the Sāṃkhyas and others.
That position is unreasonable.
Why is this so? Because it would follow that all phenomena do not possess intrinsic nature.

If all things possessed a single nature whose essence was without distinction, it would contradict the fact that the three *guṇas* have distinct essences, and it would also contradict the distinctions among all phenomena in the world.
Furthermore, if form and so forth were identical to the nature of form and so forth, then form and so forth should not possess differences such as blue, yellow, and the like.
2. Second, there are those, such as the Vaiśeṣikas, who maintain that the entity of a dharma and its existence (sattā) and so forth are definitely distinct in substance.
Their position is irrational. Why is this?
Do not [assert this], for it would follow that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Just as that which has already ceased and is non-existent cannot have its essence apprehended, [your position] would contradict the fact that real entities and so forth do not lack their own essence, and it would also contradict what is directly perceived in the world—that things exist.
Furthermore, if form and so forth were not of the nature of form and so forth, they would—like sound and so forth—not be objects of the eye and other sense faculties.
Third, there are those who maintain that a phenomenon (dharma) and its existence (sattā), etc., are both identical and different, as in the case of shamelessness and the like.
That position is irrational.

Why? Because it would entail the same fallacies of identity and difference as previously discussed; because their characteristics being contradictory implies their substances must be distinct; and because the identities of both unity and difference cannot be established simultaneously.
Do not hold that all phenomena are of a single essence, or that their identity or difference is merely conventional and not real, yet you cling to it as real; such a position is logically untenable.
Fourth, there are those, such as the Ājīvikas, who maintain that the existent phenomenon and its nature of existence are neither identical nor different.
That position is irrational.
Why? Because the grasping at identity and difference would entail that identity and difference are one and the same.
Regarding the expressions "not one" and "not different," do they function as negations or as affirmations?
If they were solely affirmative, they would not be a double negation.
If they were merely negative, there would be no underlying conceptual adherence.
If it were both exclusion (*apoha*) and manifestation (*pradarśana*), they would necessarily contradict one another.
If it were neither manifestation nor exclusion, it would result in mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Furthermore, it is neither identical nor different; this contradicts common worldly knowledge that things exist as either identical or different, and it also contradicts your own school’s tenet that dharmas such as form (*rūpa*) are definitively and substantially real.
Therefore, that statement is merely a deceptive evasion of fault; let no wise person mistakenly grant it credence.
How could the various dharmas, such as form and so forth, which are clung to by other vehicles as being real and existing apart from consciousness, not be non-existent?
The matter, non-associated formations, and various unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) that they grasp at do not exist according to reason.
Furthermore, the matter they grasp at is of two general types:
first, that which is resistant (sapratigha), composed of atoms (paramāṇu); [and second, that which is non-resistant].
Second, that which is non-resistant is not composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
That resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) is certainly not substantially real, because the atoms that compose it are not substantially real.
This is to say: if atoms possessed material obstruction (*sapratighatva*), they would—like vases and the like—be merely nominal and not substantial.
If they were devoid of resistance, they would be like non-material phenomena; how then could they aggregate to form things such as jars or garments?
Furthermore, if atoms possessed spatial dimensions, they would necessarily be divisible, and thus could not be substantially real.
If atoms lacked spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*), they would be like non-material phenomena; how then could they aggregate to receive light and cast shadows?

When the sun rises and shines upon a pillar or similar object, light and shadow appear on its eastern and western sides respectively. Since the locations where light is received and shadows are cast are distinct, the atoms you maintain must certainly possess spatial dimensions.

Furthermore, when one perceives or touches objects such as walls, one perceives only this side and not that part; since a composite object consists of atoms, these atoms must necessarily possess spatial dimensions (digbhāga).

Furthermore, each atom (paramāṇu), according to its location, must necessarily possess distinctions of above, below, and the four cardinal directions; otherwise, there would be no sense of their mutual aggregation, or they would interpenetrate one another, such that gross objects could not be formed. Therefore, atoms certainly possess spatial dimensions (digbhāga).
That which you maintain to be resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*) consists of atoms (*paramāṇu*). If these atoms lacked spatial extension (*digbhāga*), they would lack obstruction;

if that were so, they would not be resistant by way of obstruction. Therefore, the atoms you maintain must possess spatial extension. Because they possess spatial extension, they can be analyzed and are certainly not substantially real (*dravyasat*); thus, the substantial existence of resistant matter is not established.
Do the five consciousnesses not have a basis and an objective condition consisting of form?
Although they are not non-material, they are transformations of consciousness.

That is to say, when consciousness arises, through the power of internal causes and conditions, it transforms and manifests as appearances resembling the eye and other organs, as well as forms and other objects; these very appearances serve as its basis and objective condition.

However, the sense organs such as the eye are not apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); rather, their existence is inferred because they can give rise to consciousness. These are merely functional capacities and are not produced by external [matter].
Since the principle that external, resistant form (*rūpa*) exists is logically untenable, it must therefore be a manifestation of internal consciousness alone.

The arising of visual consciousness and the other consciousnesses is termed the "visual faculty" and so forth; these serve as the basis for the production of visual consciousness and the others. Since it is logically impossible for there to be external objects of perception (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for these visual consciousnesses and the rest, one must certainly admit that what is transformed by one's own consciousness serves as the object-condition. That is to say, you maintain that whatever can induce a representation resembling its own consciousness is the object-condition for that consciousness.

It is not merely that [the object] can produce [the cognition]; rather, one must not consider conditions such as causes and objects to be the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for this consciousness.
This is because when the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, cognize form and so forth, they only take as their object a composite [state] that resembles those [objects].

The composite characteristic does not possess a real intrinsic nature distinct from the various atoms, because when those [atoms] are analyzed, the consciousness that appears as that [composite] characteristic certainly does not arise.

Since that composite characteristic is not truly existent, it cannot be said to be the object-condition (*ālambana*) of the five consciousnesses; otherwise, a second moon and the like would also be able to produce the five consciousnesses.
Atoms in a state of mutual conjunction cannot each serve as the objective support for the five consciousnesses, because the characteristics of atoms do not exist within these consciousnesses.
Nor do atoms possess the characteristic of conjunction, because this characteristic does not exist when they are not in conjunction.

The state of aggregation and the time of non-aggregation do not differ in the essential nature and characteristics of these atoms; therefore, just as at the time of non-aggregation, the atoms of form and so forth are not the objects of the five consciousnesses during the state of aggregation.

There are those who maintain that when individual atoms (*paramāṇu*) of form and so forth are not aggregated, they are not the objects of the five consciousnesses; however, when they are in a state of mutual aggregation and support one another, a coarse characteristic (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*) arises, which serves as the object of these consciousnesses. They hold that this characteristic is substantially existent and constitutes the objective referent (*ālambana*) for them.
That position is incorrect, because the entity and its characteristics remain identical whether it is in a state of collective aggregation or not yet aggregated.
Furthermore, regarding objects such as jars and bowls, or atoms and the like, the consciousnesses that take them as their objective conditions would otherwise have no distinction between them.
In an aggregate of atoms, each individual atom would have to relinquish its subtle and spherical characteristics.

Furthermore, a consciousness characterized by coarse features cannot take a subtle characteristic as its object; otherwise, a consciousness directed toward one object would be taking another object, and a single consciousness would consequently have to perceive all objects.
If even the concession that atoms exist leads to this fault, how much more so when there are no real atoms external to consciousness?

From this, it is definitively known that the appearance of form and so forth, which is transformed by one's own consciousness, serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); for the seeing [of that object] arises in dependence upon it and bears its image.

However, when consciousness undergoes transformation, it manifests a single image instantaneously according to the size of the object; it does not separately transform into a multitude of atoms that combine to form a single entity.

For those who cling to the notion that coarse matter possesses a substantial reality, the Buddha taught the concept of atoms to enable them to analyze and deconstruct it; he did not mean to say that various forms of matter actually consist of real atoms.

Yogācāras, by means of conceptual wisdom (*parikalpita-prajñā*), gradually analyze and deconstruct coarse material forms until they reach a point where further analysis is impossible; this is conventionally designated as the "ultimate atom" (*paramāṇu*).

Although these ultimate atoms still possess spatial dimensions and cannot be further divided, if one were to divide them further, they would appear as mere space and would no longer be called "form" (*rūpa*); therefore, it is said that the ultimate atom is the limit of form.
From this it should be known that all resistant forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*) are manifestations of consciousness and are not composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Since other non-resistant forms (*apratigha-rūpa*) belong to this same category, they too do not exist substantially.
Alternatively, because they lack resistance (*sapratigha*), like the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), they certainly cannot be real matter (*rūpa*).

While all resistant matter manifests with the characteristics of form, even when investigated through reasoning, it does not exist apart from consciousness; how much less so for non-resistant matter, which lacks the manifest characteristics of form—how could that be said to be a truly real material phenomenon?
Are informative and non-informative matter not truly existent?
They are not truly existent. Why is this so?
Furthermore, if bodily informative matter (*kāyavijñaptirūpa*) were substantially existent, what would its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) be?
If you say it is shape (*saṃsthāna*), then it is not substantially existent, because it is analyzable and because atoms (*paramāṇu*) of length and so forth cannot be apprehended.
If one says this is "motion," it is likewise not truly existent, because it perishes as soon as it arises and thus lacks the meaning of motion.
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena do not depend on a cause for their cessation; if cessation were to depend on a cause, it would not be true cessation.

If it is claimed that there is a form which is neither color nor shape, produced by the mind and capable of moving the hands and so forth, and is thus called "bodily informative action" (*kāya-vijñapti-karman*), this is also logically untenable;
for if this were movement, the argument would be refuted as previously demonstrated.
If it were a cause of motion, it would be identical to the wind element; yet, since wind lacks informative representation (*vijñapti*), it should not be called "informative.

Furthermore, tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) should not be categorized as either wholesome or unwholesome, nor does it manifest odor or taste; by analogy with these cases, tangibility should be understood accordingly. Therefore, bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karma*) is certainly not substantially existent.

However, with the mind as the cause, the material forms such as hands transformed by consciousness arise and cease in a continuous succession, moving toward other locations; because they appear to perform actions that represent the mind, they are conventionally designated as "bodily intimation" (kāyavijñapti).

Vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) is also not substantially existent as a nature of sound, because a single momentary sound lacks the capacity for signification, a multi-momentary continuum is not substantially real, and external resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) has already been refuted previously.

However, because of the mind, consciousness transforms into something resembling sound that arises and ceases in a continuous succession, appearing as if it expresses meaning; this is conventionally termed "vocal intimation" (*vāgvijñapti*), which does not contradict reason.
Since intimation is in fact non-existent, how could non-intimation (*avijñapti*) possibly be real?
Nevertheless, there is no logical contradiction in provisionally establishing the non-informative (*avijñapti*) based on the limits of wholesome or unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*) and aspirations.

That is to say, this is established either in the stage where the seeds of wholesome or unwholesome volitions that initiate superior bodily and vocal actions increase, or in the stage of meditative concentration where volitions that cause the actual occurrence of unwholesome bodily and vocal actions cease; therefore, it is a provisional existence (*prajñaptisat*).
The World-Honored One stated in the sūtras that there are three types of karma; does this not contradict the sūtras by negating the existence of bodily and vocal karma?
It does not negate them as being non-existent, but merely states that they are not form (*rūpa*).

The volition (*cetanā*) capable of moving the body is called bodily karma; the volition capable of producing speech is called vocal karma; and because the two types of deliberative volition are associated with the mind and cause the mind to act and move, they are called mental karma.
The volitional formations (*cetanā*) of body and speech that produce activity are called "karma" (*karman*).

Because they are traversed by this definitive volition (*niścaya-cetanā*) and because they universally produce the maturation fruits (*vipāka-phala*) of suffering and pleasure, they are also called "paths" (*mārga*). Therefore, the first seven paths of action also have volition as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Alternatively, because bodily and vocal intimation are produced by volition (*cetanā*), they are metaphorically designated as "action" (*karman*).
Because they are traversed by volition, they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*).
From this it should be understood that there is no external form (*rūpa*) in reality; rather, only internal consciousness transforms and arises in the semblance of form.
The non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are likewise not substantially real. Why is this so?

Because factors such as acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) do not possess a substantial characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that can be apprehended like that of matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), or mental factors (*caitasika*); nor can their activity be apprehended as something distinct from matter, mind, and mental factors. For these reasons, it is known that they are certainly not substantially real, but are merely conventionally established based on the states (*avasthā*) of matter and the other aggregates.

This meditative absorption is certainly not a distinct entity or function apart from matter, mind, and mental factors, because it is admitted to be subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), just like matter and mind.
Alternatively, since mind, mental factors, and matter are not subsumed by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), this absorption—like absolute non-existence—is certainly not substantially real.
Alternatively, because they are not subsumed under other real dharmas, they lack a real substantial entity, just like other conventional dharmas.
Furthermore, how do you know that acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) possess a real substantial function distinct from form, mind, and so forth?
Because it is stated in the sūtras.
As it is said: "Such a person is endowed with both good and evil; the noble one is endowed with the ten dharmas of one beyond training.
Furthermore, it says that ordinary beings are not endowed with the dharmas of the noble ones, and that all arhats are not endowed with afflictions.
The statement regarding "attainment" (prāpti) and "non-attainment" (aprāpti) reveals that these do not exist as substantial entities.
The Sūtra does not state that these possess a real substance or function distinct from form, mind, and so forth; thus, it cannot serve as proof for their existence.
Furthermore, the Sūtra speaks of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin) attaining the seven jewels; how could this possibly mean he attains the bodies of others or insentient objects?
If you claim that mastery over the [seven] treasures constitutes "attainment" by way of metaphorical designation,
why do you not likewise allow this for wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, yet insist instead on a literal attainment?

If you argue that the seven treasures can be metaphorically designated as "attained" because they exist in the present, how can you know that the wholesome and unwholesome dharmas which are attained do not likewise exist apart from the present?
Because that which is divorced from actual dharmas does not exist, and because there must currently exist seeds of goodness and so forth.
Furthermore, what superior function does "acquisition" (prāpti) have with respect to dharmas?

If you say it can cause [dharmas] to arise, then it should also cause unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) to arise; all insentient things would never arise, and those not yet acquired or already lost would never be produced again.
If acquisition (*prāpti*) arising simultaneously [with a dharma] were the cause for its origination, then the two types of birth (*jāti*) that you postulate would be useless.

Furthermore, if one possessed the acquisitions of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral dharmas, then these wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral states should all manifest simultaneously; if, however, they must await other causes, then acquisition itself is useless.
If the attainment of dharmas were the cause for their non-loss, it would be because sentient beings achieve them by means of it.

Since all dharmas that can be achieved are not separate from sentient beings—and if they were separated from sentient beings, they could not truly be found—then the attainment of dharmas would be useless in both cases.

Since attainment (*prāpti*) does not exist in reality, non-attainment (*aprāpti*) likewise does not exist; however, based on sentient beings and the various phenomena that can be established, three types of "accomplishment" (*samanvāgama*) are provisionally designated according to their respective states:
first, accomplishment as seeds (*bīja-samanvāgama*); second, accomplishment through mastery (*vaśitā-samanvāgama*); and third, accomplishment as manifest activity (*samudācāra-samanvāgama*).
The term "non-accomplishment" (*aprāpti*) is established as the opposite of this.

Although there are many such categories, it is specifically at the stage when the seeds of what is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) within the three realms have not yet been permanently destroyed that "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) is conventionally designated as "the nature of an ordinary person" (*pṛthagjanatva*), because one has not yet accomplished any of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
Furthermore, how is it known that distinct forms, minds, and so forth possess real *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity)?
Because it is stated in the Sūtra.
As the Sūtra says: "This is the homogeneity of devas; this is the homogeneity of humans," and so on at length.
This sūtra does not state that there exists a real *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) distinct from form, mind, and so forth; thus, it fails as proof.
If you argue that real existence is known because the cause for identical cognition and speech arises from it, then grass, trees, and the like should also possess *sabhāgatā*.

Furthermore, if one claims that the term "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) arises from a cognition of similarity, then homogeneity itself would require another distinct homogeneity. Since that is not the case, how could this be so?

If it is argued that a real entity must exist because it serves as the cause for the arising of a common desire for activity, this reasoning is also untenable; for if habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) serve as the cause for the arising of a common desire for activity, why insist on the separate existence of a real homogeneity?
Nevertheless, based on the distinctions among the similar states of the bodies and minds of sentient beings, "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) is provisionally established.
Furthermore, how is it known that there exists a real life-faculty (jīvitendriya) distinct from form, mind, and so forth?
Because it is stated in the sūtras. As the sūtra states:
"One should know that among the triad of life-span (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), what is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is designated as 'life-span'.
This sūtra does not state that there exists a real entity of life-span distinct from matter, mind, and so forth; therefore, it fails to serve as proof [for your position].
Furthermore, since it has already been established that form is not separate from consciousness, there should likewise be no distinct life-faculty (jīvitendriya) apart from consciousness.
Moreover, if the life-faculty were a real entity distinct from consciousness, it would follow that—just like sensation (vedanā) and so forth—it would not be a real life-faculty.
If that is so, why does the Sūtra speak of three factors?
They are spoken of as three because their meanings are distinct, just as in the case of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Furthermore, in the state of being without mind (*acittaka*), life-force (*jīvita*) and warmth (*uṣman*) would necessarily be absent.
Is it not stated in the sūtras that consciousness does not depart from the body?
If this is so, how can these be called states without mind?

They [the states without mind] cease the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), but they are not the Ālaya-vijñāna; the reason for the existence of this consciousness will be explained extensively later.

This consciousness is sufficient to serve as the substance of the realms, destinies, and births, because it is the pervasive, continuous, and resultant fruit of maturation (*vipāka*); therefore, there is no need to laboriously postulate a separate, real life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Rather, the life-faculty is conventionally established based on the seeds that directly produce this consciousness, which—due to the specific functional capacity induced by karma—determine the duration of its persistence.

Furthermore, how is it known that the two mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) and the maturation of non-conception (*āsaṃjñika-vipāka*) possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) distinct from matter, mind, and so forth?
If they lacked a real intrinsic nature, they would be unable to obstruct the mind and mental factors so that they do not manifest.

If, in the state of no-mind, there were a distinct, real dharma—different from matter, mind, and so forth—that could obstruct the mind and is called "mindless absorption," then at the time of no-form, there should likewise be a distinct, real dharma—different from matter, mind, and so forth—that could obstruct matter and be called "formless absorption."
Since that is not the case, how could this be so?
Furthermore, why must that which obstructs the mind be a real entity (*dravyadharma*)?
Even something provisional (*prajñapti*), such as a dam or a levee, is capable of obstruction.

This means that when practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because one feels aversion toward the coarse movement of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of concentration, one generates a superior aspiration to restrain the mind and mental factors, causing them to become increasingly subtle and refined.

At the time of the subtle mind, it perfumes the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), forming seeds for an extremely predominant state of aversion toward the mind and so forth. Because these seeds damage and suppress the seeds of the mind and its associates, the coarse and mobile states of mind do not manifest for a time; based on this state, the two meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) are provisionally established. Since these seeds are virtuous, the absorptions are also called virtuous.

Because one seeks the fruit of non-conceptualization prior to the attainment of the state of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the seeds perfumed thereby bring about that ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna).
Based on this meditative absorption, coarse and active ideation and so forth do not function; thus, the designation "non-conceptual" (asaṃjñin) is provisionally established for this particular state.
Established based on maturation (*vipāka*), they receive the name "maturation.
Therefore, these three dharmas are also not substantially existent.

Furthermore, how is it known that the various conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) possess a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) distinct from matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth?
Because it is stated in the Sūtras. As the Sūtra says:
"There are three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned," and so forth, as explained at length.
This sutra does not state that form, mind, and so on, possess a real intrinsic nature; therefore, it cannot serve as proof [for such a claim].
The use of the sixth grammatical case does not signify that they are distinct entities, because the substance of matter and mind is precisely matter and mind themselves.

Nor is it the case that the nature of the characteristic must necessarily differ from the characterized object, lest the characteristics such as solidity and so forth differ from the elements such as earth and so forth.

If the characteristics of the conditioned were distinct from the substance of that which is characterized, then the substance of the characteristics of the unconditioned would likewise be distinct from that which is characterized.
Furthermore, if characteristics such as arising were substantially co-existent [with their substratum], they would necessarily exercise their functions simultaneously at all times.
If their functions do not arise simultaneously because they are mutually contradictory, then their essential natures must also be mutually contradictory; how then could they coexist?

Furthermore, the functions of duration, change, and cessation should not occur simultaneously, yet the natures of the characterizers (lakṣaṇas) and the characterized (lakṣya) both exist inherently from the outset;
the same should apply to their functions as well, since there is no distinct nature [between them].
If it is argued that those [characteristics] themselves depend on further causes and conditions, then the causes and conditions upon which they depend would not be inherently existent.
Furthermore, if one maintains that arising and so forth are useless because the characterized entity exists eternally yet is conjoined with arising and so forth,
then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) would also possess arising and so forth, since no distinct cause for such a difference between them can be found.
Furthermore, the past and future are neither manifest nor eternal; they should resemble flowers in the sky and lack the nature of real existence.
Since "arising" is defined as existence, how could it exist in the future?
Since "ceasing" is defined as non-existence, it should not be present in the present.
If cessation were not non-existent, then arising would not be existent.
Furthermore, since cessation contradicts abiding, how could one insist that they are simultaneous?
Since abiding does not contradict arising, why should they be restricted to different times?
Therefore, their positions, whether advancing or retreating, are irrational.

However, because conditioned phenomena arise through the power of causes and conditions, they exist now having not existed before, and having briefly existed, they return to non-existence; to distinguish them from unconditioned phenomena, four characteristics are provisionally established:
"existence now having not existed before" is the state called arising (*jāti*); [the remaining characteristics are defined accordingly].
The temporary suspension of the state of arising is termed "abiding";
the differentiation of abiding according to its prior and subsequent moments is further designated by the name "change";
and the moment when that which was temporarily present returns to non-existence is called "cessation."
The first three exist, and therefore they are all present; the last one is non-existent, and therefore it belongs to the past.
How can that which is a non-entity (abhāva) serve as a characteristic of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa)?
What fault is there in using this subsequent non-existence as a characteristic?

Arising indicates that a dharma previously non-existent now exists; cessation indicates that a dharma which existed later becomes non-existent; changeability indicates that this dharma is not immutable; and duration indicates that this dharma possesses temporary function. Therefore, although these four characteristics are all termed "indications" (*vijñapti*) with respect to conditioned dharmas, what they indicate differs.
These four characteristics are provisionally established based on a single moment (*kṣaṇa*); they may likewise be provisionally established according to the stages of a single lifetime (*ekāvadhi*).

The initial existence is called "arising" (*jāti*); the subsequent non-existence is called "cessation" (*nirodha*); the continuity of similar states after arising is called "abiding" (*sthiti*); and the transformation of this very continuity is called "alteration" (*anyathātva*). Therefore, all four characteristics are merely provisional designations.
Furthermore, how is it known that there exist real collections of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) that express distinct colors, minds, and so forth?
Because it is stated in the *Sūtra*. As the *Sūtra* says:
The Buddha has attained rare collections of names, phrases, and syllables.
This sūtra does not state that there are real names and so forth distinct from matter, mind, and other phenomena; therefore, the proof is unestablished.
If names, phrases, and syllables were substantially existent as something distinct from sound, they would—like matter and so forth—not be actual signifiers.

If it is claimed that sound is what produces names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*), then this sound must necessarily possess variations in its vocal modulations; since these are sufficient to convey meaning, what further use would there be for names and so forth?

If one were to claim that the variations in vocal modulations within sound are themselves the names, phrases, and phonemes, then by analogy with the visible forms (*rūpa*) where variations in shape and dimension are perceived as distinct from the color itself, there would have to be a separate substantial entity existing apart from the locus of the color.

If it is argued that the modulations of tone within sound—such as those produced by stringed or wind instruments—are not expressive, then these [modulations] should be like that [instrumental] sound, and names and so forth would not arise separately from them.
Furthermore, who says that those [modulations] are definitively incapable of expression?

If sound were capable of signifying meaning, then the sounds of wind-chimes and the like should possess the function of signification; these, like those [sounds of speech], would not separately produce real sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*).
If it is only the sound of speech that can produce names and so forth, why do you not admit that only speech is capable of signifying meaning?
By what reasoning is it definitively known that the expressive [word] is identical to speech? How can one know that there exists an expressive [word] distinct from speech?

That speech is not different from the expressive [word] is understood by both humans and gods; those who insist that the expressive [word] is distinct from speech are "heavenly lovers" (devānāṃpriya) and no others.

Nevertheless, based on the distinctions in the temporal states of vocal sounds, one conventionally establishes the sets of names (nāma-kāya), phrases (pada-kāya), and phonemes (vyañjana-kāya): a name expresses an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), a phrase expresses a specific distinction (viśeṣa), and a phoneme—namely, a syllable—is the basis for both.
Although these three—[the phonemes, names, and phrases]—are not distinct entities apart from sound, they differ in their status as conventional or real and are not identical to sound itself.

Consequently, there is a distinction between the objects of the two analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) of dharmas and words; likewise, the inclusion of sound, names, and so forth within the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) also differs for each.

Furthermore, it is taught according to this world-system that names, phrases, and syllables are conventionally established based on sound; however, this does not apply to all cases, for in other buddha-fields, these three are also conventionally established based on light, exquisite fragrances, flavors, and so forth.

There are those who maintain that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are distinct from the mind and mental factors and are subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from the mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
This is also unreasonable, because they are designated by names such as "greed" (*rāga*); just like manifest greed and so forth, they are not dissociated [from the mind].
The assertion that there exist other distinct, non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) should likewise be refuted according to the same reasoning as before.
Furthermore, it is logically untenable for any unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) to exist as determinate, substantial entities apart from form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth.
Furthermore, there are briefly three types of phenomena that definitely exist:
first, phenomena known through direct perception, such as form, mind, and so forth;
second, phenomena experienced through use, such as jars, clothing, and so forth.
These two types of phenomena are commonly known by the world to exist, without depending on logical proof through causes.
Third, there are phenomena characterized by functional activity, such as the eyes, ears, and so forth; their existence is established and known through their respective functions.

Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not universally known by the world to definitely exist; furthermore, they lack functional activity like that of the eyes or ears. Even if one were to grant them functional activity, they would necessarily be impermanent. Therefore, one must not maintain that unconditioned phenomena definitely exist.

However, because all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta) possess the nature of being objects of knowledge, or because they possess a nature manifested by form, mind, and so forth—just like form and mind—one should not cling to them as being real unconditioned entities existing apart from form, mind, and the like.
Furthermore, are space and so forth one or many?
If their essence were one and pervasive across all locations,
then because space accommodates phenomena such as form, the essence of space would necessarily become manifold in accordance with the entities it accommodates.
Because that which occupies one location cannot occupy another, otherwise all phenomena would mutually pervade one another.
If it is argued that space does not conjoin with phenomena, then it should not be a receptacle, just like other unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Furthermore, does space exist within form and the other aggregates?
If it exists, they would necessarily intermingle; if it does not exist, it would not be all-pervasive.
Moreover, when the fetters of one category and one grade are abandoned, one would consequently attain the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the remaining categories and grades.

When a single phenomenon fails to arise due to the absence of its conditions, one should attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) with respect to all [phenomena], because it is logically consistent that their substance is one.

If their substance were manifold, they would possess distinct categories and, like form (*rūpa*) and so forth, would not be truly unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); furthermore, space (*ākāśa*) would likewise not be omnipresent or capable of containing all things.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entities asserted by other schools to exist substantially apart from mind and mental factors should be refuted according to the previous [arguments].
Furthermore, since all unconditioned phenomena are admitted to lack cause and effect, they must—like a rabbit’s horn—not exist as something distinct from mind and its concomitants.
However, the sūtras state that there are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) such as space (*ākāśa*).
Briefly, these unconditioned phenomena are of two kinds:

first, those that exist as provisional designations based on the transformation of consciousness. This means that because one has previously heard the names "space" and so forth, the mental images of space and so forth arise in accordance with conceptualization; through the power of repeated habituation, when the mind and its associates arise, they manifest in the likeness of unconditioned phenomena such as space.
These manifested appearances are similar before and after without undergoing change; they are conventionally designated as "permanent.

Second, they are provisionally established based on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); that is, the true suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by emptiness and selflessness, which is neither existent nor non-existent, transcends the paths of mind and speech, and is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena. Because it is the ultimate truth of phenomena, it is called the "nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*); because it is free from all obstructions, it is called "space" (*ākāśa*).

Because it is the ultimate realization through which all defilements are extinguished by the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), it is called "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Because it is naturally pure without depending on the power of discernment, or is manifested through the absence of conditions, it is called "cessation not through discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Because the sensations of suffering and pleasure have ceased, it is called "immovable" (*āniñjya*). Because ideation and sensation do not function, it is called the "cessation of ideation and sensation" (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*).

These five are all provisionally established based upon *tathatā* (suchness); *tathatā* itself is also a provisional designation. It is said to "exist" in order to preclude the denial that it is non-existent, and it is said to be "empty" in order to preclude the attachment that it is existent.

Do not say that because it is empty and illusory, it is therefore taught as real; rather, because its principle is neither false nor inverted, it is called *tathatā* (suchness). This differs from other schools which claim that apart from matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), there exists a real, eternal dharma named *tathatā*; therefore, the various unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are not definitively substantially existent.

The various phenomena (dharmas) grasped by non-Buddhists and those of other vehicles do not possess a real intrinsic nature distinct from mind and mental factors, because they are objects of apprehension (*grāhya*), just like mind and mental factors.
Furthermore, the cognition that apprehends them does not take them as its object, because it is itself an apprehending subject (*grāhaka*).
Just as these cognitions are based upon their objects, so too all minds and mental factors, being dependently originated, are like magical illusions and do not exist in reality.
To dispel the false attachment that there are real objects existing external to the mind and its mental factors, it is said that "there is only consciousness."
If one holds that consciousness-only truly exists, such grasping at it as an external object is likewise an attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
Briefly stated, there are two types of attachment to dharmas:
first, the innate (*sahaja*); second, the conceptual (*vikalpita*).

The innate grasping at phenomena as real (*sahaja-dharmagrāha*) arises from the internal causal force of false habitual perfuming since beginningless time; it is always coexistent with the body, functioning spontaneously without depending on false teachings or false discrimination, and is therefore called "innate."
This, moreover, is of two kinds:

first, that which is constantly continuous, residing in the seventh consciousness; taking the eighth consciousness as its object, it gives rise to the appearances of its own mind and clings to them as real dharmas.
