When the preceding cause is in the state of cessation, the subsequent effect arises immediately, like the simultaneous rising and falling of the two ends of a scale. Thus, the continuity of cause and effect flows like a stream; why rely on the concepts of "going" and "coming" for this continuity to be established as non-interruption?
When the cause exists in the present state, the subsequent effect has not yet arisen; of what, then, is it the cause?
When the effect exists in the present state, the preceding cause has already ceased; of what, then, is it the effect?
Since cause and effect do not exist, who can avoid the extremes of nihilism and eternalism?
If the subsequent effect already existed at the time of the cause, and the effect was thus inherently present from the beginning, why would it depend on a preceding cause?
Since the meaning of "cause" is non-existent, how could the meaning of "effect" possibly exist?
If there were neither cause nor effect, how could one avoid the extremes of nihilism and eternalism?
Since the principle of cause and effect is established through the functioning of phenomena according to the Dharma, your objections do not apply to our school.

If the essence (*tattva*) is inherently existent, its function must likewise be so, for the causes and conditions upon which it depends are also inherently existent. Consequently, your position that cause and effect are definitively non-existent is untenable; you should therefore believe in the correct principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as taught in the Mahāyāna.

This means that this correct principle is profound and subtle, transcending verbal expression; terms such as "cause" and "effect" are all merely provisional designations. Observing that present phenomena possess the capacity to project subsequent states, one provisionally establishes a "future effect" in contrast to speak of a "present cause."
Observing that present phenomena possess characteristics that correspond to preceding conditions, we provisionally posit a "prior cause" in contrast to the "present effect.
"Provisional" means that the present consciousness manifests appearing as those [past] characteristics.
Thus, the principle of cause and effect is clearly evident; remaining free from the two extremes, it accords with the Middle Way. All wise persons should practice and study accordingly.
Other schools (nikāya) maintain that although the past and future do not exist, there is still the principle of the constant continuity of cause and effect.

They argue that even for a present phenomenon that is extremely rapid, there are still two moments: the initial moment of arising and the final moment of cessation. At the time of arising, it repays the cause; at the time of cessation, it draws forth the fruit. Although these two moments exist, their substance is one.

When the preceding cause is in the process of ceasing and the subsequent effect is in the process of arising, although their essential natures and characteristics differ, both are equally existent. Such a relationship of cause and effect is not a mere conceptual construct; yet it avoids the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and is free from the aforementioned difficulties. What wise person would reject this and believe in anything else?
Those words are empty and possess no real meaning at all.
How could there be two times within a single thought-moment?
Since arising and ceasing are mutually contradictory, how could they be identical to the present?
If cessation were present, then arising would have to be future.
Since it exists and is therefore called "arising," why would it not be past when it does not exist and is therefore called "cessation"?
If cessation were not non-existent, then arising would not be existent.
Since arising is currently manifest, cessation ought to be currently non-existent.
Furthermore, how can these two opposites be one in essence?
Such a thing is not observed in the case of suffering, pleasure, and so forth.
If arising and ceasing were identical, then time would not be dual;
if arising and ceasing were distinct, how could one say their substance is the same?
Therefore, it is logically impossible for arising and ceasing to both exist simultaneously in the present, depending upon a single identical substance.

The Sautrāntikas and others also fail to establish the principle of the continuity of cause and effect, because they do not admit the existence of the ālayavijñāna capable of sustaining seeds; therefore, one should believe in the correct principle of the continuity of cause and effect as taught in the Mahāyāna regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This consciousness has been revolving continuously like a stream from beginningless time; until what stage is it finally abandoned?
It is finally abandoned at the stage of an Arhat.

That is to say, when the noble ones have completely severed the afflictive obstructions (kleśāvaraṇa), they are called Arhats; at that time, because this consciousness is forever separated from the heavy residues (dausthulya) of the afflictions, it is said to be abandoned.

The Arhats mentioned here encompass the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of all three vehicles; for they have all eternally destroyed the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*), are worthy of receiving the sublime offerings of the world, and will never again undergo birth within the realm of segmented existence (*prādeśika-jāti*).
How is this known to be so?
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states that all Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas do not possess the ālayavijñāna.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* further states that when Bodhisattvas attain enlightenment, they simultaneously sever the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), thereby becoming Arhats and Tathāgatas.
If that were so, since Bodhisattvas have not yet permanently severed all seeds of affliction and are not Arhats, they should all possess the ālayavijñāna. Why is this?
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states that even non-retrogressive bodhisattvas do not possess the *ālayavijñāna*.

It explains that those of the two vehicles who, at the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*), turn their minds toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), are necessarily called "non-retrogressive bodhisattvas" because they will never again retrogressively give rise to afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and because they are proceeding toward enlightenment. Thus, they receive this new designation.
Those who have not yet perfected the *ālayavijñāna* are included within this category of *arhats*; therefore, that treatise does not contradict this meaning.

Furthermore, because all afflictions (*kleśa*) never again arise for Bodhisattvas from the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) upward, because they proceed spontaneously within the swift current of the Dharma, because they can initiate all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) amidst all conditioned activities, and because they advance and increase moment by moment, it is only at this stage that they are called "non-retrogressive" (*avaivartika*) Bodhisattvas.

However, although this bodhisattva has not yet completely eliminated the seeds of affliction within the *vipākavijñāna*, the self-view, self-love, and other such factors that take this consciousness as their object no longer grasp it as a hidden internal self. Because they have thereby permanently relinquished the name "ālaya," it is said that they do not constitute an *ālayavijñāna*; thus, they are also referred to as an "arhat."

There is another interpretation: Bodhisattvas from the first bhūmi upward have already realized the principle revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, have already attained the two types of sublime wisdom, and have already severed the two categories of afflictive and cognitive obstacles that arise from conceptualization. Because they are able to give rise to all modes of conduct within a single mode of conduct, even when they give rise to various afflictions for the sake of benefiting others, those afflictions do not produce the faults of affliction; therefore, these are also called "non-retrogressive bodhisattvas."

However, although this bodhisattva has not yet completely severed the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), they no longer grasp or store this consciousness as their own internal self through the conceptual views of self, self-love, and so forth that take it as an object; by virtue of this, they also relinquish the name "ālayavijñāna," and thus it is said that the ālayavijñāna is no longer established for them. This person is also called an arhat.

Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: although a Bodhisattva on the ten stages has not yet permanently severed all afflictions (*kleśa*), these afflictions are like poisons suppressed by mantras or medicine; they do not give rise to any of the faults of the afflictions.
"In all stages [of the bodhisattva], because they have abandoned the afflictions just as an arhat has, they are also called 'arhats. This statement is irrational;

since the seventh stage and below, there still exists the innate view of self, craving, and so forth, which grasp this consciousness as their own internal self—how could the name *ālaya* have already been relinquished?"

If it were said that the name "ālaya" is abandoned because the conceptualization of a self, self-love, and so forth no longer cling and store [within it], then those in the stages of training, such as stream-enterers and others, would also have already abandoned the name "ālayavijñāna"; to accept this would contradict what is taught in all the treatises.

The afflictions that arise in Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi) do not constitute faults because they are accompanied by correct knowledge (saṃprajanya); such a thing does not occur for Stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and others—how, then, could one use them as an analogy for these Bodhisattvas?

Although the afflictions arising within those six consciousnesses do not constitute faults due to correct knowledge, the seventh consciousness—in its state as a tainted mind—spontaneously manifests and clings to this [eighth] consciousness as its storehouse; how could it not be the same as that of a stream-enterer?
For this reason, it is known that their explanation is irrational.

However, because an Arhat has completely and ultimately severed the afflictions and their latent predispositions (*dausthulya*) within this consciousness, he no longer clings to the *ālayavijñāna* as his internal self. Consequently, having permanently lost the name "ālaya," it is said to be "abandoned"; yet this does not mean that the substance of the eighth consciousness is entirely abandoned. Otherwise, an Arhat would lack a consciousness to sustain the seeds, and he would immediately enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* at that very moment.

Although the eighth consciousness is fully possessed by all sentient beings, it is established under various names according to its specific functions: it is called "mind" (*citta*) because it is the accumulation of seeds perfumed by various phenomena;
it is called "appropriator" (*ādāna*) because it grasps and maintains the seeds and the material sense organs so that they do not perish;
and it is called the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeyāśraya*) because it serves as the support for all knowable phenomena, both defiled and pure.
It is also called the "seed-consciousness" (*bīja-vijñāna*), because it universally sustains all seeds of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
These various names apply throughout all stages [of existence].

It is also called the *ālaya*, because it gathers and stores all factors belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) so that they are not lost, and because it is grasped as one's own internal self by means of self-view, self-love, and so forth.

This name applies only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*), for it does not apply to those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) or non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, as they lack the sense of being a storehouse (*ālaya*) for the grasping of defiled phenomena.
Alternatively, it is called the "maturation consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*), because it is the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) of wholesome and unwholesome karma that draws forth birth and death.

This name applies only to the stages of ordinary beings, the two vehicles, and the various bodhisattvas, because the stage of a Tathāgata does not still possess dharmas that are maturation-born and indeterminate.
Alternatively, it is called the "Stainless Consciousness" (amala-vijñāna), because it is the support for all most extremely pure, untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.

This name exists only in the stage of the Tathāgata; for those in the stages of Bodhisattvas, the two vehicles, and ordinary beings possess contaminated seeds that are susceptible to perfuming, as they have not yet attained the perfectly pure eighth consciousness.
As stated in the Sūtra:
The Tathāgata’s stainless consciousness Is the pure, outflow-free realm;
Liberated from all obscurations, It is associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
The name *ālaya* is emphasized here because its faults are grave and it is the first to be abandoned;

as for the substance of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), it is abandoned by Bodhisattvas when they are about to attain enlightenment, and it is abandoned by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas upon entering the nirvāṇa without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*).
The essence of the immaculate consciousness (amala-vijñāna) never undergoes abandonment, for there is no time when its benefit and happiness of sentient beings are exhausted.
Since it is common to the mind and other [mental factors], it should be explained according to the specific context.
However, the eighth consciousness generally comprises two states:

First, in the state with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is subsumed under the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and is associated only with five factors, namely contact (*sparśa*) and so forth; it takes as its object only the previously mentioned spheres of appropriation (*upātta*).

Second, in the state without outflows (*anāsrava*), it is subsumed exclusively under the wholesome nature (*kuśala*) and is associated with twenty-one mental factors: specifically, the five universal (*sarvatraga*) and five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors, plus the eleven wholesome factors. This is because [the latter] are always associated with all minds, because one constantly delights in realizing the objects observed by wisdom, because one constantly maintains a firm impression of the objects observed, and because one constantly and clearly remembers objects previously experienced.

Because the Blessed One possesses no unconcentrated mind, because he constantly exercises discernment regarding all phenomena, because he is always associated with supreme pure faith and so forth, because he is free from defilement, and because he is free from distraction, this [mind] is associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), as it functions spontaneously and perpetually in a state of equilibrium.
All phenomena serve as its objective referents, because the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) universally takes all phenomena as its objects.
How should one understand that this eighth consciousness has a distinct substantial entity apart from the visual consciousness and the others?
Because the sacred teachings and correct reasoning serve as the valid authorities, it is said in the *Mahāyānābhidharma-sūtra*:
"The element from beginningless time is the common support for all phenomena."
From this arise the various realms of existence as well as the realization of nirvāṇa.
Because the intrinsic nature of this eighth consciousness is subtle, it is manifested through its functional activities.

In the verse, the first half reveals the eighth consciousness as functioning as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), while the second half reveals its functioning as the support (*āśraya*) for both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

"Dhātu" (realm/element) has the meaning of "cause"; it refers to the seed-consciousness which, from beginningless time, has continued in a successive stream and directly gives rise to all phenomena; therefore, it is called the "cause."
Based on the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*), this refers to the appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*). Since beginningless time, it has served as the basis for all phenomena;

therefore, it is called a "condition. This means that because it is able to maintain all seeds and serves as the support for manifest phenomena, it both transforms into those [phenomena] and acts as their basis.
"Transforming into that" refers to transforming into the receptacle world and the body endowed with sense organs.

"Acting as the support for that" means serving as the basis for the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), because it is able to maintain (*upādāna*) the five material sense organs; thus, the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, evolve in dependence upon it.
Furthermore, because it serves as the support for the manas, the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna) functions in dependence upon it.

Since the manas is subsumed under the category of evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), it is like the visual and other sensory consciousnesses, which depend upon their simultaneously existing bases (sahabhū-indriya).
Because the eighth [consciousness] ought logically to be of the nature of consciousness, it likewise takes the seventh as its simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).
This is called the function of this consciousness as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
"By virtue of which there is" means by virtue of the existence of this consciousness.
Regarding the existence of various realms of rebirth, there are both wholesome and unwholesome realms.

This means that because of the existence of this eighth consciousness, it maintains all phenomena conducive to the process of transmigration, thereby causing sentient beings to wander through birth and death.
Although afflictions, karma, and birth are all part of the process of saṃsāra, it is the *gati* (destinies) that are specifically mentioned because they are the most prominent as the fruit.
Alternatively, the term "destinies" (*gati*) may refer to both the subject who goes and the destination itself; thus, even the requisites for the destinies can be designated by the name "destiny."
All afflictions, karma, and births depend upon this consciousness; thus, it serves as the support for the process of saṃsāra.
Furthermore, regarding the realization of nirvāṇa, it is because this consciousness exists that the realization of nirvāṇa occurs.
This means that because this eighth consciousness exists, it maintains all phenomena conducive to cessation (*nivṛtti*), enabling practitioners to realize nirvāṇa.
Here, only the path capable of realizing [nirvāṇa] is mentioned, because nirvāṇa itself does not exist in dependence upon this consciousness.
Alternatively, this refers only to the nirvāṇa that is realized, because it is the primary object sought by the practitioner.
Alternatively, this speaks of both nirvāṇa and the path, as both are subsumed within the category of cessation (*nirodha*).
The term "nirvāṇa" indicates the cessation that is realized, while the subsequent term "attainment" indicates the path by which it is attained.

Since nirvāṇa is realized at the stage where the path capable of severing has completely exhausted the afflictions to be severed, both the path that severs and the cessation realized depend upon this consciousness; thus, it serves as the supporting basis for the process of returning to extinction (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Furthermore, in this verse, the first line demonstrates that the intrinsic nature of this consciousness exists eternally from beginningless time; the subsequent three lines demonstrate that it serves as the general and specific basis for the two categories of phenomena: defilement and purification.
Defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) refer to the truths of suffering and its origin; that is, the states of rebirth and the karma and afflictions that lead to them.
Pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*) refer to the truths of cessation and the path; that is, the nirvana to be realized and the path by which it is realized.
Both of those exist in dependence upon this consciousness, for the principle [of their existence] based on the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and so forth is not established.

Alternatively, the first phrase reveals that the substance of this consciousness is a beginningless continuity, while the latter three reveal its status as the basis for the three natures—namely, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)—which should be understood in their respective order.
The various meanings explained in this verse cannot exist apart from the eighth consciousness.
Furthermore, that same sutra states:
"Because it stores all dharmas, it is the consciousness of all seeds."
Therefore it is named *ālaya*; this I have revealed for the sake of the Victors.
Because this fundamental consciousness possesses all seeds, it is able to store and conceal all defiled phenomena; based on this, the name *ālayavijñāna* is established.
It is not like the *pradhāna* (Primal Nature) transforming into the *mahat* and so forth, because the seed and its fruit are not of one substance;

because the support and that which is supported arise and perish together; and because it mutually contains and hides the defiled dharmas, while sentient beings also grasp it as their self—therefore, this consciousness is called the *ālaya*.

The assembly of Bodhisattvas who have already entered the path of vision (darśanamārga) and attained true realization (abhisamaya) are called "Victors" (jināḥ); because they are able to realize and understand the ālayavijñāna, our World-Honored One has correctly revealed it for their sake.

Alternatively, all bodhisattvas are termed "victors" (*jin*); although prior to the path of seeing they have not yet realized or understood the *ālayavijñāna*, they are able to believe in and understand it while seeking its fundamental transformation (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), and therefore it is taught to them as well.
The various evolving consciousnesses do not possess such characteristics; as the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* also states:
"The ādānavijñāna is profound and subtle; Containing all seeds, it is like a torrential stream.
I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, Fearing they would conceptualize and grasp it as a self."

Because it can maintain the seeds of all phenomena, can appropriate the basis of the material sense-faculties, and can also grasp the continuity of rebirth, this consciousness is called the *ādāna* (appropriating) consciousness.
Because sentient beings lacking the [Buddha-]nature cannot fathom its depths, it is called "profound.
Because those of the lineage intent on tranquility cannot penetrate it, it is called "extremely subtle.
It is the true seed of all phenomena; when struck by conditions, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses arise, flowing constantly and without interruption like a torrential stream.

"Ordinary beings are devoid of intrinsic nature, and fools are inclined toward quiescence; fearing that they might give rise to conceptual attachment regarding this [teaching], thereby falling into the evil destinies and obstructing the arising of the Noble Path, my World-Honored One did not expound it for them."
Only the eighth consciousness possesses such characteristics; the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* also states:
"Just as when the ocean encounters the condition of wind, / Various waves arise, / Manifesting their functioning in the present, / Without a moment's interruption."
The ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise;
struck by the winds of objects and so forth, it constantly gives rise to the waves of the various consciousnesses, which manifest and function in their transformations.

Since the visual and other sensory consciousnesses do not possess the continuous, uninterrupted succession of the great ocean that gives rise to the waves of the various consciousnesses, we know that there exists a distinct nature of the eighth consciousness.
Within these immeasurable Mahāyāna sūtras, it is specifically taught that this eighth consciousness exists.

All Mahāyāna sūtras accord with selflessness and oppose the *pudgala*; they turn away from saṃsāra and incline toward nirvāṇa; they praise the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha and disparage all non-Buddhists; they manifest phenomena such as the aggregates and negate [independent entities] such as the *pradhāna* (primordial matter).

Those who delight in the Mahāyāna maintain that it can be demonstrated as such, because it is subsumed within the sūtras that accord with the non-erroneous principle, just as the *Ekottarika-āgama* and others are subsumed within the category of authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*).
Furthermore, the noble Maitreya established through seven reasons that the Mahāyāna sūtras are truly the word of the Buddha.
First, because it was not previously predicted.

If the Mahāyāna sūtras were spoken by others after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa for the purpose of destroying the True Dharma, why did the World-Honored One not, as he did with future events that would cause terror, first provide a prediction?
2. Because they have coexisted from the beginning.
The teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna have coexisted from the very outset; how, then, can one know that the Mahāyāna alone is not the Buddha’s teaching?
3. Because it is not the domain of others.

The Mahāyāna teachings are vast and profound; they are not within the sphere of conceptualization for non-Buddhists and others, nor have they ever been taught in their scriptures or treatises. Even if such teachings were explained to them, they would not believe or accept them. Therefore, it is not the case that the Mahāyāna sūtras were not spoken by the Buddha.
Fourth, because it must be universally established.

If one were to claim that the Mahāyāna was spoken by other Buddhas and is not the word of the present Buddha, then the principle that the Mahāyāna teaching is indeed the word of the Buddha would be universally established [as the only alternative].
5. Because of the existence or non-existence [of the Mahāyāna].
If the Mahāyāna exists, one should believe that these various Mahāyāna teachings were spoken by the Buddha, because apart from this Mahāyāna, nothing else can be found.
If the Mahāyāna does not exist, then even the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle would not exist, because apart from the Mahāyāna, there is definitively no principle for attaining Buddhahood.
Who appears in the world to teach the Śrāvaka-yāna?
Therefore, the Śrāvaka-yāna is what was taught by the Buddha; it is not a Mahāyāna teaching, as it does not accord with correct principle.
Sixth, because it serves as an antidote.

Those who diligently practice according to the Mahāyāna sūtras are all able to induce non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which can correctly counteract all afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, one should believe that this was spoken by the Buddha.
Seventh, because the meaning differs from the literal expression.

The intended significance (*abhiprāya*) taught in the Mahāyāna is extremely profound; one cannot grasp its meaning by following the literal phrasing alone. Otherwise, one would give rise to slander, claiming it is not the word of the Buddha. Therefore, the Mahāyāna is truly the word of the Buddha.
As the verse in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra-alaṃkāra* expresses this meaning:
"Because it was not previously predicted that they coexist, because they are not the objective domain of others,
and because the antidotes differ in their phrasing, existence and non-existence are established."

In the sūtras of other schools as well, the ālayavijñāna is taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*) to possess a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Specifically, in the Āgamas of the Mahāsāṃghika school, it is intentionally designated as the "root-consciousness" (*mūlavijñāna*), because it is the support (*āśraya*) for the visual consciousness and the others, just as a tree root is the basis for the trunk and so forth;
this is not the case for the visual and other [sensory] consciousnesses.
Both the Theravādins and the *Vibhaṅga* scholars maintain that this is the "bhavāṅgavijñāna" (constituent-of-existence consciousness) spoken of with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
"Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the three realms of existence; "constituent" (*aṅga*) has the sense of a cause. This alone is eternally and universally the cause of the three realms of existence.

The Mahīśāsaka school asserts that this is called the "aggregate that exhausts birth and death" (*ātyantika-saṃsāra-skandha*). Apart from the eighth consciousness, there is no other aggregate-dharma that remains uninterrupted until the limit of birth and death.

This is because, while material form is interrupted in the Formless Realm, and the various minds and mental factors cease in states such as the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), it has already been established that non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) have no distinct intrinsic nature apart from matter, mind, and so forth; therefore, only this consciousness is termed the "aggregate that exhausts birth and death."

In the *Ekottarika-āgama* of the Sarvāstivāda school, it is also taught with intentional meaning that this is called the ālaya, stating: "one loves the ālaya, delights in the ālaya, rejoices in the ālaya, and finds pleasure in the ālaya."

That is to say, because the ālayavijñāna is the object of craving—both collectively and individually—across the three periods of time, these four names are established for it; for sentient beings grasp it as their true internal self, and as long as this grasping is not severed, they constantly generate attachment toward it.
The *ālayavijñāna* is the locus of true attachment; one should not cling to the other five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*).

This is because those born in a realm of exclusively painful sensation do not give rise to attachment toward the other five appropriated aggregates; rather, they constantly loathe and oppose them, thinking, "When shall I cast off this life, this commonality of existence (*nikāyasabhāga*), and this body and mind of suffering, so that I may freely experience happiness?"
The five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) are also not the locus of true attachment; for even those who have abandoned desire do not crave them, yet they still love the self (*ātman*).

Likewise, pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is not the locus of true attachment; for even those who are free from the defilements of the third dhyāna, though they loathe pleasant feeling, still love the self.

The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is also not a locus of true attachment; for those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and have faith in non-self, although they do not give rise to craving for the view of a self-body, they still give rise to love for the internal self.

The evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and so forth are also not the locus of true attachment; for those who have not yet attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and seek the cessation of the mind, although they may loathe the evolving consciousnesses, they still love the self.

Likewise, the physical body (*rūpakāya*) is also not the locus of true attachment; for one who is free from the defilement of form (*rūparāga*), although they may loathe the physical body, they still love the self.
The dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) lack a distinct intrinsic nature apart from form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth; therefore, they are also not the locus of true attachment.

When ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*) give rise to self-love (*ātmasneha*), although they may have love or non-love toward the other aggregates, self-love necessarily arises toward this consciousness; thus, this alone is the true locus of attachment.
Therefore, that which is designated by the name *ālaya* definitely refers only to this *ālayavijñāna*.

Having cited the authoritative scriptures (*āgama*), the correct reasoning (*yukti*) shall now be demonstrated: it is said in the Sūtras that because it is the locus where the seeds of all defiled and purified phenomena (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-dharma*) are gathered and arise, it is called "mind" (*citta*).
If this consciousness did not exist, that mind which maintains the seeds would not be possible.

This is because the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are interrupted in states such as the meditative attainment of cessation; because they easily shift and arise through the distinct categories of sense organs, objects, mental attention, and wholesome factors; and because, like flashes of lightning, they do not abide steadfastly. Thus, they cannot be perfumed (*vāsya*), cannot maintain seeds, and are not the minds in which the seeds of defilement and purity are accumulated and produced.

This consciousness is of a single type, constant, and uninterrupted; like a sesame seed, it is stable and capable of being perfumed, which accords with the meaning of "mind" (*citta*) as taught in that sutra.
If one does not admit the existence of a mind that can maintain the seeds, it would contradict not only the sutras but also correct reasoning.

This means that regarding all phenomena arising within the categories of defilement and purity, because there is nothing to be perfumed, they would not perfume to form seeds; consequently, the effort expended in producing them would be in vain.

Since there would be no causal seeds at the time these defiled and pure states arise, it would follow that one holds a view identical to the non-Buddhists who maintain that things arise spontaneously (*svabhāva*).

Because form (*rūpa*) is not associated with mind and is not of the nature of mind—just like sound, light, and so forth—it cannot, according to principle, be perfumed by internal dharmas that are either defiled or pure; how then could it maintain seeds?
Furthermore, since such [form] lacks a real intrinsic nature apart from consciousness, how can it be maintained as the support for internal seeds?

The mental factors associated with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) cannot maintain seeds nor undergo perfuming (*vāsanā*), because they arise intermittently and are easily abandoned, because they lack autonomy, and because they are not of the nature of mind (*cittatva*). Therefore, there must exist a distinct mind that maintains the seeds.

Some say that since beginningless time, although the six consciousnesses undergo transformations in their states across successive moments based on faculties, objects, and so forth, there is no difference in their essential nature; thus, they are what are perfumed and can maintain seeds. By this means, both the causes and effects of defilement and purity are established. Why, then, insist on the existence of an eighth consciousness-nature?
That statement is meaningless.

Why is this so? If one maintains that the category (*jāti*) is real, it is identical to the non-Buddhist schools; if one allows that the category is merely provisional, it would lack superior efficacy and thus could not sustain the real seeds of internal phenomena.
Furthermore, as for the category of consciousness that you maintain [to exist], by what nature is it subsumed?
If it were wholesome or unwholesome, it should not be susceptible to perfuming, because you admit it is determinate (*vyākṛta*), just like cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If it were indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), then at the time of wholesome or unwholesome minds there would be no indeterminate mind, and this category [of indeterminate phenomena] should be abandoned.
It is not the case that the category of wholesome or unwholesome things can be indeterminate; for a distinct category must necessarily share the same nature as its distinct basis.

Furthermore, in states of mindlessness (*acittaka*), this kind [of consciousness] is definitely absent; since there is such interruption, its nature is not stable. How, then, could it be maintained that it can hold seeds or receive perfuming (*vāsanā*)?

Moreover, because the types of consciousness are identical, the minds of Arhats or ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) would necessarily be perfumed by all defiled and untainted dharmas, which, if admitted, would lead to logical fallacies.

Furthermore, the sense organs such as the eye, or other dharmas, share the same category of being "roots" with the consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness; thus, they ought to mutually perfuse one another.
Yet you do not admit this; therefore, you should not maintain that the category of consciousness is what receives perfuming.

Furthermore, regarding the six groups of consciousness, whether in terms of their substance or their categories, since two moments—preceding and succeeding—are not simultaneous, they cannot mutually perfuse one another like moments separated by an interval; for the perfuming agent and the object perfumed must necessarily exist at the same time.

Those who maintain that only the six consciousnesses arise simultaneously argue that, according to the preceding reasoning, since they are not objects of perfuming (*bhāvyatva*), they likewise lack the capacity to sustain seeds.

Furthermore, some maintain that the causal relationship is established such that the preceding moment of a given category of matter or mind serves as the seed for its subsequent moment; therefore, the previously stated proofs do not hold.
That position is irrational because there is no perfuming (*vāsanā*).
That is to say, since there is no perfuming within their own category, how can one maintain that the preceding moment serves as the seed for the subsequent one?

Furthermore, that which has been interrupted would not arise again, and those in the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*) among the two vehicles would lack future aggregates, because it is the matter and mind at the moment of death that serve as the seeds for what follows.

Furthermore, one should not maintain that matter and mind arise by serving as seeds for one another in turn; for it has already been stated previously that evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and material form (*rūpa*), etc., are not objects of perfuming (*vāsya*).

Some say: "All dharmas of the three periods of time exist, and the mutual response between cause and effect is entirely established; why then labor to maintain that there is a 'seed-holding consciousness' (*bīja-dhāra-vijñāna*)?"
However, as for the scriptural statement that the mind is the seed, this is because it possesses a potent efficacy in giving rise to both defiled and pure phenomena.
That [position] is irrational; for the past and future are neither permanent nor present, being like flowers in the sky and so forth, and thus are not substantially existent.
Furthermore, it lacks functional activity and cannot be apprehended as having the nature of a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
If there were no consciousness capable of sustaining the seeds of defilement and purity, all causes and effects would fail to be established.

There are those who hold that the Mahāyāna principle of emptiness through the elimination of signs is ultimate; relying on fallacious inference, they deny the existence of this consciousness as well as all phenomena, which specifically contradicts and harms the sūtras cited previously.

To hold that the causes and effects of defilement and purity—namely, wisdom, abandonment, realization, and cultivation—are all unreal constitutes a great false view; for while non-Buddhists also slander the causes and effects of defilement and purity, they do not claim they are entirely non-existent, but merely hold them to be unreal.
If all phenomena were not truly existent, the Bodhisattva would not need to diligently cultivate and accumulate the provisions for enlightenment in order to abandon birth and death.
What wise person would seek the son of a barren woman to serve as an army in order to eliminate an illusory enemy?

Therefore, one should believe that there exists a mind capable of maintaining seeds, upon which the causal relationship of defilement and purity is established; that mind is precisely this eighth consciousness.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that there is a maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*) produced by the influence of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
If this consciousness did not exist, that resultant mind (*vipāka-citta*) would not be possible.

This is because the visual and other sensory consciousnesses are intermittent and do not constitute the fruit of karma at all times; thus, like flashes of lightning and the like, they are not the resultant mind. Furthermore, a resultant mind should not be interrupted and then resume, for such a phenomenon does not occur in the case of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth.

The six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, which are produced by karma, are like sound and other such phenomena; because they do not continue in an uninterrupted stream, they are "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*), but they are not the "true maturation" (*vipāka*).

One must necessarily admit the existence of a true maturation-consciousness that compensates for the projecting karma, being pervasive and uninterrupted, transforming itself into the body and the environment to serve as the support for sentient beings. This is because the body and the environment cannot exist apart from mind, because non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) lack substantial reality, and because the various evolving consciousnesses are not constantly present.
If this mind did not exist, who would transform the body and its environment?
Furthermore, based on what dharma would sentient beings perpetually be established?
Moreover, whether in a state of meditative concentration or not, during moments of deliberate thought or thoughtlessness, it stands to reason that numerous physical sensations arise.
If this [mind] were non-existent, there should not be physical well-being or exhaustion at a later time.
If a truly resultant mind (*vipākacitta*) does not exist constantly, how could such bodily sensation exist in that state?

When a Buddha gives rise to other virtuous states of mind and so forth, he must necessarily manifest a truly ripened (*vipāka*) consciousness, because at the time such [other minds] arise, he is still a sentient being who is not yet a Buddha.
Consequently, there is always a truly resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), and that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that sentient beings transmigrate through the five destinies and four modes of birth.
If this consciousness did not exist, the substantial entity of birth in those realms would not be possible.

That is to say, it is only when there exists something real, permanent, pervasive, and unmixed that one can establish those phenomena as the authentic and actual states of birth in the various realms.
Non-vipāka dharmas do not lead to a confusion of destinies and births, because while one dwells in a particular destiny, they can give rise to the dharmas of other destinies and births.

Furthermore, the various material forms that are the results of karma within the five consciousnesses do not pervade all destinies and births, for they are entirely absent in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding those born through the maturation of karma within the wholesome states and the mental consciousness, although they proceed toward all destinies without confusion, they do not exist constantly.
Since non-associated formations lack a real intrinsic nature, none of them can be established as truly real destinies.
Only the ripening consciousness (*vipākacitta*) and its associated mental factors (*caitasika*) are truly constant, pervasive, and unmixed; these constitute the actual states of rebirth (*gati*).

If this [ripening] mind were absent, then when one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and gives rise to wholesome states and the like, those births would not be considered states of rebirth.

If one were to concede that the destinies (*gati*) and births (*upapatti*) encompass all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*), then when one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and gives rise to an uncontaminated mind (*anāsravacitta*), that state would not be a destiny or a birth, which would contradict correct reasoning.
To avoid both the aforementioned fault and this error, it follows that only those phenomena which are maturation (*vipāka*) are truly and substantially destinies and births.

Therefore, the Tathāgata is not subsumed under the realms of rebirth (*gati*), because a Buddha possesses no resultant indeterminate (*vipāka-avyākṛta*) dharmas; nor is he subsumed under the elements (*dhātu*), because he is without outflows (*anāsrava*); for the World-Honored One has already abandoned the truths of suffering and its origin, and all seeds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) have been eternally severed.

Since the actual states of birth and existence consist solely of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*), the existence of those consciousnesses and mental factors cannot be logically established apart from the eighth consciousness; therefore, one knows that this distinct eighth consciousness exists.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that the body possessing the material sense-faculties is "appropriated" (*upātta*).
If this consciousness did not exist, such appropriation would be impossible.
That is to say, the five material sense-faculties and their physical bases are appropriated only in the present life; this is necessarily due to the existence of a mind capable of appropriating them.

Only the maturation-consciousness (vipākacitta), which is induced by prior karma and is neither virtuous nor defiled, is capable of maintaining a uniform continuity and appropriating the body endowed with material sense-faculties; the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), such as the eye-consciousness and others, do not possess this quality.

The meaning of this statement is to show that the evolving consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth, lack any single category capable of pervasively maintaining (*upādāna*) one's own internal body composed of material sense-faculties throughout its continuity; it does not, however, intend to show that only the ripening (*vipāka*) mind is capable of such maintenance, lest it imply that the material bodies of Buddhas lack such maintenance.
However, it is only the retributive consciousness (*vipākacitta*) that can grasp and maintain the contaminated physical body; therefore, this statement is made.

This means that because the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise based on present conditions—just like sound, wind, and so forth—their states of being wholesome or defiled are not drawn by karma, just as non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is not.

That which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) cannot appropriate a contaminated physical body (*sāsrava-rūpakāya*), because it is not itself a maturation, because it is not a universal support, and because it does not continue in a series, like a flash of lightning and so forth.

The term "all mind-consciousnesses" (*citta-vijñāna*) also includes mental factors (*caitta*), because they are necessarily associated [with consciousness], just as the term "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) does.

It is not possible for the material sense-faculties or the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) to appropriate the body possessing material sense-faculties, because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*), like space and so forth.
Therefore, there must be a distinct mind capable of appropriation, and that mind is precisely this eighth consciousness.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these three—mutually support one another to enable continued existence.
If this consciousness did not exist, there would be no consciousness capable of sustaining vitality (*āyuṣ*) and warmth (*uṣman*) so that they endure for a long time;

for the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are intermittent and subject to change, like sound or wind. They lack the function of constant sustenance and cannot therefore be established as the consciousness that maintains vitality and warmth.

Only the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is uninterrupted and unchanging, like vitality and heat; because it possesses the function of constant maintenance, it can be established as the consciousness that sustains vitality and heat.
The Sūtra states that these three factors mutually support one another, yet vitality and heat continue as a single stream.
The theory of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) is not like this; how could it possibly accord with correct reasoning?

Although you claim that the three factors mutually support one another, you admit that "warmth" alone does not pervade the three realms; why then do you not admit that consciousness alone can exist in intermittent occurrence?
This does not constitute a fault or difficulty regarding the preceding reasoning.

That is to say, only where these three factors are present and function in immediate succession can they maintain one another constantly; otherwise, they lack the capacity for constant mutual maintenance.

Previously, by means of this principle, it was demonstrated that the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) used in the context of the three natures does not refer to the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). Even if one were to employ a more relaxed or non-comprehensive phrasing, how could that undermine the aforementioned principle?
Therefore, the reasoning set forth previously is fully established.

Furthermore, among the three factors [of life, heat, and consciousness], since both vitality (*āyuṣ*) and heat (*uṣman*) are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is known that consciousness (*vijñāna*)—like vitality and heat—is certainly not uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). When one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and gives rise to an uncontaminated mind, at that time, what consciousness could maintain that vitality?

From this it is known that there is a single type of maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) which is constant and pervasive, capable of sustaining life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*); that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness.

Furthermore, the sūtras state that when sentient beings are born or die, they necessarily abide in a distracted state of mind (*vikṣiptacitta*), not in a mindless meditative absorption (*acittakasamāpatti*).
If this consciousness did not exist, the mind at the time of birth and death would not be possible;

for at the time of birth and death, the body and mind are obscure and dull, like being asleep without dreaming or in a state of extreme fainting, when the clearly manifest evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna) certainly do not arise.

Furthermore, because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) of the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) cannot be known within this state, they certainly do not manifest, just as in the state of being without mind (*acittaka*).
This is because the modes of activity and objects of the six evolving consciousnesses must be knowable, as is the case at other times.

Because the true ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is extremely subtle, its modes of activity (*ākāra*) and objects of perception (*ālambana*) are both imperceptible; it is the fruit of projecting karma that continues throughout a single lifetime, remaining constantly without change. It is the consciousness present during the state of non-concentrated mind, termed the "mind of birth-and-death," which does not contradict correct reasoning.

Some say that at this stage, the five consciousnesses definitely do not exist, and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not apprehend objects either; because the various causes for its arising—whether due to the five consciousnesses, due to the instruction of others, or due to meditative concentration—cannot be found, the mental consciousness at the stage of rebirth is likewise non-existent.
If that were so, once sentient beings are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), their mental consciousness (manovijñāna) would never arise again at a later time.

This is because a concentrated mind (samāhita-citta) must necessarily be induced by a distracted mental consciousness; yet in that realm, the five sensory consciousnesses and external instruction are both absent, leaving no means for a distracted mind to arise and thereby induce concentration.
If you claim that it necessarily manifests later through the power of habitual practice (*abhyāsa*), why does it not manifest at the very moment of its initial arising?
Furthermore, at the time of first taking birth in the desire or form realms, the habituated mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) should likewise manifest.
If [the subtle consciousness] has not yet appeared due to being obscured by torpor, this is simply the aforementioned cause; why then labor to state it separately?

Other schools maintain that within the states of birth and death, there exists a distinct class of subtle mental consciousness whose mode of activity (*ākāra*) and object (*ālambana*) are both imperceptible.
It should be understood that this is precisely the eighth consciousness, for the well-established *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) is not like this.

Furthermore, at the time of death, due to wholesome or unwholesome karma, the sensation of cold gradually arises from either the lower or upper parts of the body; if this consciousness did not exist, that phenomenon would be impossible.

The evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) cannot maintain the body because the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, each rely on their own distinct bases or do not function [simultaneously].

Furthermore, the sixth mental consciousness does not abide in the body; its objects are indeterminate, and it dwells pervasively throughout the body in constant succession. Therefore, cold contact should not arise gradually by means of that [consciousness].

Only the resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*), by the power of prior karma, constantly and universally maintains a continuous stream that appropriates the physical body; when this appropriation is relinquished, the sensation of coldness arises at that location.
Because life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are inseparable from one another, the place where the sensation of coldness arises is no longer a sentient being.
Although it undergoes transformation, it is a condition (*pratyaya*) yet not appropriated (*anupātta*); therefore, one knows that this eighth consciousness definitely exists.

Furthermore, a sūtra states: "Consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and name-and-form conditions consciousness; these two dharmas thus depend upon each other reciprocally, like a bundle of reeds turning together at the same time."
If this consciousness did not exist, the intrinsic nature of that [other] consciousness would not be possible;
for that very sūtra provides its own explanation, stating that "name" refers to the four non-material aggregates, while "form" refers to the kalala and so forth.
These two exist in mutual dependence upon consciousness, like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another as reciprocal conditions; they always evolve simultaneously and never separate.
Since the evolving consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, are subsumed within "name," if this [ālayavijñāna] were non-existent, what would you call "consciousness"?

Nor can it be said that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) refers to the five groups of sensory consciousness, while "consciousness" refers to the sixth [mental consciousness]. This is because the five sensory consciousnesses do not exist at the stage of the *kalala*.

Furthermore, since the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) arise intermittently, they lack the power to constantly sustain name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); how, then, could they be said to always serve as the condition for name-and-form?
Therefore, the term "that consciousness" (tad-vijñāna) indicates the eighth consciousness.

Furthermore, a sūtra states that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment.
If this consciousness did not exist, the substance of that consciousness-food would not be possible;
for the Sūtra states that there are four kinds of nutriment:
first, edible food, which has the characteristic of transformation and decay.

This means that the three—odor, flavor, and tangible objects—belonging to the desire realm can function as food at the time of transformation; for this reason, the sense-base of visible form is not included within substantial food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), because visible form has no utility at the time of transformation.
The second is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*), which has the characteristic of contacting objects.
This means that when tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*) first apprehends an object, it grasps joy and so forth, thereby functioning as nutriment.

Although this contact is associated with all consciousnesses, its status as a nutriment is most prominent in relation to the six consciousnesses; for it grasps coarse and manifest objects, and because it excels in nourishing by taking up joy, pleasure, and beneficial equanimity.
The third is the nutriment of mental volition (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*), which has aspiration as its characteristic.
This refers to contaminated volition that operates in conjunction with desire; by aspiring toward desirable objects, it functions as a form of nutriment.

Although this volition is associated with all [six] consciousnesses, its function as nutriment is predominant when it belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because the mental consciousness possesses a superior capacity for aspiration toward objects.
The fourth is the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), characterized by maintenance.

This refers to contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) which, through the power of edible food, contact, and volition, increases and is able to function as nutriment. Although this consciousness generally pertains to the nature of all [eight] consciousnesses, the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is predominant in the sense of being nutriment, because it maintains a continuous stream and excels in the function of maintenance.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that these four nutriments are subsumed within three aggregates (*skandha*), five bases (*āyatana*), and eleven elements (*dhātu*).
These four are called "nutriments" because they are able to sustain the bodies and lives of sentient beings, preventing them from being destroyed or severed.

Edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) is functional only within the desire realm (kāmadhātu). Although the sustenance of contact (sparśa-āhāra) and the sustenance of mental volition (manaḥsaṃcetanā-āhāra) pervade all three realms, they function in dependence upon consciousness and exist or cease according to the presence or absence of that consciousness.

The evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, are intermittent and subject to transformation; they cannot universally and constantly sustain the body and life, because they are interrupted during mindless meditative absorptions (acittaka-samāpatti), sleep, fainting, and among the gods of the heaven of non-conception (asaṃjñisattva-deva).

If there were only the states of consciousness, because they undergo transformation according to their respective bases, objects, natures, elements, stages, and so forth, they would not be pervasive or constant in sustaining the body and life.
For those who maintain that there is no eighth consciousness, upon what kind of nutriment (*āhāra*) does the Sūtra base its statement: "All sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment"?

It is not the case that consciousness and so forth of the past or future serve as nutriment during states of non-consciousness; for they are neither present nor permanent, lacking both substance and function like flowers in the sky.
Even if they possessed substance and function, they would not be subsumed under the present, and thus—like space and such—they would not possess the nature of nutriment.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that the mind in meditative absorption and so forth serve as nutriment for sentient beings in a state of non-consciousness, because at the time they abide in that non-conscious state, those [minds] have already ceased; and it is already fully established that what is past is not nutriment.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that non-associated formations such as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) constitute their nutriment, because they are not included among the four nutriments—edible food and the rest—and because non-associated dharmas do not exist as substantial entities.

Some maintain that even in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and similar states, the sixth consciousness still exists and can function as nutriment for those sentient beings.
This position is irrational and will be refuted in detail later.
Furthermore, it must be explained what serves as nutriment when one gives rise to untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousness while born in the two higher realms;
for since untainted consciousness and its associates destroy existence (*bhava*), they cannot serve as nutriment for that body and life.

Nor can it be maintained that there are contaminated seeds within uncontaminated consciousness that serve as its nutriment, because uncontaminated consciousness and the like are like nirvāṇa and cannot maintain contaminated seeds.

Furthermore, it cannot be said that the body and life-force of sentient beings in the higher realms sustain one another as mutual food, because those bodies and life-forces are not subsumed within the four types of nutriment.

Moreover, in the formless realm there is no body, and since there is no body, there is nothing capable of sustaining the life-force; this is because the *nikāya-sabhāga* (homogeneous character) and so forth lack substantial reality.

From this, it is known with certainty that there exists a maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna) distinct from the various evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), which is uniform, constant, and pervasive, and which sustains the body and life-force so that they do not perish or cease. It is based on this that the Blessed One made the statement: "All sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment."

Sentient beings are established solely on the basis of the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*); since the Buddha is without outflows (*anāsrava*), he is not included among sentient beings. Therefore, when it is said that sentient beings abide by relying on nutriment, one should know that all such statements are made based on his manifesting emanations (*nirmāṇa*).
Since the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is by nature the supreme nutriment, that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness.

Furthermore, a sūtra states: "For one who abides in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the activities of body, speech, and mind are all extinguished; yet life-force (*āyus*) is not extinguished, nor is warmth (*uṣman*) departed, the sense faculties (*indriya*) do not undergo transformation or decay, and consciousness does not depart from the body."
If this consciousness did not exist, then for one abiding in the meditative attainment of cessation, a consciousness that does not depart from the body would be impossible.

This is because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the visual and other sensory consciousnesses are coarse and mobile; they necessarily involve mental exertion when arising toward their respective objects.

Because one seeks temporary cessation due to weariness with that [consciousness], and gradually suppresses and eliminates it until reaching the stage of total exhaustion, the designation "one who abides in the meditative attainment of cessation" is established based on this stage; therefore, within this attainment, all those consciousnesses are extinguished.

If it is not admitted that there exists a subtle, uniform, and pervasive consciousness that constantly and universally sustains life-span (*āyus*) and so forth, on what basis can it be said that "consciousness does not depart from the body"?

If you argue that because that consciousness arises again at a later time—just as a tertian malaria is said to "not leave" the body—it is therefore called "not departing," then one should not say that "mental formations have ceased. This is because consciousness would arise and cease simultaneously with perception (*saṃjñā*) and the other aggregates. Furthermore, life-span, warmth, and the sense-faculties would likewise be identical to consciousness, which would lead to a great error.
Therefore, one must admit that consciousness, like vitality and warmth, is in reality not separate from the body.

Furthermore, if there were no consciousness whatsoever in this state, it would—like a clod of earth or a stone—not be reckoned among sentient beings; how then could it be said that one is "abiding in the meditative attainment of cessation"?
Furthermore, if the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) were absent at this stage, who would be able to sustain the sense faculties, vitality, and warmth?
Lacking such sustenance, they would all perish and disintegrate, like a corpse that possesses no vitality and the like.
Since subsequent consciousnesses will certainly not arise again, if it is said that [the ālayavijñāna] does not depart from the body, to what would it belong?
For once the various ripening consciousnesses (*vipākavijñāna*) have abandoned this body, there is no rebirth of another body apart from those consciousnesses.
Furthermore, if there were no consciousness that maintains the seeds at this stage, how could subsequent consciousness arise without seeds?
This is because it has already been fully established that past and future phenomena, as well as non-associated formations, do not possess real substantial entities.
Furthermore, since it has already been refuted that dharmas such as various forms exist apart from consciousness and yet undergo perfuming or maintain seeds, [consciousness must exist].

Moreover, in mindless states such as the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), consciousness truly exists just as it does in states with mind, because these states possess the faculties, life-force, and warmth, and are thus subsumed within the category of sentient beings.
By this reasoning, it is certain that for one abiding in the meditative attainment of cessation, consciousness truly does not depart from the body.

If it were argued that the sixth consciousness exists in this state and thus is called "not departing from the body," this would also be unreasonable, because this meditative attainment is also termed the "mindless attainment" (*acittaka-samāpatti*).

If one were to define "mindless" (acittaka) as being without the five consciousnesses, then all meditative absorptions (samāpatti) should be called mindless, because in all such absorptions the five consciousness-bodies are absent.
Since the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is included among the six evolving consciousnesses, it would likewise not exist in the absorption where the five consciousness-bodies have ceased.

Alternatively, because the mental aspect (*ākāra*) and the object (*ālambana*) of consciousness in this state are unknowable, it is like vitality (*āyus*) or heat (*uṣman*), which are not the sixth consciousness.

If there were consciousness in this state with a knowable mental aspect and object, it would—like other states—not be included within this state; for this meditative absorption is entered precisely so that consciousness, whose aspects and objects are discernible, may be brought to rest.
Furthermore, if the sixth consciousness exists in this state, do its mental factors exist or not?

If mental factors were present, the sūtra should not state that for one abiding in this meditative absorption, all mental activities (*citta-saṃskāra*) have ceased, nor should it be called the "absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).

The preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of this meditative absorption involves only the cultivation of revulsion toward feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*); therefore, within this absorption, only feeling and perception cease.

Since these two factors—feeling and perception—are powerful supports for the mind and are uniquely termed "mental formations" (*citta-saṃskāra*) among all mental concomitants, what contradiction is there in stating that the mental formations cease?
In the state of non-percipient absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), only perception (*saṃjñā*) should cease, because one merely feels aversion toward perception.

Yet you do not admit this; since feeling (*vedanā*) and perception alone provide such strong support for the mind, when these two cease, the mind should likewise cease. Just as the body remains even when bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*) have ceased, why must you insist that the mind must cease along with them?
If that were so, when the formations of speech (*vāk-saṃskāra*)—namely vitarka and vicāra—cease, speech itself should not cease; yet this is not what is accepted.

However, among the formations associated with phenomena, there are those that are pervasive (*vyāpaka*) and those that are non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). When pervasive formations cease, the phenomena necessarily cease along with them; when non-pervasive formations cease, the phenomena may still remain.
They are not omnipresent; that is to say, inhalation and exhalation are not omnipresent because the body still remains when the breath ceases.
Vitarka and vicāra are included among the omnipresent factors of speech, for when they cease, speech necessarily ceases as well.

Since feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are also admitted to be included among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), just like volition (*cetanā*) and the others, the mind must necessarily cease when feeling and perception cease; how, then, can it be said that the mind remains when they have ceased?

Furthermore, since volition (*cetanā*) and the other [mental factors] are admitted to be universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), they too should cease when sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*) cease.
This being so, faith (*śraddhā*) and the others would likewise be absent in this state, because it is not possible for something to remain when that which is universal has ceased.
How can it be said that there are remaining mental factors?

Since you admit that volition (*cetanā*) and so forth are not absent in this state, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) must likewise be present, as they are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
Furthermore, if volition and the like exist within this meditative absorption, there must also be contact (*sparśa*), because no other mental factors arise without depending on the power of contact.
If you admit that contact exists, then feeling must also exist, because feeling is conditioned by contact.
Since you admit that feeling exists, perception must also arise, for they are inseparable, just as craving is conditioned by feeling.

Not all feelings are capable of giving rise to craving; therefore, it is not the case that every contact conditions feeling, nor that every contact can produce feeling. Consequently, the objection raised is logically untenable.
The opponent replies:
"That is not so, because there is a distinction.

That is to say, the Buddha himself specified that craving arises with only those feelings produced by contact associated with ignorance as its condition; however, there is no instance where he ever specified that contact produces feeling [in general]. Therefore, wherever there is contact, feeling necessarily arises, and it is a settled principle that feeling is concomitant with perception."
Alternatively, as in other stages, feeling and perception would also not be extinguished, because one maintains that volition and so forth exist within this stage.

To accept this would contradict the statement regarding the cessation of mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra-nirodha*), and it would also fail to establish the meditative attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha-samāpatti*).

If there were no mental factors (caitta), consciousness (vijñāna) would likewise not exist; for we do not observe any other mind that is devoid of mental factors, because other universal factors (sarvatraga) perish along with the perishing of their associated states, because feeling (vedanā) and the rest would not then be "great ground" factors (mahābhūmika), and because this consciousness would not be an associated phenomenon (saṃprayukta-dharma).

If this were granted, it would follow that [the mind] lacks a basis (*āśraya*) and an object-condition (*ālambana*), because it would not be a mental phenomenon (*citta*) like form (*rūpa*) and other such dharmas.

Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "With the mind (*manas*) and dharmas as conditions, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact (*sparśa*) occurs, and together with contact, there arise feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)."

If there were mental consciousness within this meditative absorption, then because of the conjunction of the three [faculties], contact would necessarily arise; since contact is invariably accompanied by feeling, perception, and volition, how could there be consciousness without these mental factors?

If it is argued that at other times the triad of conditions possesses the power to constitute contact, and that contact, having arisen, can give rise to sensation and so forth, and that for this reason, because one has cultivated a mind of aversion toward mental factors prior to this concentration, the three factors lack the capacity within the state of meditative absorption such that contact does not arise and there is no sensation and so forth; [this is not tenable].

If that were so, it should be called a "meditative absorption that extinguishes mental factors" (citta-saṃskāra-nirodha-samādhi); why then is it described as merely "extinguishing feeling and perception" (vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha)?

If you argue that at the time of aversion one is only averse to feeling and perception, and because these two are extinguished, all mental factors are extinguished, and thus the name of the absorption is established based on what was previously averse to; [we reply:]...

If that were so, the mind within this state should also be extinguished, because it is associated with what is being suppressed, just like other mental factors (*caitta*). If this were not the case, how could it be called the "mindless absorption" (*acittaka-samāpatti*)?
Furthermore, what kind of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) exists within this state of meditative concentration?
It cannot be of a defiled or indeterminate nature, because such things do not exist within any wholesome meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, all other defiled or indeterminate minds must necessarily be accompanied by mental factors (*caitasika*); nor can one who seeks to cultivate the wholesome give rise to defilement and the like out of weariness; nor can one who seeks tranquility (*śānti*) instead give rise to distraction (*vikṣepa*).
If it is claimed that this [mind] is virtuous because it is associated with virtue, then it should be associated with the roots of virtue such as non-attachment;
yet this mind cannot be virtuous by nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*) or ultimately virtuous (*paramārtha-kuśala*), for that would contradict your own tenets, as it is neither a root of virtue nor nirvāṇa.

If it is argued that this mind is "wholesome by origination" (*samutthāna-kuśala*) because it is induced by the wholesome roots of preparatory effort (*prayoga*), this is also logically incorrect, as it contradicts your own tenet; for, like other wholesome minds, it is not [wholesome] by way of origination.
A wholesome mind can arise immediately after a mind of any of the three natures; how, then, could that wholesome mind be produced by a preceding [unwholesome or neutral] motivation?
Therefore, the mind is wholesome by virtue of the power of association (*samprayoga*).
If this is so, it must necessarily be associated with the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); how then can you say that this mind alone lacks mental factors (*caitta*)?
Therefore, if there were no mental factors (*caitta*), the mind (*citta*) itself would also not exist.

By such reasoning, one can infer that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), such as the eye-consciousness and so forth, do not remain separated from the body during the state of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Thus, when the Sūtra states that [consciousness] is "not separated from the body," that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness.
When entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), it does not cease, because this is the extremely tranquil *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness).
One should understand that the same applies to states such as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Furthermore, a sūtra states: "Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is purified, sentient beings are purified."
If this consciousness did not exist, those defiled and pure minds would not be possible.

This is because defiled and pure phenomena take the mind as their basis; they arise from the mind and abide in dependence upon the mind, for it is the mind that receives their perfuming and sustains their seeds.
However, defiled phenomena are briefly of three kinds, distinguished by their categories of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and fruits.

If this consciousness did not exist, then after returning from one realm or stage to another while holding the seeds of afflictions within an undefiled mind, the arising of various afflictions would necessarily be without cause; for no other phenomenon can maintain those seeds, and because the past and future are not substantially existent.
