If the various afflictions were to arise without a cause, then there would be no fruits of the three vehicles for those in training or those beyond training, because all [afflictions] that have already been severed would necessarily arise again.

Furthermore, if this consciousness did not sustain the seeds of karmic fruits, then after one has moved between different realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi*) or after heterogeneous dharmas have passed, the arising of various karmic fruits would likewise be without a cause; this is because other seeds and other causes have already been refuted previously.

If various karmic fruits were to arise without a cause, then even after entering the realm of nirvana without remainder, the karmic fruits of the three realms would arise once again, and afflictions likewise would arise without a cause.

Furthermore, the conditionality of *saṃskāras* for consciousness (*vijñāna*) would fail to be established, because it has already been refuted that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) receive perfuming.

Moreover, the defiled consciousness at the moment of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) is not produced by the influence of *saṃskāras*; therefore, one must state that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) has *saṃskāras* as its condition.
Because there is no possibility [of connection] due to the vast separation of time, this [prior case] is not established; since it is not established, the subsequent case is also not established.
Furthermore, all pure phenomena (*viśuddha-dharma*) are also of three kinds, distinguished by the mundane and supramundane paths and their respective fruits of abandonment.

If this consciousness did not exist to sustain the seeds of the mundane and supramundane pure paths, then those pure phenomena arising after a heterogeneous state of mind would all be without cause, for the other causes you have proposed have already been refuted.

If those two pure paths were to arise without a cause, then after one has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder, those two pure paths would have to arise once again, and their basis as well would have to arise without a cause.

Furthermore, the supramundane path should not arise at the outset, because there is no dharma to sustain it, as it is by its very nature a seed; because the categories of contaminated dharmas are not its cause; and because arising without a cause would not be consistent with the principles of the Śākya lineage.
Since there is no arising at the beginning, there would likewise be no arising at the end; thus, the fruits of the paths of the three vehicles would not exist.
If this consciousness did not maintain the seeds of affliction, the fruit of transformation and abandonment could not be accomplished either.
This means that when the Path arises, neither the manifest afflictions nor their seeds exist;

because the defiled and pure minds do not arise simultaneously, the mind associated with the Path does not sustain those seeds, as its nature is diametrically opposed to them, like *nirvāṇa*; and because past, future, or acquisitions (*prāpti*) are not substantially existent, the principle of other phenomena sustaining the seeds is untenable.
Since there is nothing to be abandoned (*prahātavya*), the abandoner (*prahātr*) also does not exist; upon what, and by means of what, could the fruit of abandonment (*prahāṇaphala*) be established?

If it were argued that the fruit of abandonment is established because subsequent afflictions do not arise through the power of the Path (*mārga*), then the first arising of the Path would constitute the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), for all subsequent afflictions would already lack a cause and never arise again.
If this consciousness is admitted, everything is established, for it alone is capable of sustaining the seeds of both the defiled and the pure.
Although there are boundless logical arguments proving the existence of this consciousness, fearing that excessive detail would weary the reader, I have briefly outlined the essential points.
That there exists this distinct consciousness is evident from both scripture and reasoning; all wise persons should accept this with deep faith.
Thus has been explained the aspect of the first transformation.
What is the aspect of the second transformation?
The verse says:
The second transformative consciousness, which follows in sequence, is named *manas*.
It evolves depending upon that [first consciousness] and takes it as its object; its nature and characteristic consist in mentation.

6. Four afflictions are always co-present: namely, self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), as well as self-pride (*ātma-māna*) and self-love (*ātma-sneha*), along with others such as contact (*sparśa*). 7.
They are subsumed under the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*); they follow whatever [realm] is produced and whatever [level] they are bound to.
The Arhat’s meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*) do not possess [this].
The commentary states:

Following the explanation of the first type of transformative consciousness, which is the maturation consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), one should now analyze the characteristics of the transformative consciousness that consists of mental activity (*manas*).
This consciousness is given the specific name *manas* in the sacred teachings because it excels other consciousnesses in its constant and thorough deliberation (*santīraṇa*).
How does this name differ from that of the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?

This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound; just as with the name "store-consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*), here "consciousness" itself is the "mind" (*manas*). Thus, consciousness is identical to mind.
This is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound, just as in the case of "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so forth, because consciousness is distinct from the mind (*manas*).
However, because various sacred teachings fear that this [consciousness] might be confused with that [mind], they apply the name "mind" (*manas*) exclusively to the seventh [consciousness].
Furthermore, it is designated as "mind" (*manas*) to distinguish it from consciousness (*vijñāna*), because it accumulates and discerns more weakly than other forms of consciousness.
Alternatively, it is called simply "mind" to show that it serves as the immediate support for that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
"Dependent upon that which transforms" clarifies the basis (*āśraya*) of this [manas].

"That" refers to the aforementioned first transforming consciousness (*pariṇāma-vijñāna*), for the Noble Ones have taught that this consciousness depends upon the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

According to one interpretation, this manas takes the seeds of that consciousness as its basis, rather than the manifest consciousness itself; for this [manas] is uninterrupted and does not require the manifest consciousness as a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) in order to arise.

There is another interpretation: this *manas* takes both the seeds of that consciousness and that manifest consciousness as its simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*). Although it is uninterrupted, it is called a "transforming consciousness" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) because it undergoes transformation; thus, it necessarily requires the manifest consciousness as a simultaneous support in order to arise.
"Transformation" refers to the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*), which demonstrates that this consciousness constantly relies upon that [storehouse] consciousness to apprehend its objects.
All minds and mental factors possess a support (*āśraya*); however, there are generally three types of such supports:

first, the causal support (*hetu-pratyaya-āśraya*), which refers to one's own seeds. All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) rely upon this support, for they would necessarily not arise were it separated from their own causal conditions.

Second is the basis of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), which refers to the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). All minds and mental factors depend upon this basis, for they would necessarily not proceed were it not for their simultaneous roots (*sahabhū-indriya*).

Third is the basis of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which refers to the mind that has just ceased. All minds and mental factors depend upon this basis, for they would necessarily not arise were it not for their leading root (*nairmāṇika-indriya*).
Only the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) are said to possess a basis (*sāśraya*) because they are endowed with three types of bases;

other phenomena do not. Regarding the first basis, that of the seed (*bīja*), some say that the manifest fruit can only arise once the seed has already ceased, because the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that what has already arisen cannot exist without a seed, and because the seed and the sprout, etc., do not coexist.

There is an interpretation that the proof cited by him is unestablished: because his statement relies on the production of subsequent seeds; because the production of sprouts from seeds and so forth is not ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); because the destruction of the seed and the arising of the sprout are not universally established; and because the flame and the wick are simultaneous causes for one another.
However, while the cause and effect of seeds within their own category do not coexist, the arising of seeds and manifest phenomena is necessarily simultaneous.

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that impermanent dharmas serve as causes for other natures and also serve as causes for their own subsequent moments; this is the meaning of "conditioned cause" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The term "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) indicates that seeds of the same category serve as causes for one another, where the preceding serves as the cause for the succeeding. The term "extrinsic nature" (*parabhāva*) indicates the sense that seeds and manifest phenomena act as mutual causes for one another.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* also states this: the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and defiled phenomena act as mutual causes and conditions, existing simultaneously like bundles of reeds.
Furthermore, it is taught that the seed and its fruit must necessarily coexist; therefore, the basis of the seed is certainly not prior or posterior.
If there are instances where it is said that the seed and fruit are sequential, one should know that these are all merely "conformative" (anuvartana) modes of exposition.
Thus, these eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (caitta) each definitely have their own distinct seeds as a basis (*āśraya*).

Next, regarding the simultaneous basis (*sahabhv-āśraya*), some state that the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, take the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as their basis, because when these [five] arise in the present, that [mental consciousness] necessarily exists.
There are no separate eye-faculties and so forth that serve as simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*), because the five faculties—the eye and the rest—are themselves the seeds.
As stated in a verse of the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
"Consciousness arises from its own seeds and evolves appearing in the likeness of an object."
To establish the internal and external bases (*āyatana*), the Buddha taught them as ten.

The meaning of that verse is that the World-Honored One, in order to establish the twelve bases, taught that the seeds of the five consciousnesses are the faculties such as the eye, and that the objective aspects of the five consciousnesses are the objects such as form; therefore, the faculties such as the eye are themselves the seeds of the five consciousnesses.
The *Ālambanaparīkṣā* also states:
"The capacity for form within consciousness Is reasonably termed the five faculties;
This capacity and the objective form Have been mutual causes from time immemorial."

The meaning of that verse is as follows: the functional capacity of the seeds within the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) that can produce the visual consciousness and other sensory cognitions of form is designated as the five faculties; there are no separate [physical] eyes and so forth.
The seeds and the consciousnesses of form are constantly mutual causes for one another, because the perfuming agents and the seeds serve as reciprocal causes.
The seventh and eighth consciousnesses have no separate basis other than this [storehouse consciousness], for they evolve in constant continuity with superior intrinsic power.
The sixth consciousness has a distinct basis of its own, for it must rely upon the *manas* to arise.

According to one interpretation, that [previous] explanation contradicts both reason and scripture; if the five material sense-faculties were themselves the seeds of the five consciousnesses, then the seeds of the eighteen elements would become confused and disordered.
However, each of the eighteen elements has its own distinct seeds, as this is stated in various places throughout the holy teachings.

Furthermore, the seeds of the five consciousnesses each possess distinct capacities to produce the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*); with respect to which of these do you maintain that the name "eye-faculty" and so forth applies?

If it were the seeds of the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), they should be subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); if they were the seeds of the object-portion (*nimitta-bhāga*), they should be subsumed under the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
This would contradict the sacred teaching that the five faculties, such as the eye, are all subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).

Furthermore, if the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) were themselves the seeds of the five consciousnesses, then the five organs would have to be the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition) of the five consciousnesses, and they should not be described as being subsumed under the category of *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition).

Moreover, if the nose and tongue organs were themselves the seeds of their respective two consciousnesses, then the nose and tongue organs would necessarily be bound exclusively to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), or else those two consciousnesses would have to be admitted as extending to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). To accept either of these would contradict the sacred teachings.
The eye, ear, and body faculties are the seeds of the three consciousnesses; the same difficulty applies regarding the two realms and five stages.
Furthermore, since the seeds of the five consciousnesses pertain to both the wholesome and the unwholesome, the five material faculties should not be exclusively indeterminate.
Furthermore, since the seeds of the five consciousnesses are not comprised within what is appropriated (*upātta*), the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) should likewise not be appropriated.

Moreover, if the five material sense-faculties were the seeds of the five consciousnesses, then the seeds of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would have to be the *manas*, because they [the proponent] treats the five faculties as being of the same nature (*sadharmya*).

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the visual and other consciousnesses all possess three bases (*āśraya*). If the five material sense organs were merely the seeds of the five consciousnesses, then there would only be two bases.

Moreover, various sacred teachings state that the visual and other faculties encompass both the manifest and the seed; to maintain that they are exclusively seeds would contradict all such authoritative scriptures.

There are those who, wishing to avoid the aforementioned difficulties and refutations, align themselves with that [opposing] position and further offer this defense: "The seeds of predominant karma capable of inducing the five consciousnesses within the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) are termed the 'five material faculties' (*pañca-rūpīndriyāṇi*); they do not act as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the production of the seeds of the five consciousnesses. This perfectly accords with the two verses and is well-consistent with the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*."
His words are empty and devoid of any real meaning, for it would follow that the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) are not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Furthermore, it would follow that they are not merely appropriated (*upātta*), are not subsumed solely within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and are not merely internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
The nose and tongue would have to be bound exclusively to the desire realm; the [other] three faculties would not be bound to the five stages;

the karma that produces the mental consciousness would have to be the manas; the eyes and so forth would not be comprised of both the manifest and the seeds; and furthermore, the eyes and so forth would not be material faculties.
Furthermore, if all five sensory consciousnesses were produced by karma, they would necessarily be categorized as exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Since the wholesome and other types of the five consciousnesses are not produced by karma, they would lack the eye and other organs as their co-existent supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*). Therefore, what has been said does not constitute a sound rebuttal.

Furthermore, it is stated throughout various authoritative scriptures that the ālayavijñāna transforms into what appears as the material sense faculties (rūpīndriya), as well as their physical bases and the receptacle world (bhājanaloka).
How can you deny the existence of the material sense faculties?

It is permissible to allow that the visual and other consciousnesses transform into the semblance of form and so forth, but it is not permissible to allow that the visual and other [faculties] are transformations of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Such confusion deeply contradicts both scripture and reasoning.

However, when the *Gāthā* states that the functional capacity of seeds is called the "five faculties," this is intended to refute the notion of real material sense-faculties existing apart from consciousness.

Regarding that which is transformed by consciousness and appears as the eye-faculty and so forth, because it possesses the function of generating the five consciousnesses, it is metaphorically designated as "seeds" and "the functional capacity of matter"; this does not mean that the material faculties are themselves the karmic seeds of consciousness.

Furthermore, the clearly manifest mental consciousness that takes the five objects as its conditions should have the five sensory consciousnesses as its simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), because it necessarily coexists with them.

If that [mental consciousness] were not supported by the eye-consciousness and the others, it would likewise not serve as a support for the five consciousnesses, because the strength of their mutual dependence is equal.

Furthermore, although the seventh consciousness is uninterrupted, since it undergoes transformation during the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) and other stages, it must have a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), just as the six consciousnesses do.
Otherwise, it would not be subsumed under the "transforming consciousnesses" (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which would contradict the sacred teaching that there are seven transforming consciousnesses.
Therefore, one must admit that it has a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), which is comprised within the eighth consciousness in its active state (*pravṛtti*).
As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Because the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) exists, there is the manas; with the manas as its support, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises."

The intended meaning of that treatise is as follows: because it takes the manifest storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as its support, the manas exists; it does not arise from its own seeds. Otherwise, one would have to say that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) arises because the storehouse consciousness exists.
Therefore, that [previous] explanation contradicts both reason and scripture.

Consequently, it should be stated that the first five evolving consciousnesses each necessarily have two simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*): namely, the five material sense-faculties and the simultaneously arising mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The sixth evolving consciousness definitely and constantly has one simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), namely the seventh consciousness.
If it arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses, it also takes those five consciousnesses as its simultaneous support.
The seventh evolving consciousness definitely has only one coexistent support, namely, the eighth consciousness.
Since only the eighth consciousness is eternally without transformation and is self-sustaining, it has no coexistent support.

There is an interpretation that this explanation has not yet exhausted the principle: since the eighth consciousness and the others are identical in their nature as consciousness, why is it not admitted that they possess simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*)?
Since the seventh and eighth consciousnesses always function in conjunction, what fault would there be in them serving as mutual supports for one another?

Just as it is accepted that manifest consciousness takes seeds as its support, one must likewise accept that the seeds of consciousness depend upon manifest consciousness; for the perfuming [consciousness] and the maturation [consciousness] serve as the supports for the growth and persistence of seeds, since seeds do not grow or persist apart from them.
Furthermore, the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), functions by maintaining the body and depending upon the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
As stated in the sūtras, the ālayavijñāna is wafted by the winds of karma and flows continuously, ever-present, in dependence upon all the sense faculties.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* also states that because the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, each have their own distinct supports, they cannot grasp and maintain the physical body endowed with material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*).

If the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) did not pervasively rely upon all the material sense organs, it would—like the six consciousnesses—not be capable of grasping and maintaining [the body], or else the reason established [for its existence] would suffer from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Therefore, when the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) manifests, it necessarily has one support, namely the seventh consciousness; furthermore, in the realms possessing form, it also relies upon the material sense organs.

When it is the seeds of consciousness, they likewise necessarily have one support, namely the retributive consciousness (vipākavijñāna); at the stage of initial perfuming, they also rely upon the perfuming agent. The rest is as previously explained.
There is another interpretation: what was stated previously is all unreasonable, because it fails to distinguish between the "basis" (*āśraya*) and the "support" (*niśraya*).

"Support" refers to all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, which attain birth and abiding by relying upon causes and depending upon conditions; all such things relied upon and depended upon are called supports, as in the case of a king and his ministers supporting one another.

If a phenomenon is definitively possessed of an object and acts as a sovereign, causing the mind and mental factors to apprehend their respective objects, it is then the "basis" (*āśraya*), namely the six internal bases (*ādhyātmika-ṣaḍāyatana*).
Others are not possessed of an object and do not definitively act as sovereigns; thus, these [bases] are like kings, not like ministers and the like.

Therefore, in all the holy teachings, only mind and mental factors are said to "possess a basis" (*sāśraya*), and not material phenomena (*rūpa*) and so forth, because the latter lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
It is taught that mental factors take the mind as their basis, but it is not taught that mental factors serve as the basis for the mind, because they are not the primary factor.
However, there are places where it is said that "the supported is the basis" or "the basis is the support"; these are all conventional designations made according to the circumstances.

Consequently, the simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*) of the five consciousnesses are necessarily of four kinds: namely, the five material sense-faculties, and the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses. This is because if any one of these is missing, the consciousness will certainly not arise; furthermore, their supports are distinct as the basis for the common object, for discrimination, for defilement, and for purity, respectively.

The holy teachings state that [the five sensory consciousnesses] rely solely upon the five sense faculties because these are their unique bases (*asādhāraṇa*), and because they must share the same object (*sama-viṣaya*) due to their close conformity.

As for the sixth mental consciousness, its simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*) are of only two kinds, namely the seventh and eighth consciousnesses; for if either one were missing, it would necessarily not arise.
Although the five consciousnesses clearly apprehend their objects when they arise together with [the manas], they do not necessarily exist [at all times]; therefore, they are not the support.

The holy teachings state that [the manas] depends solely on the seventh [consciousness] because it is the support for both defilement and purity, is subsumed under the same category of evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), and is closely concordant with it.
The seventh consciousness has only one type of simultaneous support, namely the eighth consciousness; for if the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) were absent, it would certainly not function.
As a gāthā says: "Depending upon the ālaya, the manas functions."
Relying upon the mind (*citta*) and the intellect (*manas*), the other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise.

The *ālayavijñāna* likewise has only one type of simultaneous support, namely the seventh consciousness; for if that consciousness were absent, [the *ālaya*] would certainly not evolve, as the treatises state that the storehouse consciousness always evolves simultaneously with the *manas*.
Furthermore, it is said that the ālayavijñāna always relies upon defilement; this is precisely the manas.

As for the statement that the manas is absent during the three stages, this is spoken with reference to the obscured [manas]; just as one might say that the ālaya is absent during the four stages without meaning that the eighth consciousness does not exist, so too should this be understood.
Although the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) also relies upon the five sense faculties, these are not necessarily present there; thus, they are not included among the supports (*āśraya*).
While the seeds of consciousness can manifest and grasp their respective objects—thereby possessing the sense of being a support—they lack the status of being supported (*āśrita*).
The basis (*āśraya*) of mental factors (*caitta*) should be explained as corresponding to that of consciousness (*vijñāna*), with the addition of their own respective associated mind (*citta*).
If one explains it in this way, it perfectly accords with both reason and scripture.

Regarding the subsequent "opening and guiding" basis (*prāviveka-āśraya*), there is an interpretation that because the five consciousnesses do not continue from themselves or others in a preceding-to-succeeding sequence and must necessarily be induced and produced by the sixth consciousness, the sixth consciousness alone serves as the opening and guiding basis.

Because the sixth consciousness continues its own stream and is also produced by being induced by the five sensory consciousnesses, it takes the first six consciousnesses as its "opening and guiding support" (āśraya).

Because the seventh and eighth consciousnesses continue their own streams and do not depend on being induced by other consciousnesses, they take only their own kind as their opening and guiding support.

There is an interpretation that the previous explanation has not yet fully investigated the principle. For the time being, it may be as stated regarding the first five consciousnesses when they are in a state of non-mastery and encounter non-superior objects.

However, in a state of mastery—such as that of the Buddhas and others who possess mastery over their objects—the various faculties function interchangeably; they operate spontaneously and with certainty without requiring deliberate seeking. In such a case, how could those five consciousness-bodies not be continuous?

Since the five sensory consciousnesses that are outflows are produced by the force of determinate attention—whether defiled or pure—and while they remain focused on their objects without yet having relinquished them, how could one not admit that they continue in a succession of many moments?

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that defilement and purity occur only after the mind has reached a state of determination; it is only thereafter that the resultant eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) arises as either wholesome or unwholesome. This [resultant consciousness] does not arise through its own power of discrimination; rather, as long as this mental faculty (*manas*) does not turn toward another object, for that duration the eye-consciousness and the mental consciousness continue to evolve in a stream, being either wholesome or defiled.
It should be understood that the same applies from the arising of visual consciousness up to tactile consciousness.

That [text] clearly indicates that for such a duration, both the visual and mental consciousnesses proceed in a continuous stream; since there is no absence of mental consciousness at the time of visual consciousness, it is not the case that these two consciousnesses arise as a mutual succession.

If an intensely powerful object appears in continuous succession, such that it overwhelms the body and mind and cannot be momentarily relinquished, then the five groups of sensory consciousnesses must necessarily continue in succession, as in the case of those in the Hot Hells or the gods of the Heaven of Forgetfulness through Play.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If these six consciousnesses serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for those [subsequent] six consciousnesses, they are then designated by the name 'mental faculty' (*manas-indriya*).
Between the preceding and succeeding moments of the five sensory consciousnesses, there is invariably only the mental consciousness."
That treatise should state: "If this single consciousness serves as the equal-and-immediate condition for those six consciousnesses," or it should state:
"If these six consciousnesses serve as the equal-and-immediate condition for that single consciousness."

Since this is not the case, we know that the five consciousnesses possess the quality of continuity; when the five consciousnesses arise, there must necessarily be a mental consciousness capable of inducing the subsequent moment of mental consciousness to arise. Why, then, would one need to rely upon the five consciousnesses as the "opening and guiding" support (*āśraya*)?

When the mental consciousness has been interrupted during states such as mindlessness, sleep, or fainting, and subsequently arises again, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and the manas, which are both constantly continuous, should also serve as its *āśraya* of guidance (*āvāhaka*).
If that [manas] is induced by its own preceding class, why do you not allow the same for the five sensory consciousnesses?
Since this is not the case here, how can it be so there?
The manas associated with the wisdom of equality must initially arise dependent upon the sixth mental consciousness; therefore, it too should take that as its inducing support (*āśraya*).
The eighth pure consciousness, which co-exists with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, must initially be induced by the provisional means of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.

Furthermore, since the maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*) relies upon the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*), or upon a virtuous mind associated with compassion and vows, it follows that one must necessarily admit that the eighth consciousness also takes the sixth and seventh consciousnesses as its "opening and guiding" support (*āśraya*).

Consequently, those [previous] statements have not thoroughly investigated the underlying principles; one should rather state that, among the first six consciousnesses, whichever consciousness functions as the immediately preceding condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*) serves as the "opening and guiding support" (*kṣaṇika-āśraya*). Specifically, the sixth mental consciousness takes its own preceding class or the seventh or eighth consciousnesses as its opening and guiding support; the seventh manas-consciousness takes its own preceding class or the sixth consciousness as its opening and guiding support; and the ādāna-consciousness takes its own preceding class, as well as the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, as its opening and guiding support.
All [of these] do not contradict reason, because of what was stated previously.
According to another interpretation, this explanation is also unreasonable.

Regarding the "opening-and-guiding support" (*āśraya-avakāśa-pradāna*): it refers to a conditioned dharma that acts as the primary cause capable of functioning as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Because it opens up space for and guides the subsequent arising of mind and mental factors, it is called the opening-and-guiding support.
This [the *āśraya-pratyaya*] belongs exclusively to the mind (*citta*) and not to mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth.
If this [mind] and that [mind] lack the sense of arising simultaneously, it is said that the former possesses the power of opening and guiding for the latter.
Since the eight consciousnesses within a single body can arise together, how can those of different categories serve as the opening and guiding support (*āśraya*) for one another?

If it were admitted that [matter] serves as a basis, then [the various consciousnesses] would not arise simultaneously, which would be identical to the position of other schools that minds do not arise concurrently.

Furthermore, within a single body, the number of consciousnesses arising together is indeterminate; if it were permitted for them to act as one another’s equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), then the same would apply to form and so forth, thereby contradicting the noble teaching that the equal-and-immediate condition pertains exclusively to mind and mental factors.

However, when the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that matter (*rūpa*) may also possess the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), this is a statement employing both concession and refutation. It means that, while provisionally conceding to the Hīnayāna view that matter and mind possess the immediately preceding condition in their successive sequence, it refutes [the Hīnayāna position] regarding the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*). Otherwise, the term "also" (*api*) would be rendered useless.

If you claim that the word "equal" (*samanantara*) does not exclude differences in number but merely indicates similarity of type, you would contradict your own tenet that consciousnesses of different types serve as equal and immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*).

Therefore, it is deeply consistent with both scripture and reasoning that each of the eight consciousnesses takes only its own kind as its opening-and-guiding support (*āśraya*), because it is impossible for members of the same kind to arise simultaneously.
The mental factors (*caitta*) that depend upon this [mind] should be explained in accordance with the consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Although the mind and its mental factors arise simultaneously as distinct categories, they are mutually associated and harmonized such that they appear as one; they necessarily arise and perish together, their activities are invariably identical, and when one provides the opening and guidance, the others do so as well. Therefore, they act as one another’s immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are not like this, and thus should not be used as an analogy.
Furthermore, mental factors (*caitta*) are not "opening-and-leading" supports (*āśraya*), because they lack the principle of being the primary cause for what is produced.

If the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for each of the mind and mental factors were restricted solely to their own respective categories, then at the time of the initial transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, the corresponding mental factors such as faith (*śraddhā*) would lack this condition; this would contradict the holy teaching that all minds and mental factors arise from four conditions.

Although the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is interrupted during states such as mindlessness, sleep, or fainting, when it arises again, its "opening and guiding" support (*āśraya*) is simply its own preceding class.

It should be understood that the same applies to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*): they are called "uninterrupted" (*anantara*) because there is no intervening mind of their own kind between them.

Since that [preceding consciousness] has already served as the introductory guide for the present consciousness at the time of its own cessation, why trouble to posit a different category as the introductory support (*āśraya*)?

However, when the sacred teachings state that the first six consciousnesses mutually induce one another, or that the seventh and eighth depend on the sixth and seventh to arise, these are all said in reference to a particularly potent dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), not the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); therefore, there is no contradiction.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If, immediately following this consciousness, various consciousnesses necessarily arise, this [preceding consciousness] is called the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for them.

Furthermore, regarding these six consciousnesses serving as the equal-and-immediate condition for those [subsequent] six consciousnesses, the designation of this [condition] as the "mental faculty" (*manas-indriya*) does not contradict the principle that while the expression is general, its intended meaning is specific.
Therefore, having relied upon the profound accord between the teachings and the principles, this auxiliary discussion is concluded; we should now proceed to analyze the main treatise.

Although this transforming consciousness possesses three types of supports (*āśraya*), the statement that it "evolves based on them" refers only to the first two. This is to demonstrate that the support and the object-condition (*ālambana*) of this consciousness are identical, and because these first two supports possess superior functional utility, or because the "opening and guiding" support (*unmīlana-āśraya*) is easier to understand.
Thus, the support (*āśraya*) of this consciousness has already been explained.
What is its object (*ālambana*)?
It is that very same [consciousness] which serves as its support; for the Noble Ones have taught that this consciousness takes the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object.

There is an interpretation that this [ignorance] takes as its object both the substance of that consciousness and its associated mental factors, because the treatise states that the grasping at "I" and "mine" is always associated with them.
That is to say, taking their substance and associated factors as objects, one respectively clings to them as the self and as what belongs to the self.
However, since mental factors are not separate from consciousness, there is no contradiction with the teachings regarding the expression "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
One interpretation holds that such a claim is logically untenable, as there is nowhere it is stated that [the mind] takes contact (*sparśa*) and so forth as its object.

It should be said that this manas takes only the seeing and image portions (*nimitta-bhāga*) of those consciousnesses as its objects, respectively grasping them as "self" and "what belongs to the self.
Since both the image and the seeing portions have consciousness as their substance, this does not contradict the teaching of the Sage.

There is another interpretation which holds that this statement is also illogical, because the five material sense-faculties and their objects do not belong to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Furthermore, it would follow that [this manas] must also take external objects as its domain—just like the five sensory consciousnesses—and must take common objects as its domain—just like the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Moreover, it would follow that those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) would not grasp at "mine" (*mama*), and that those who have become weary of form and are born there would not transform their form. Therefore, one should say that this manas takes only the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and its seeds as its objects, grasping them respectively as "self" (*ātman*) and "mine" (*ātmiya*).
Since the seeds are simply the functional capacities of that consciousness and are not substantially existent entities, this does not contradict the sacred teachings.
According to another interpretation, the previous explanations are all unreasonable, because the seeds of form and so forth do not belong to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Since the treatises state that seeds are substantially existent (*dravyasat*), it follows that what is merely nominal (*prajñapti*) must be like a non-entity and thus cannot serve as a causal condition.

Furthermore, since the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) co-arising with this consciousness arises spontaneously, as a single class, and continues in constant succession, how could one possibly maintain a separate grasping for a self or what belongs to a self?

This is because, within a single moment of mind, there is no possibility of two distinct objects—such as permanence and annihilation—being apprehended simultaneously by two separate grasping cognitions.
Furthermore, one should not say that these two graspings occur sequentially, for they have been evolving as a single, uniform flavor since beginningless time.
It should be understood that this manas takes only the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) as its object, and nothing else.

This is because [the storehouse consciousness] has been a homogeneous continuum since beginningless time, appearing as if it were permanent and unitary, and because it serves as the constant basis for all phenomena.
This [view] merely grasps that [object] as one's own internal self; the expression "mine" (ātmīya) is used here by force of the linguistic momentum.
Alternatively, this [view] grasps that [object] as the self of my self; thus, two expressions are employed for the single meaning of the view.

If one speaks in this way, it accords well with the teachings and reasoning, for many passages state that there is only the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), and because the grasping at "I" and "mine" do not arise simultaneously.

In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), [the mirror-like wisdom] takes only the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object; once the basis has been transformed, it also takes true suchness (*tathatā*) and other phenomena as its objects. This is because the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) realizes ten kinds of equality and knows the differences in the inclinations (*adhimukti*) of all sentient beings, manifesting various images of the Buddha.

This discussion refers, for the time being, to the state prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); therefore, it is said that this [consciousness] takes that storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object.
This is because the principles governing awakening and delusion, as well as their universal or limited scope, must necessarily be so.
Since the objects of selflessness and self are respectively pervasive and non-pervasive, how could this consciousness take its own support as its object?
If there is a subsequent consciousness that takes the preceding mind as its object, since that is already established, what fault could there be in this case?
The verse states that "reflection is its nature and characteristic," which simultaneously reveals both the self-nature and the mode of activity of this consciousness.

Because the mind (*manas*) has deliberation as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and because it employs that very [nature] as its mode of activity (*ākāra*), this simultaneously explains its specific designation.

It is called *manas* because it is capable of precise deliberation; for in the state prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it constantly and precisely deliberates upon the characteristics of the grasped self, while in the state after the transformation of the basis, it likewise precisely deliberates upon the characteristic of non-self.
How many mental factors (caitta) are associated with this manas?
Briefly, it is always accompanied by four types of afflictions; here, the term "accompanied" (saha) signifies the sense of association (samprayoga).

That is to say, from beginningless time until the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), this manas spontaneously and constantly takes the ālayavijñāna as its object and is associated with the four fundamental afflictions.
What are these four? They are self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), and self-love (*ātma-sneha*); these are called the four kinds.
Self-delusion refers to ignorance (*avidyā*); because one is deluded regarding the characteristics of a self and confused about the principle of non-self, it is called self-delusion.
The view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) refers to the grasping at a self; because one falsely conceptualizes non-self phenomena as being a self, it is called the view of self.
Self-conceit (*asmimāna*) refers to arrogance; because one relies upon the grasped self to cause the mind to become uplifted and haughty, it is called self-conceit.

"Self-love" (*ātmasneha*) refers to self-grasping; it is called "self-love" because one develops deep attachment toward the self that is grasped. This term also indicates that pride and craving coexist with views and pride, thereby refuting the position of other schools who maintain that there is no such principle of association (*samprayoga*).

These four constantly arise to disturb and turbidify the internal mind, causing the external evolving consciousnesses to perpetually become defiled; because sentient beings cannot escape the cycle of birth and death due to this, they are called afflictions (*kleśa*).
Those [afflictions] are of ten kinds; why are there only four here?
Because when the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is present, other views do not arise, as two types of wisdom cannot coexist within a single moment of mind.
How, then, can this consciousness necessarily possess the view of self?
The two types of grasping and false views arise solely from discrimination and are abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
The afflictions associated with these are exclusively innate (*sahaja*), as they are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

The view of extremes regarding "mine" arises dependent upon the view of self; however, the view associated with this [innate grasping] does not arise dependent upon that [discriminated view of self], because it constantly clings to an internal self. Therefore, the view of self must necessarily be present, for since this view is definitive and decisive, there is no room for doubt to arise.
Because one is attached to a self, hatred cannot arise; therefore, there are only four afflictions associated with this consciousness.
How can the three—view, pride, and attachment—arise together?
Since their modes of activity (*ākāra*) do not conflict, what fault is there in their arising simultaneously?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that greed causes the mind to sink, while pride causes the mind to be uplifted.
How is this not contradictory?

There is no conflict between these texts and their meanings, for there are distinctions of coarseness and subtlety regarding the objects of disparagement and reliance—namely, whether they are external objects or internal objects, and whether they are conceptually constructed or innate.
Are there only these four mental factors associated with this manas? No;
for it is also accompanied by others, such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth.

According to one interpretation, there are only nine mental factors associated with this manas: the aforementioned four, plus the other five dharmas—namely, contact, attention (*manaskāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—because the manas is necessarily associated with the universal (*sarvatraga*) factors.

It was previously stated that contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] coexist with the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*); however, fearing that they might be considered—just as before—to be "unobscured-neutral" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), the word "others" (*anya*) is employed to distinguish them from that.
The particle "and" (*ca*) signifies a collection of meanings: it combines the four preceding and the five succeeding [factors], because they are always associated with the *manas*.
For what reason does this manas lack other mental factors?

It is because desire (*chanda*) is the aspiration for an object that has not yet been attained; since this consciousness spontaneously takes as its object an entity already attained, it lacks anything to aspire to, and thus desire is absent.

Adhimokṣa (resolute determination) maintains an object that has not yet been ascertained; this consciousness, however, has from beginningless time constantly taken a fixed object as its referent because it is maintained by the sūtras, and thus lacks adhimokṣa.

Smṛti (mindfulness) is the mere recollection of things previously experienced; this consciousness constantly takes as its object a present experience and has nothing to recollect, and therefore lacks smṛti.

Concentration (*samādhi*) consists solely of binding the mind to focus on a single object; since this consciousness operates spontaneously, perceiving different objects from moment to moment, it is not one-pointed and thus lacks concentration.
As for wisdom (*prajñā*), because it is identical to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), it is not mentioned separately.
Because virtue is pure, it does not coexist with this consciousness.

The arising of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) is necessarily established based on the distinctions between preceding and succeeding states dependent upon primary afflictions (*kleśa*). Since this consciousness is always associated with the four primary afflictions and its preceding and succeeding states are of a single, undifferentiated type, there are no secondary afflictions associated with this consciousness.

Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) involves regretting actions previously committed; this consciousness, however, functions spontaneously and constantly takes present objects as its domain. Since it does not regret past actions, remorse is absent here.

Sleep necessarily depends upon the heaviness and dullness of body and mind, and arises only occasionally through the power of external conditions; this consciousness, being of a single type from beginningless time, internally grasps without depending on external conditions, and therefore sleep is not present there.

Vitarka and vicāra both function by way of the external door, involving shallow or deep deliberation and coarse or subtle verbal expression; this consciousness, however, functions solely by way of the internal door, being of a single type that clings to a self, and is therefore not associated with them.
There is an interpretation that his explanation of the "remaining" [defilements] is irrational, because the verse separately states that these are subsumed under the "obscured" (nivṛta).

Furthermore, it would lack the secondary afflictions (upakleśa) that coexist with the mind; since primary afflictions (kleśa) necessarily coexist with secondary afflictions, the term "the remaining" here indicates the secondary afflictions.
Regarding this, there is one interpretation: the five secondary afflictions are universally associated with all defiled minds.
As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, torpor, restlessness, lack of faith, laziness, and heedlessness are always and invariably associated with all categories of defiled states.
If they were separated from the lack of pliancy (*akarmaṇyatā*) and other such factors, it would be impossible for defilement to arise;
since the mind is already defiled at the moment afflictions (*kleśa*) emerge, those five factors must necessarily be present during the state of a defiled mind.
When afflictions arise, they necessarily do so due to lack of fitness, agitation, lack of faith, laziness, and negligence.
Although restlessness pervades all defiled states of mind, it increases specifically during the state of greed; therefore, it is described as a derivative of greed.

For example, although sleep (*middha*) and regret (*kaukṛtya*) pervade minds of all three moral natures, they are said to be "parts of delusion" (*moha-bhāga*) because they increase specifically during the state of delusion.

Although other sources state that there are six or ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that pervade all defiled minds, those statements of pervasiveness are made based on specific contextual meanings; it is not the case that they actually pervade every defiled mind.

That is to say, based on the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), six are explained by taking those whose understanding encompasses both the coarse and the subtle, as well as those that are neutral (*avyākṛta*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*), which manifest as obstacles to concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Based on the twenty-two secondary afflictions, ten are explained by taking those whose understanding encompasses both the coarse and the subtle and both natures (*dvi-vidha*). Therefore, these two explanations do not contradict one another.

However, there are fifteen mental factors associated with this manas, namely: the nine previously mentioned factors, the five secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the discernment (*prajñā*) from among the object-specific factors (*viṣayaviśeṣa*).

Although the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is subsumed under the object-specific discernment, it is divided into two within the fifty-one mental factors because there is a functional distinction between them.
For what reason does this manas lack other mental factors?
It is because the ten [factors] such as anger (*krodha*) have coarse and agitated aspects, whereas this consciousness is subtle and refined; therefore, it does not coexist with them.

Furthermore, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), whereas this [manas] is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); therefore, it is not associated with them.

Distraction causes the mind to flow outward toward external objects; this [state] arises by constantly grasping internally at a single type of object and does not flow outward, and therefore it does not exist [therein].

Lack of clear comprehension refers to the arising of bodily, vocal, and mental activities directed toward the external world that transgress established norms; since this involves only internal grasping, it does not coexist with that [distraction].
There are no other mental factors [associated with all defiled minds], as the meaning has been explained previously.

According to another interpretation, one should state that six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are universally associated with all defiled minds, because the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and faulty wisdom (*dausprajñā*) are associated with all defiled minds.
If forgetfulness, distraction, and impaired wisdom did not exist, the mind would certainly be unable to give rise to the various afflictions (*kleśa*).

This is because it is only by taking as an object a category of previously experienced phenomena that one gives rise to forgetfulness and erroneous discernment, which in turn cause the afflictions such as craving (*rāga*) to arise.
When afflictions arise, the mind necessarily wanders, for they all cause distraction with respect to their objects.
Lethargy and restlessness are mutually contradictory in their modes of activity; thus, they cannot arise simultaneously in every defiled state of mind.

Regarding the treatise’s statement that five factors pervade all defiled minds: this interpretation applies to both coarse and subtle [defilements] because they contradict exclusively wholesome dharmas; furthermore, since the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) pervade both natures (wholesome and unwholesome), the meaning of the term "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*) is as previously explained.

However, there are nineteen mental factors associated with this [mental consciousness], namely: the nine previously mentioned factors, the six secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), along with mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the addition of lethargy (*styāna*).
This separate mention of mindfulness is to be explained according to the previous explanation of wisdom.
Furthermore, it is "concentrated" because it focuses exclusively on the object of the grasped self without ever relinquishing it.
It is "accompanied by torpor" because the ignorance associated with this consciousness is particularly heavy, causing the mind to be dull and lethargic.
Because it is the opposite of that, there is no restlessness (*auddhatya*).
As stated above, one should understand that there are no other mental factors [present].

Another interpretation further states that ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are universally associated with all defiled minds. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "Laxity (*pramāda*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lethargy (*styāna*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), indolence (*kausīdya*), wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*), wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*), wrong mindfulness (*mithyā-smṛti*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and wrong awareness (*asamprajanya*)—these ten arise in all defiled minds, as they pervade all locations and are bound to all three realms."

If there were no wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*) or wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*), the mind would certainly be unable to give rise to the various afflictions (*kleśa*); for it is only when one grasps the characteristics of an object through the desire for union or separation that afflictions such as greed arise.

Those who harbor doubts regarding principles (tattva) certainly have no hesitation concerning objective entities such as form (rūpa); therefore, even doubt associated with [other mental states] possesses resolute conviction (adhimokṣa).
As for those who also hesitate regarding the objective entity itself, this is not the affliction of doubt (vicikitsā), such as when one hesitates between [perceiving] a person or a tree stump.

The reason these two are not said to be universal in other contexts is that, when the mind is associated with doubt regarding an unattractive object, its wrong desire and resolve are not coarse or manifest.
As for the mutual presence or absence of the others, the meaning is as previously explained.

In this manas, there are twenty-four mental factors (*caitta*), namely: the nine aforementioned factors, the ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the five object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*).
Following the reasoning explained previously, it should be understood that there are no other mental factors as described above.

There is another interpretation: the previous explanations have not fully exhausted the reasoning. Furthermore, while one may doubt whether the next world exists or not, what characteristic of desire or resolute conviction (adhimokṣa) could there be therein?
If mental torpor (styāna) were absent at the moment afflictions arise, then the state of being unamenable to cultivation (akarmanyatā) would necessarily not be present.
If restlessness were absent, there would be no agitation, and it would consequently be like a virtuous state or other non-afflicted states.
If there were no distraction within an afflicted mind, it would follow that it is neither a state of wandering nor an afflicted mind.
If there were no loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), how could afflictions arise and manifest?

Therefore, every defiled mind necessarily arises in association with the eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*): namely, lethargy (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*).

Forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*) and lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), which have mindfulness (*smṛti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature, do not pervade all defiled minds; for not all defiled minds take previously experienced objects as their cognitive focus through the process of discernment (*viveka*).
If ignorance were its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would arise pervasively throughout all defiled minds, as previously stated.

However, this [ignorance] is associated with eighteen mental factors (*caitta*), namely: the nine aforementioned dharmas, the eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the wisdom (*prajñā*) of the object-specific category (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*).
The absence of other mental factors and the three passages from the treatise should be explained according to the preceding [analysis].
If one explains it in this way, it does not contradict reason or scripture.

With which feeling (*vedanā*) is this afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*) associated?

One interpretation holds that it is associated exclusively with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*), because it constantly grasps at an internal self, giving rise to attachment and delight. Another interpretation maintains that this is not so;
for one must admit that the feeling of joy extends even to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), as otherwise it would contradict the words of the Noble Ones (*ārya*).

It should be said that this mind is associated with four types of feeling: namely, when born in the miserable realms, it is associated with the feeling of sorrow, because it takes as its object the fruit induced by unwholesome karma;

when born among humans, in the desire realm heavens, or in the first two dhyānas, it is associated with the feeling of joy, because it takes as its object the fruit of wholesome karma belonging to stages characterized by joy;
and in the third dhyāna, it is associated with the feeling of pleasure, because it takes as its object the fruit of wholesome karma belonging to stages characterized by pleasure.

From the fourth dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), [the mind] is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because it takes as its object only the wholesome karmic fruit of the stage of equanimity.

According to another interpretation, that explanation is also unreasonable; for since beginningless time, this [mind] has spontaneously belonged to a single category, taking the internal as its object and grasping at a self, remaining constantly without change and thus being incompatible with fluctuating sensations (*vipariṇāma-vedanā*).

Furthermore, regarding this manas, those points where its meaning differs from that of the previously mentioned ālayavijñāna are all explained separately; if it were associated with the four types of sensation, they too would have been explained separately. Since they are not explained separately, it is certain that it is the same as the latter; therefore, this [manas] is associated only with the sensation of equanimity (upekṣā).

In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it is associated with the aforementioned mental factors; in the stage where the basis has been transformed, it arises simultaneously with only twenty-one mental factors, namely: the five universal (*sarvatraga*), the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), and the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*) factors.

Just as the eighth consciousness, in its state where the basis has been transformed (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), is associated exclusively with neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*) because it functions spontaneously and always operates with equanimity toward its objects,
by what nature are the mental factors (*caitta*) of the manas subsumed?
It is subsumed under the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta), and not otherwise.
Because these four afflictions and so forth associated with this manas are defiled phenomena, they obstruct the Noble Path and conceal one's own mind; thus, they are called "obscured.
Since they are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, they are termed "unspecified" (avyākṛta).

As with the various afflictions and so forth of the two upper realms mentioned above, those which are gathered and concealed by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are categorized as neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Because they are the subtle basis for the defiled dharmas associated with them and because they proceed spontaneously, they are also categorized as neutral; however, once the basis has been transformed (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), they possess exclusively a virtuous nature.
To which stage (*bhūmi*) are the mental factors (*caitta*) of the manas bound?
They are bound to the stage in accordance with the stage where they arise.

That is to say, the mental factors associated with the active manas when one is born in the desire realm are bound to the desire realm; it should be understood that this is likewise up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This is because [the manas] spontaneously and constantly takes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object, grasping it as an internal self, and not [taking] another stage as its object.
If the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the maturation (*vipāka*) of that stage, arises and manifests before one, it is said that one is "born" in that stage.
When the afflicted manas takes that as its object and clings to it as a self, it is bound to that stage; thus, it is said to be "bound" by that stage.
If it is bound by the various afflictions and so forth of that stage, it is said to be "bound by them.
Once the basis has been transformed (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it is no longer bound.
This afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) continues in succession from beginningless time; at what stage is it permanently severed or temporarily interrupted?
The Arhat, the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), and the supramundane path do not possess [the afflicted manas].
"Arhat" generally indicates the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-phala) within the three vehicles.
In this stage, both the seeds and the active manifestations of the afflicted manas are permanently severed and extinguished; therefore, it is said that they do not exist.

In the state of an arhat, in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and within the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), it is temporarily suppressed and ceased; therefore, it is said that it does not exist [in those states].

This is because the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*), which has been evolving in a subtle, homogeneous, and spontaneous manner since beginningless time, cannot be suppressed or ceased by any mundane paths with outflows (*sāsravamārga*).
The noble paths of the three vehicles possess the sense of suppressing and extinguishing [afflictions], because the true realization of selflessness contradicts the grasping at a self.
When the subsequently attained non-outflow wisdom manifests, it is its outflow and likewise contradicts this [grasping].
Because both the realization of true non-self and its subsequently attained wisdom are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are called the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*).

Since the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is an outflow (*nisyanda*) of the noble path and is characterized by extreme tranquility, it likewise does not exist [as a distinct entity].

Because these seeds have not been permanently severed, once one has emerged from the noble path following the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), these [afflictions] manifest again until they are finally extinguished.
Furthermore, because these afflictions associated with the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) are innate (*sahaja*), they are not abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*);
yet, because they are defiled (*kliṣṭa*), they are not non-abandonable (*aprahātavya*).
Because they are extremely subtle, all seeds [of these afflictions] are abandoned simultaneously and instantaneously along with the lowest-of-the-low afflictions of the *bhavāgra* stage;
this is because their potencies are equal.

When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests, these seeds are abandoned all at once, and one becomes an Arhat; therefore, in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they never arise again.

When those of the two vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning turn toward the Mahāyāna, from their initial generation of the bodhicitta until they attain Buddhahood, although they are in reality bodhisattvas, they are also called arhats; because their meaning [of being worthy] and so forth are equivalent, they are not mentioned separately.

Regarding this, there is one interpretation: the manas is associated only with the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because all the holy teachings state that it is absent in three states, because they say it is constantly associated with the four delusions, and because they describe it as the basis for the defilement of consciousness.
There is another interpretation: that [previous] explanation contradicts both scripture and reasoning, because the sutras state that the supramundane manas exists.
Furthermore, just as when it is defiled, the undefiled manovijñāna must necessarily have a co-nascent, non-common support.

The treatise states that the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is invariably accompanied by one consciousness, namely the manas; when the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) arises, then two consciousnesses operate together, namely the mental consciousness and the manas; if any one of the five sensory consciousnesses arises among them, then three consciousnesses operate together; and so on, until at times all five sensory consciousnesses arise simultaneously, in which case seven consciousnesses operate together.

If the seventh consciousness did not exist during the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), then at that time the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) would lack a concomitant consciousness; thus, it would not be the case that it always necessarily evolves in conjunction with exactly one consciousness.

Furthermore, if the seventh consciousness were absent during the abiding in the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), then at that time the storehouse consciousness would be accompanied by only one consciousness. How, then, could it be said that when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises, the storehouse consciousness necessarily evolves in conjunction with two?
The *Xianyang lun* states that the manas is constantly associated with four afflictions.

Alternatively, it may manifest as conduct characterized by arrogance based on those associations, or as conduct of equanimity; thus, one knows that this manas encompasses both the defiled and the non-defiled.

If, because the treatises state that the stage of an Arhat lacks the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), it follows that there is no seventh consciousness, then by the same logic, because the treatises state that at the stage of an Arhat one abandons the *ālayavijñāna*, it would follow that there is no eighth consciousness.
Since that [consciousness] is not so, how could this be otherwise?
Furthermore, various treatises state that by transforming the seventh consciousness, one attains the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).

Just as that wisdom, like other forms of wisdom, must necessarily have a basis (*āśraya*), associated mental factors (*samprayukta*), and a pure consciousness, if this [seventh] consciousness were absent, that wisdom would likewise be non-existent; for there can be no supported entity (*āśrita*) apart from its basis (*āśraya*).

It cannot be said that [the Buddha] relies upon the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), for it is admitted that the Buddha’s activity is constant, like the Great Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
Furthermore, if the seventh consciousness did not exist in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*), that eighth consciousness would lack a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*);
yet such a support must necessarily exist, because its nature is the same as that of the other consciousnesses.

Furthermore, just as the grasping at a self (ātma-grāha) constantly operates for those who have not yet realized the selflessness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya), so too should the grasping at a self of phenomena (dharma-ātma-grāha) constantly operate for those who have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya).
If this consciousness did not exist, upon what consciousness would that [attainment] rely? It cannot rely on the eighth consciousness, because the latter lacks discernment (*prajñā*).

Therefore, one should believe that for the noble paths of the two vehicles, the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), this consciousness functions constantly; for they have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Furthermore, in various treatises, the five [consciousnesses] being of the same nature (pañca-samāna-dharma) is used as a proof that there exists a seventh [consciousness] serving as the support for the sixth.

At the time when the Noble Path arises and during the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa), if there were no seventh consciousness to serve as the support for the sixth, then both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the logical reason (*hetu*) established would be fallacious; alternatively, it would follow that the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) would likewise be without a support.

Just as the five [consciousnesses] always have a support, the sixth should likewise do so; therefore, there must certainly exist an undefiled manas that constantly arises and manifests throughout the three aforementioned states.

To say that it does not exist refers to the defiled manas; this is just as when it is said that the four states lack the ālayavijñāna—it does not mean that the eighth consciousness is non-existent. This case should be understood in the same way.
This differentiation of the manas is briefly of three kinds:

first, that associated with the view of a personal self (pudgala-ātman); second, that associated with the view of a self in phenomena (dharma-ātman); and third, that associated with the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna).

Initially, it is present throughout the mental continuums of all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the learners (*śaikṣa*) of the two vehicles, and a class of bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage during their stages of contaminated mind (*sāsravacitta*); in these states, they give rise to the view of a personal self (*pudgalātman*) by taking the ālayavijñāna as its object.

Next, it pervades the mental continuums of all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, as well as all bodhisattvas during stages when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena has not yet manifested; in those states, they give rise to the view of a self in phenomena based upon the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

Subsequently, throughout the continuums of all Tathāgatas and during the stages of the Path of Seeing and the Path of Meditation for Bodhisattvas, when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena manifests before them, they give rise to the Wisdom of Equality by taking the stainless ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and so forth as their object.

At the stage when the view of a person (pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi) arises, the view of a self in phenomena (dharma-ātma-dṛṣṭi) must also necessarily be present; for the grasping at a self necessarily arises based on the grasping at phenomena, just as one mistakes a tree stump for a person in the dark.

Although the functions of the two views—the view of self and the view of phenomena—are distinct, they do not contradict one another, as both rely upon the same wisdom. This is because, just as the substance of visual consciousness and so forth is a single entity while its various functions, such as the discernment of blue and other colors, are not mutually exclusive, this case should be understood in the same way.

When the noble path of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, or the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), is present before them; when a bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment is at the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); and when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is present before a Śrāvaka of gradual enlightenment—all of these instances involve the arising of only the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), because the clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*) has already been suppressed.

When the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena has not yet manifested for those in the stage of no-more-learning of the two vehicles or for those who have attained gradual enlightenment, they likewise give rise only to the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), because the grasping at a self (*ātman*) has already been severed.
