Within these three stages, the five faculties beginning with faith have the nature of these [mental] faculties: namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), joy (*sukha*), pleasure (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Furthermore, during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) and so forth, there is also the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*), as one feels sorrowful while seeking to realize subsequent superior dharmas; however, because it is not a fundamentally wholesome faculty, it is generally not mentioned.
Those in the first three formless realms who possess this faculty do so because they have acquired it as a secondary cultivation alongside the superior path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

Alternatively, for those of the two vehicles who turn toward the Great Vehicle, in order to realize the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), they also give rise to the untainted [wisdom] of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*)—which is subsumed under the nine stages—even prior to the [first] bhūmi.

Since all those [faculties] are subsumed under these faculties of a bodhisattva, the bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) also possesses these faculties; however, they are mentioned only in relation to the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi because that period is brief.

From the final moment of the path of seeing up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), all nine untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*), such as faith and the rest, are of the nature of the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Those who have not yet abandoned desire experience sorrow and distress when seeking to realize the higher liberations; these also possess the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), but because it is not a fundamentally wholesome faculty, it is generally not mentioned.
In all stages of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the nine untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) are entirely of the nature of the faculty of one who has fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Although the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) possesses the untainted (*anāsrava*) contemplations (*vihāra*), they are not clear or sharp; thus, it does not possess the latter three faculties.
Such is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the twenty-two faculties.
Other meanings regarding various categories should be understood as explained in the treatise (*śāstra*).
*Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only), Fascicle Seven; *Cheng weishi lun*, Fascicle Eight.
Composed by Dharmapāla and other Bodhisattvas.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
These four conditions, based on the distinctions in meaning across fifteen bases, are established as ten causes.
How are these established based on the fifteen bases?

The first basis for speech (*vāk-sthāna*) refers to the nature of speech arising from the conceptualization of names for phenomena; it is upon this basis that the cause of conventional designation (*anuvyavahāra-hetu*) is established, because by means of this speech one designates various objects according to what has been seen, heard, and so forth. Thus, this [speech] which is the speaker serves as the cause for that which is spoken.

Some treatises state that this consists of name, concept, and view; because one grasps signs according to names and adheres to them, speech subsequently arises. If one follows that explanation, it becomes evident that this cause is the basis for speech.

Second is the basis for experiencing, which refers to the nature of being that which is depended upon by the experiencer and the experienced; it is based on this very basis that the "condition of dependence" (*apekṣā-hetu*) is established. That is to say, when something causes another thing to arise, persist, be accomplished, or be attained through dependence upon it, this is the condition of dependence for that [latter] thing.

The locus of the three types of habitual tendencies refers to the stage when internal and external seeds have not yet matured; it is upon this very locus that the projecting cause (ākṣepahetu) is established, because it is capable of projecting its own distant result.

The fourth is the basis for seeds with moisture, which refers to the stage when internal and external seeds have reached maturity; it is upon this basis that the "arising cause" is established, because it is capable of giving rise to its immediate result.
The fifth is the basis of immediate cessation, which refers to the condition as the immediately preceding moment for the mind and mental factors.
The sixth is the basis of the objective sphere, which refers to the object-condition for the mind and mental factors.
The locus of the seven faculties refers to the six faculties upon which the mind and mental factors depend.

The locus of the eight functional activities refers to the instrumental functions regarding the actions performed; that is, with the exception of seeds, it refers to other auxiliary manifest conditions.

Ninth is the basis of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), which refers to the agent’s activity regarding the action performed; that is, with the exception of seeds, it refers to other present conditions that act as causes.

Tenth is the basis of seeing reality (*tattvadarśana*), which refers to untainted vision (*anāsravadarśana*); excluding the drawing forth of its own seeds, it is able to assist in the drawing forth and realization of untainted phenomena.

Based collectively on these six, the "appropriating cause" (*parigraha-hetu*) is established; that is to say, the five [bases] appropriate the conditioned phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava*), while all six together appropriate those without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the eleven bases of conformity (*anukūla-sthāna*), this refers to neutral, defiled, or wholesome manifest, seed, or formative factors (*saṃskāra*) that can conform to similar or superior categories of phenomena; it is precisely based on these bases that the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) is established.
This means that it is capable of giving rise to similar and superior practices and is capable of inducing unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas.

Regarding the twelve bases for differentiated functional capacities: conditioned dharmas each possess a specific power to give rise to and realize their own respective results; it is based on this that the cause of "determination" (*pratiniyama-hetu*) is established, meaning that each is able to produce its own results within its respective realm and so forth, and each is able to attain the fruits of its own vehicle.

The thirteenth is the basis of harmony (*sāmagrī-adhiṣṭhāna*), which refers to the bases ranging from "reception" (*anubhava*) to "distinctive function" (*viśeṣa-karman*). Within the process of the production, abiding, accomplishment, and attainment of a result, there is a power of harmony; it is upon this basis that the "cause of common purpose" (*ekārtha-hetu*) is established. This means that from "contingency" (*apekṣā*) through "specific determination" (*pratiniyama*), all share the same activity, such as arising and so forth.

The fourteen bases of obstruction refer to those factors that can obstruct the processes of arising, abiding, accomplishing, and attaining; it is based on these bases that the "contradictory cause" (*viruddha-hetu*) is established, because they are able to contradict such processes as arising and so forth.

The fifteenth is the basis of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa-adhiṣṭhāna*), which refers to those factors that do not obstruct the processes of arising, abiding, accomplishment, and attainment; it is upon this basis that the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*) is established, because those factors do not contradict the processes of arising and so forth.
Thus, these ten causes are subsumed under two types:
first, the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*), and second, the instrumental cause (*upāya-hetu*).

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that the "projecting seed" (*ākṣepaka-bīja*) and the "actualizing seed" (*abhinirvartaka-bīja*) are called the productive cause, while all remaining causes are subsumed under the instrumental cause.

This explains the various causal seeds among attraction (*ākṣepa*), production (*abhinirvṛtti*), leading forth (*āvāhaka*), determination (*pratiniyama*), simultaneous action (*ekakāryatva*), and non-contradiction (*avirodha*): those in the stage of non-maturation are called seeds of attraction, while those in the stage of maturation are called seeds of production.
Because all seeds of the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) among those six causes are subsumed within these two categories, we have omitted them here;
for apart from those that actually arise, they are "generative causes" (*janaka-hetu*), such as the four causes that produce their own seeds, yet these are frequently interrupted.
Alternatively, even that which directly produces a result may be designated by the term "seed," as when one speaks of the seeds of currently manifesting rice or wheat.

As for the remaining causes—namely the first, second, fifth, and ninth, as well as those among the six causes that are not *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions)—these are all the remainder of the seeds of the productive and ripening conditions; therefore, they are collectively said to be subsumed under the category of the "expedient cause" (*upāya-hetu*).
These two types do not belong exclusively to those two causes, because among the other four causes there are also seeds that function as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
Nor are those eight [causes] exclusively what is termed "remaining causes" (*avaśeṣa-hetu*), for even those two [primary] causes include factors that are not causal conditions.

The *Savitarkādi-bhūmi* states that the "cause of origination" (*janana-hetu*) is the "productive cause" (*janaka-hetu*), while the others are subsumed under the category of "expedient means" (*upāya*).

The meaning of this passage is that among the six causes, those seeds and manifest phenomena that constitute the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) are all termed "causes of origination," because they can directly produce their own corresponding results.

These remaining causes are all subsumed under the category of expedient means; it is not that this arising belongs exclusively to those [nine] causes, because among the other five causes there are also causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
It is not only those nine that are called "remaining causes," because within those arising causes there are factors that are not causal conditions.
Alternatively, the seeds of attraction and production mentioned in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* correspond to those two causes; the remaining causes correspond to the other eight.

Although within these two causes there are factors that are not productive causes (*janakahetu*), they are specifically mentioned here because the seeds of the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) are predominant and manifest.
Although among the other causes there are those that are not "causes of application" (*prayoga-hetu*), they are mentioned specifically because the predominant ones are most clearly manifest.

In the *Savitarkādi-bhūmi*, it is stated that the "cause of origination" (*utpatti-hetu*) is the "productive cause" (*janaka-hetu*), while the others are "causes of application. One should understand that "origination" here refers precisely to that "cause of origination," and the "other causes" refer to the remaining nine causes.
Although the seeds of causal conditions exist within the projecting [karma] (*ākṣepaka*), they are not mentioned because they are distant from the fruit and thus remain hidden;

whereas although the seeds of causal conditions do not exist within the actualizing [karma] (*abhinirvartaka*), they are mentioned specifically because they are proximate to the fruit and thus made manifest.
The inclusion of other skillful means should be understood by analogy with what has been stated above.
Upon what basis are the four conditions established as taught?
Furthermore, how are they subsumed within the ten causes and the two causes?

The treatise states that causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya) are established based on seeds; immediately preceding conditions (samanantara-pratyaya) are established based on what has ceased without interval; objective conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) are established based on the object; and dominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya) are established based on the remainder.
Among these, the seeds are subsumed under the causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya) within the bases (āśraya) numbered three, four, eleven, twelve, thirteen, fifteen, and sixteen.
Although these four stages also have causes and conditions, they are frequently interrupted; therefore, they are not mentioned here in brief.
Alternatively, even those [stages] can directly produce their own results—just as external things such as barley are—and thus may also be designated by the name "seed."
Alternatively, the term "seed" may apply exclusively to the fourth [condition], with the distinctions of directness or indirectness, and concealment or manifestation, as previously described.

Regarding the statement that the "immediately preceding cessation" and the "object" constitute the bases, one should understand that this collectively indicates that the bases for the two conditions are not limited to five or six; for within the remaining bases, there also exists the sense of the two intermediate conditions.
Alternatively, there may be only five or six; although they exist in other contexts, they are omitted here because they are somewhat obscure.

The treatise states that the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is subsumed under the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*); the nature of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is the instrumental cause (*upāya-hetu*); and the two intermediate conditions are subsumed under the supportive cause (*parigraha-hetu*).
Although the means (*upāya*) internally possesses the latter three conditions, it is predominant; therefore, it is specifically mentioned here.
The other causes also possess the two intermediate conditions, but because they are manifested within "appropriation" (*parigraha*), they are specifically mentioned there.
Regarding the initial capacity to produce [results], the inclusion and exclusion are as previously stated; the causes and conditions that have been explained must necessarily have results.
How many such results are there?
In what locations are they obtained?
There are five kinds of results:

first, the ripened result (*vipāka*), which refers to the indeterminate states produced by maturation (*vipākaja*) within one's own continuum, brought about by contaminated wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.

Second, the outflowing result (*niṣyanda*), which refers to that which is drawn forth as a similar type through the practice of wholesome [dharmas] and so forth, or that which follows along as a subsequent fruit resembling its prior karma.

Third is disjunction (*visamyoga*), which refers to the wholesome unconditioned phenomena (*asamskṛta-dharma*) realized through the abandonment of hindrances by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Fourth is human effort (*puruṣakāra*), which refers to the tasks accomplished by various agents employing various instruments.
Fifth is the predominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), which refers to the fruits obtained other than the preceding four.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state that the basis of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) yields the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*); the conforming basis yields the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*); the basis of true vision yields the fruit of disjunction (*visamyogaphala*); the basis of human effort yields the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*); and the remaining bases yield the predominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

The term "locus of habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā-sthāna*) indicates all the functional capacities of the various bases for producing the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*); the term "locus of conformity" (*anuvṛtti-sthāna*) indicates all the functional capacities of the various bases for drawing forth the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*); the term "locus of true vision" (*samyag-darśana-sthāna*) indicates all the functional capacities of the various bases for realizing the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*); the term "locus of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-sthāna*) indicates all the functional capacities of the various bases for bringing about the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); and the term "remaining loci" indicates all the functional capacities of the various bases for obtaining the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Otherwise, [the definition] would be either too broad or too narrow.

Alternatively, if one holds that "habitual tendencies" (vāsanā) belong exclusively to the third category, even though they exist elsewhere as maturation causes (*vipāka-hetu*), and although there are maturation causes in this context that are not habitual tendencies, the habitual tendency is mentioned here specifically because it is distant from its fruit in the same manner as a maturation cause.

Conformity (anuloma) belongs exclusively to the eleventh base (*āyatana*). Although its result of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) may be obtained in other bases, and this base may also obtain results that are not of outflow, it is the cause for this [base] that brings about a particularly distinguished mode of activity; since conformity is likewise so, it is mentioned specifically.

The statement that the "true locus of vision" (*samyagdarśana*) refers exclusively to the tenth stage is because, although the realization of dissociation (*visamyoga*) can also occur in other stages, and this stage can also attain what is not dissociation, it is specifically mentioned here because the characteristic of realizing dissociation is most manifest at this point.

The term "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) refers exclusively to the ninth [ground]. Although the fruit of human effort is also produced in other stages, and this stage can likewise produce the fruits of increase (*adhipati-phala*) and so forth, the name and its characteristics are most prominent here; therefore, it is specifically mentioned.

The remaining [results] belong exclusively to the other eleven bases (*āyatana*). Although these eleven bases can also obtain other results, and other bases are also capable of producing the dominant result (*adhipatiphala*), it is because these eleven predominantly produce the dominant result—and since the others have already been explained—the former are mentioned specifically here.

Thus, among these five fruits, it is said that the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala) is obtained through the projecting cause (ākṣepakahetu), the producing cause (abhinirvartakahetu), the determinative cause (pratiniyamahetu), the simultaneous cause (sahabhūhetu), the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu), and the non-obstructing cause (avighnahetu), as well as through the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya).

If it is the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), it is obtained through the conditions of the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), the producing cause (*abhinirvartaka-hetu*), the supporting cause (*parigrahaka-hetu*), the inducing cause (*āvāhaka-hetu*), the specific cause (*pratiniyama-hetu*), the concurrent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the non-contradictory cause (*avirodha-hetu*), as well as the initial and final conditions.

If it is the disconnection fruit (*visamyoga-phala*), it is obtained through the conditions of the supporting cause, the inducing cause, the specific cause, the concurrent cause, and the non-contradictory cause, as well as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Regarding the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*), according to one interpretation, it is obtained through the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) by depending upon the causes of appropriation (*parigraha*), simultaneous action (*sahabhū*), and non-contradiction (*aviruddha*).

According to another interpretation, it is obtained through the remaining three conditions—excluding the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)—by depending upon the causes of attraction (*ākṣepa*), production (*abhinirvṛtti*), appropriation (*parigraha*), induction (*āvāhaka*), specific determination (*pratiniyama*), simultaneous action (*sahabhū*), and non-contradiction (*aviruddha*).
If it concerns the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), it may be obtained from all ten causes and four conditions.
This concludes the ancillary discussion; one should now analyze the primary treatise.

Within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), seeds can function as three conditions to produce manifest conceptualization (*vikalpa*), excluding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

That is to say, one's own respective seeds are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for them; as for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), they serve as the objective support for that which cognizes.
If the seeds provide assistance or do not obstruct them, they constitute the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
It should be understood that the same applies to the manifestation of pure [phenomena].
When manifesting conceptualizations are mutually related, they can serve as three conditions, excluding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That is to say, among sentient beings, self and others may mutually serve as two conditions, with the exception of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

When the eight groups of consciousness are mutually compared, they definitely possess the condition of predominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*), but they necessarily lack the condition of equal and immediate antecedence (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

As for the meaning of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it may or may not exist: the eighth [consciousness] exists as such for the [other] seven, but the seven do not exist as such for the eighth, because the remaining seven are not the objective substrata relied upon by the eighth.
The seventh [consciousness] exists in relation to six [objects], while five exist and one does not; the remaining six do not exist at all in relation to it.

The sixth [consciousness] does not exist in relation to five, while the remaining five do exist in relation to it, because the five consciousnesses rely solely upon the eighth [consciousness] as their objective aspect (*nimitta*).

Within its own class, the sixth [consciousness] may have three types of objects across preceding and succeeding moments; for the others, with the exception of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), they apprehend only present objects.

If one accepts that the five [sensory consciousnesses] perceive past characteristics, then the seventh [mental consciousness] and the five [sensory consciousnesses] also possess three conditions across preceding and succeeding moments.
The first seven [consciousnesses] can serve as perfumers for the eighth, as they establish the seeds of its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).

Although they are of different entities within the same aggregate, when viewed in relation to one another, they possess only the *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition), because the substantial bases relied upon by all associated mental factors (*samprayukta-dharma*) are identical and thus do not take one another as objects.

Alternatively, it is said that they do not mutually take one another as objects from the perspective of the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect), whereas from the perspective of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), there is the sense of mutual objectification.

This means that various objective aspects arise by taking each other as their substantial cause (*ālambana-pratyaya*). For example, the seeds within consciousness serve as the substantial cause for the objective aspects of contact (*sparśa*) and so forth; otherwise, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), those [objective aspects] would lack an object.

Even if it is granted that the transformation of color necessarily depends on seeds, let there be no confusion regarding the fact that the objects of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) do not share the same substance;

for the seeing-part and its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), which are of one essence, function as two conditions, while the seeing-part exercises only a dominant influence (*adhipati-pratyaya*) over the latter.
The relationship between the seeing [nature] and self-cognition is likewise.
As for the remaining two, they mutually serve as both types of conditions.
Here, this is not explained based on seeds or the object-aspect (nimitta-bhāga), but rather speaks only of how the manifest states act as mutual conditions for one another.

Within the purified collection of the eight consciousnesses, both self and other are mutually related and all possess objects of cognition (*ālambana*), because they are capable of universal cognition.

This excludes only the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), which does not take the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object; for logically, the image-part lacks the functional capacity to act as a cognizer.
Since manifest discrimination arises by taking seeds and manifest phenomena as conditions, it stands to reason that seeds likewise arise by taking manifest phenomena and seeds as conditions.
How many conditions can manifest phenomena and seeds act as for seeds?
Seeds certainly do not arise from the two intermediate conditions, because those two are established only in dependence upon the mind and mental factors.
The manifest [seed] acts as both conditions for its own kindred seeds, whereas it serves only as a dominant condition for those that are not its kindred.
Likewise, a seed in relation to its own kindred seeds possesses both conditions, while in relation to those that are not its kindred, it also serves only as a dominant condition.
Based on this internal consciousness, where mutual conditioning gives rise to the differentiation of cause and effect, both principle and scripture are established.

Since the external conditions you cling to are useless even if they existed, how much more so when they contradict both principle and scripture; why then do you stubbornly persist in clinging to them?

Although this general classification collectively reveals the minds and mental factors of the three realms, the various sacred teachings display them through many approaches according to their predominant characteristics, sometimes describing them as two, three, four, five, and so forth, as is fully and extensively analyzed in other treatises.
If there is only internal consciousness and no external objects, by what means does the continuity of birth and death for sentient beings occur?
The verse says: 19.
Due to the habitual tendencies of various karmas, together with the habitual tendencies of the two types of grasping, [the continuum persists].
When the previous maturation has been exhausted, another maturation arises again.
The treatise says:
"All karmas" refers to merit, non-merit, and the imperturbable; that is, the karma of volition (*cetanā*) which is either contaminated wholesome or unwholesome.
The attendants of karma are also designated by the name "karma," because they likewise bring about the ripening fruits of projection and fulfillment.

Although these [attendants] perish immediately after arising and possess no capacity to project a future ripening fruit, they perfume the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) to give rise to their own functional capacities; it is these very capacities that are called "habitual tendencies" (vāsanā).
This is formed by the perfuming of the karmic energy-portion (*karma-vāsanā*); it is termed "habitual energy" (*vāsanā*) to distinguish it from past and present karma.

Such habitual energy continues in a successive stream until, at the time of maturation, it brings about the fruit of ripening (*vipāka-phala*). This demonstrates that [the ālayavijñāna] is the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the future fruit; both the grasped-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as well as the primary and secondary aspects of that grasping, are all subsumed under the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).

The capacity, directly produced by that which has been perfumed, which is able to generate that very fundamental consciousness, is called the "habitual energy of the two graspings. This indicates the seeds of the causes and conditions for the mind of the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) in a future life, as well as the various factors associated with it.
"Both" refers to the coexistence of the seeds of karma and the seeds of the two types of grasping; this signifies that these distant and proximate conditions mutually assist one another.
Because karma gives rise to manifest birth, it is mentioned first in the verse.
"The preceding maturation" refers to the karmic maturation fruits of successive previous lives.
As for the remaining maturation (*vipāka*), it refers to the karmic maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*) of successive future births.
Although the seeds of the two grasps (*dvaya-grāha*) result in an inexhaustible experience of fruition, the experience of fruition resulting from karmic habit-energies (*vāsanā*) has an end.

Because it is difficult for a maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) to be produced from a different gender, whereas it is easy for a flow-on fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) and a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) to be induced when their natures are the same.

Since the seeds of various types of karma that induce future lives ripen, when the previously acquired maturation fruit has been fully experienced, they are further able to produce other distinct maturation fruits.
Because of this, the cycle of birth and death revolves without end; why rely on external conditions for its continuity?

The meaning of this verse is that the saṃsāric cycle of birth and death does not exist apart from consciousness, because the mind and mental factors constitute its very nature. This is due to karma and the two types of grasping.
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). These habitual tendencies are, in brief, of three kinds:
first, the habitual tendency of names and words (*nāma-vāsanā*), which refers to the specific, individual seeds of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
There are two types of conventional designation (*nāma-vyavahāra*):
first, the designation that expresses meaning, which refers to the specific distinctions of vocal sounds that signify meanings;
second, the designation that manifests objects, which refers to the mind and mental factors that cognize objects.
The seeds perfumed by the two types of linguistic expression act as the individual causes and conditions for conditioned phenomena.
The two types of habitual tendencies of self-grasping refer to the seeds of the false attachment to a self and what belongs to a self.
There are two types of self-grasping:
first, innate self-grasping, which is the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self that is abandoned through cultivation;
second, conceptual self-grasping, which is the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self that is abandoned through insight.
The seeds perfumed by the two types of self-grasping cause the distinction between self and others among sentient beings and so forth.
The habitual tendencies of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*) refer to the karmic seeds that bring about maturation (*vipāka*) within the three realms.
The members of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) are twofold:
first, tainted wholesome [karma], which is the karma capable of inviting desirable results;
second, all unwholesome [karma], which is the karma capable of inviting undesirable results.

In accordance with the seeds perfumed by the two branches of existence (*bhava-aṅga*), they cause the distinction between the various realms of rebirth (*gati*) within the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*).

One should understand that self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*), the branches of existence, and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) serve as the dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for these differentiated fruits.
Regarding the "karmic habitual tendencies" mentioned in this verse, one should understand that these are precisely the habitual tendencies of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

One should understand that the "habitual tendencies of the two types of grasping" (*dvaya-upādāna-vāsanā*) are precisely the two kinds of habitual tendencies: those of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) and those of linguistic expression (*nāma-kāya*). Because they are perfumed by grasping at "self" and "mine," as well as by grasping at linguistic expressions, they are all termed "grasping."
The meaning of the remaining text, including the word "all" (*sarva*), is as explained previously.
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) proceeds by means of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*).

The afflictions that initiate karma and moisten rebirth are called "afflictions"; the various karmas capable of inducing future existence are called "karma"; and the manifold sufferings drawn forth by karma are called "suffering."
The seeds of delusion, karma, and suffering are all termed *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies).
The first two types of *vāsanā* serve as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the suffering of birth and death, as they assist in the production of that suffering.
The third type of *vāsanā*, in relation to the suffering of birth and death, functions as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), as it directly gives rise to that suffering.
The three types of habitual tendencies (vāsanās) should be understood according to the verses.
Afflictions and suffering are termed "grasping" (upādāna) because they constitute the grasper and the grasped.
"Grasping" carries the sense of attachment; thus, karma does not receive this name.
The meaning of the remaining text, including the word "all" (*sarva*), is as explained previously.

It should be understood that these afflictions, karmas, and sufferings collectively subsume the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), namely from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), as extensively explained in the treatise.
However, the twelve links are briefly subsumed into four categories:

first, the projecting factors (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*), namely ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), because they project the seeds for the five effects, beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Among these, ignorance refers exclusively to that which can incite the performance of wholesome or unwholesome karma that will truly result in future lives.
That which is thus produced is what is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*).
For this reason, all karma to be experienced in the present life and all auxiliary karma for future lives are not the member of "volitional formations.

Regarding the two members that are "projected," these refer to the five types [of aggregates], beginning with consciousness, which are comprised within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and directly produce the future matured fruit (*vipākaphala*), because they are projected by the preceding two members.
In this context, the "seed of consciousness" refers to the cause of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Excluding the latter three causes, all other causes are subsumed within the seed of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
As for the latter three causes, they correspond respectively to the latter three types mentioned in the sequence of names.
Alternatively, "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) subsumes all five causes; within this, the other four types are established according to their predominance.
The same applies to the relationship between the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), whether taken collectively or individually.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that consciousness is also the seed of karma within the projecting consciousness, and is thus designated as the limb of "consciousness" (*vijñāna-anga*); furthermore, the seeds of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) are subsumed under "name-and-form."

The Sūtra states that the *vijñāna* link encompasses both the seeds of the projecting karma and the projected karma, as both are designated by the term "consciousness. Furthermore, consciousness is the support for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), yet it is not itself subsumed under name-and-form.

Although the five factors beginning with consciousness are in reality simultaneous due to being impelled by karma, the various sacred teachings provisionally describe them as sequential because they differ in terms of principal and attendant, general and particular, superior and inferior, and cause and effect.
Alternatively, because there is a sequence in the stages of their future arising, it is said that they have priority and posteriority.
For this reason, consciousness and the other factors are also said to be "active" (*samudācāra*), since at the time of being a cause, they necessarily lack the state of being active.
Furthermore, it is by virtue of this teaching that production and projection occur simultaneously; for the stages of being moistened and not yet moistened cannot possibly coexist.
The three factors capable of producing [the result] are craving, grasping, and existence, as they directly give rise to future birth, aging, and death.

This means that, conditioned by the delusion regarding internal maturation (*vipāka-phala*), one initiates various karmas capable of truly summoning future existence. Having acted as the condition to trigger and directly produce the seeds of the five results in the states of birth, aging, and death in the future, one then relies on the delusion regarding external dominant results (*adhipati-phala*) to give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) based on the experience of objects. Conditioned by this craving, the four types of grasping (*upādāna*), such as sensual desire, arise again. The combination of craving and grasping moistens the seeds of projecting karma and the causes of the projected [results], which are then designated as "existence" (*bhava*). Both are so called because they are able to bring about the immediate presence of the results of future existence.
In some places, only the seeds of karma are called "existence" (*bhava*), because these are what directly bring about the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Furthermore, in other places, only the five [aggregates] are called "existence," because they are the seeds that directly produce future consciousness and so forth.

The four "resultant members" (phala-aṅga) are birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarā-maraṇa*), because they are what is produced in close proximity to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*).

That is to say, from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until one reaches the fundamental existence (*maula-bhava*) before undergoing decay and transformation, all are subsumed under the member of birth; all stages of decay and transformation are collectively termed "old age," while the breaking up of the body and the end of life are termed "death."
Old age is not necessarily present; it is established as a factor in conjunction with death.
Why is illness not also a factor?
Because it is neither universal nor certain.

Although old age is not universal, it is established as a link because it is pervasive; for among all realms, destinies, and births—excluding those who die prematurely—all possess the process of decay as they approach their end.
Why, then, is name-and-form (nāmarūpa) established as a link when it is not universal?

The factors are established based on their fixed occurrence; for those born from a womb, an egg, or moisture, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are not yet complete until name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) has definitely arisen.

Furthermore, the factor of name-and-form is also universally present; even in the initial stage of birth for those of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*) who possess form, although the five faculties are complete, they have not yet become functional, and at that time they are not yet designated as the factor of the six sense bases.
Although those born in the formless realm certainly possess the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*), it is not clear and thus cannot yet be designated as the "mind-base" (*mana-āyatana*).
For this reason, the treatise states that all twelve links of dependent origination exist, at least partially, within the two higher realms.
Since craving is not present everywhere, why establish it as a distinct factor?
Those born in the evil realms do not crave them.
It is established as distinct because of its certainty; for those born in the good realms, craving is invariably present, whereas they do not seek non-existence.
One who has attained the stage of non-return does not moisten rebirth; although craving does not arise [in them], there is nonetheless a seed of it, just as with grasping.
Furthermore, craving is also universal, for even those born in the evil destinies possess craving toward their present objects of self-identity.
Based on the absence of craving for a body in the miserable realms (*apāya*), the Sūtra states that [craving] does not exist there; it does not mean that it is entirely non-existent.
For what reason are birth and old age and death established as being produced [by existence], while the five members beginning with consciousness are separately established as being projected?
Because the distinct characteristics of the causal stage are difficult to discern, five members are established separately based on the perspective of the future resultant stage.

That is to say: at the time of rebirth-linking, the characteristic of consciousness as a cause becomes manifest; next, while the sense faculties are not yet complete, the characteristic of name-and-form increases; next, when the sense faculties are complete, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) flourish; based upon these, contact arises, and from contact, sensation (vedanā) is produced; it is at that point that the fruition of sensation is said to be consummated.

Based on this resultant state (*phala-avasthā*), five factors are established as causes; for the distinctions of the resultant state are easily understood, two members are established in total to manifest the three types of suffering (*tri-duḥkha*).
However, if the resulting fruit is yet to come in the future, "birth," "aging," and "death" are taught in order to engender revulsion;
if it has reached the present, the five factors beginning with "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are taught to allow for the understanding of how the stages (*avasthā*) arise sequentially.
For what reason is ignorance established as the general factor for initiating karma, while craving and grasping are established separately for the stage of moistening karma?

Although all afflictions are capable of both initiating and moistening karma, the power of ignorance is predominant at the stage of initiating karma because it possesses eleven superior characteristics—namely, its object and so forth—as explained at length in the sūtras.

In the stage of moistening karma, the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) predominates; craving is said to be like water because it can irrigate and moisten. Only through repeated watering can the sprout of existence (*bhava*) arise.
Thus, based on the initial and final stages, craving and grasping (*upādāna*) are distinguished as two, while ignorance (*avidyā*) is established as one, as it lacks the sense of repeated arousal.

Although all afflictions are subsumed within the "appropriation" link (*upādāna*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is predominant in its capacity to moisten and nourish; therefore, it is said that craving increases.

All links of dependent origination depend upon their own respective levels (*svabhūmi*); however, there are cases where formative action (*saṃskāra*) is initiated based on the ignorance (*avidyā*) of another level, such as when the ignorance of a lower level initiates formative action of a higher level.

If that were not the case, then the higher meditative absorption (dhyāna) produced by one who has first suppressed the defilements of a lower stage would not constitute the limb of "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*), because ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to that [lower] stage has not yet arisen.

Furthermore, for one who descends from a higher stage to a lower stage or ascends from a lower stage to a higher stage, upon what kind of feeling (*vedanā*) would they base the limb of "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*)?
That craving also takes as its object the feeling of the future birth, whether in its manifest state or as a seed; this does not contradict reason.

Among these twelve links, ten causes and two fruits are necessarily of different lifetimes. Within the causes, the first seven may either be of a different lifetime from craving, grasping, and becoming, or they may be of the same lifetime; however, if [craving] consists of two, three, or seven [links], each is necessarily of the same lifetime.

Thus, these twelve factors in a single layer of cause and effect are sufficient to manifest cyclic existence and to avoid the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; to establish two layers would be truly useless, or else one might exceed this and fall into infinite regress.

Regarding these twelve links, when distinguished by their conceptual categories, nine are real and three are provisional: because the six links already moistened by craving are combined to constitute "existence" (bhava), and because the five links beginning with consciousness are designated as "birth" (jāti) and so forth based on the distinctions between the three phases of the [three] characteristics.
Five [links] constitute a single category: namely, ignorance, consciousness, contact, feeling, and craving; the remaining [links] do not constitute a single category.

This is because three [links] are exclusively of the nature of defiled afflictions (*kleśa*), seven are exclusively non-defiled maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*), and within the stages of the seven [links], the arising of defilement is possible.
The provisional designation applies to both; the remaining [factors] apply to both types.
Ignorance, craving, and grasping are called "distinctive characteristics" because they do not intermingle with other members; the others are "mixed characteristics."

Six factors are exclusively non-material (arūpa), namely: ignorance (avidyā), consciousness (vijñāna), contact (sparśa), feeling (vedanā), craving (tṛṣṇā), and grasping (upādāna). The remaining factors pertain to both categories.

All of them are with-outflow (sāsrava) and are comprised within the conditioned (saṃskṛta); those that are without-outflow (anāsrava) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) are not members of the [twelve] links because they do not constitute the conditions for existence.

Ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) pertain exclusively to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*); formations (*saṃskāra*) pertain exclusively to the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the unwholesome; existence (*bhava*) pertains to both the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*); and the remaining seven members pertain exclusively to the unobscured-unspecified.
Within the seven stages, both wholesome and defiled states also arise; although these all pertain to the three realms, they may be either partial or complete.

The factors of the higher stages can suppress those of the lower stages—namely, the six modes of activity such as "coarseness" and "suffering"—because one may give rise to them while seeking rebirth in a higher realm.
All such [actions] arise solely from non-learner and learner noble ones (*ārya*).
Because these tainted wholesome karmas take clear knowledge (*vidyā*) as their condition and oppose the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), they are not subsumed under the links of existence.

From this, it should be understood that noble ones (ārya) certainly do not perform karma that brings about rebirth in future existence, because they are neither deluded nor seek such future results of suffering.

There is no contradiction in principle regarding the fact that by utilizing the preparatory stages of meditative concentration (dhyāna), one is born in the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) and so forth through the assistance of prior karma.

One interpretation holds that ignorance (*avidyā*) is abandoned only through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*), because it must be deluded regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*) in order to initiate the performance of karma; furthermore, a noble one (*ārya*) never creates karma for future existence.
The two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), because they seek future existence and thereby moisten rebirth.
The nine types of mind at the moment of death are associated with the craving that arises simultaneously [with them]; the remaining nine are all common to both the paths of seeing and cultivation.

According to one interpretation, all of them are common to both types of abandonment, because the treatise states that while those in the fruit of stream-entry have abandoned a portion of all the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*), there is no one who has abandoned them entirely.
If the link of ignorance were to be abandoned solely by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), how could it be said that a stream-enterer has not completely abandoned it?
If the links of craving and grasping were to be abandoned solely by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), how could it be said that he has already abandoned one portion of all the links?

Furthermore, it is taught that all afflictions (*kleśa*) throughout the entire realm (*dhātu*) are capable of linking birth (*pratisandhi*). While the formations leading to rebirth in evil destinies (*durgati-gāmi-saṃskāra*) are initiated solely by afflictions arising from discrimination (*vikalpa*), it is not stated that those which moisten rebirth (*janma-sneha*) are exclusively abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Since all formations that induce future existence (*punarbhava*) are initiated by those abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*), it is known from this that the three members—ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—also pertain to both what is abandoned through insight and what is abandoned through cultivation.
However, regarding the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*), that which directly instigates [the process] is abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), while its auxiliaries are not fixed.

Regarding the two factors of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), that which directly moistens rebirth is abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), while their auxiliaries are not fixed.
Furthermore, afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*) should be abandoned by their very nature, because they are permanently severed when their antidote arises.
All contaminated (*sāsrava*) non-afflicted phenomena are not to be abandoned by nature, as they do not contradict the Path.

However, there are two senses in which it is described as "abandonment": first, because of being freed from bondage, meaning that the afflictions which take that [object] as their condition and are associated with it are abandoned;
second, because of non-arising, meaning that the basis for those [afflictions] is abandoned so that they never arise again.
Based on abandonment through detachment (*vairāgya-prahāṇa*), it is said that tainted wholesome states and non-obscured neutral states are abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Based on abandonment through non-arising (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*), it is said that the evil destinies, the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), and so forth, are abandoned only by seeing (*darśana-heya*).
Regarding the statement that the twelve links pertain to both types of abandonment, one should understand this as appropriate for each of the aforementioned abandonments.
Ten are associated with pleasure and equanimity, because feeling does not co-associate with itself.

Because in the stage of old age and death there is mostly no pleasure and it admits of equanimity (*upekṣā*), it is associated with eleven types of suffering (*duḥkha*) rather than with feeling (*vedanā*).

Eleven of these are partially subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); however, since there is mostly no pleasant feeling in the stage of old age and death, and because the suffering of change is established in dependence upon pleasure, it is not mentioned here.
Twelve [links] are partially subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), because there is the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*) within all the members.

Twelve [links] are entirely subsumed under the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), because all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are the suffering of conditioned formations.

Based on the neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*), it is said that eleven [links] constitute a portion of suffering; excluding the link of aging-and-death as explained in the context of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), this is the actual meaning.

In various scriptural teachings, the descriptions vary according to the predominance of specific characteristics, yet they are all subsumed within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), because their nature is that of the appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*).
The five [factors] are also subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), because they are of the nature of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).

When the various members (*aṅga*) are compared with one another, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) definitely exists; as for the remaining three conditions, their presence or absence is indeterminate.
The Sūtra, relying on meditative concentration, states that there is only one [link].
There is the sense of being a causal condition (*nidāna*) when craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is viewed in relation to grasping (*upādāna*), and when existence (*bhava*) is viewed in relation to birth (*jāti*).

If it were said that the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the seed of karma, then volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) would likewise act as a causal condition for consciousness; however, for the other links viewed in relation to one another, there is no sense of being a causal condition.

As for the statement in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* that ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) for formative forces (*saṃskāra*), this is said with reference to the karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) of action at the time of ignorance.
Because they coexist with ignorance, they are metaphorically designated as "ignorance," though in reality they are the seeds of formative forces.

When the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the various members [of dependent origination] lack the condition of direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) when viewed in relation to one another, this is based on the teaching that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are present only as the existence of karma (*karma-bhava*).

However, ignorance (*avidyā*) in relation to formative forces (*saṃskāra*), craving in relation to grasping, and birth (*jāti*) in relation to aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) possess the other two conditions.
Birth depends on becoming, and clinging depends on craving; they possess the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but lack the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
When other members are compared with one another, both [conditions] are absent.
This explanation is based, for the time being, on the actual dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that is proximate, sequential, and non-confused.
When these are viewed in relation to one another, their functioning as conditions is not fixed; those who are wise should reflect upon this according to reason.

Regarding the inclusion of the twelve factors within the three categories of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*): ignorance, craving, and grasping are subsumed under afflictions; formations (*saṃskāra*) and a portion of existence (*bhava*) are subsumed under karma; and seven factors and a portion of existence are subsumed under suffering.
Where it is said that karma fully encompasses existence (*bhava*), one should know that this is stated with reference to *karmabhava*.
Where it is said that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is subsumed under karma, that is because the seeds of karma are designated as the limb of consciousness.
That which is summoned by delusion and karma is designated solely as "suffering" because it is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) for the purpose of engendering revulsion.
Since delusion, karma, and suffering constitute the twelve links [of dependent origination], these are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.
Furthermore, the continuity of birth and death arises from internal causes and conditions and does not depend on external conditions; therefore, there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
"Cause" refers to the two types of karma—impure (*sāsrava*) and pure (*anāsrava*)—which directly induce birth and death, and are thus designated as the cause.
The "conditions" (pratyaya) refer to the two obstacles—the afflictive and the cognitive—which assist in bringing about birth and death; therefore, they are called conditions.
Why is this so? Because there are two kinds of birth and death:

First is birth-and-death by segments (*prādeśika-maraṇa*). This refers to the coarse, heterogeneous maturation fruits (*vipāka-phala*) within the three realms, which are produced by various contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome and unwholesome karmas through the auxiliary power of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Because the duration of one's body and life has fixed limits determined by the force of causes and conditions, it is called "segmented."

Second is the inconceivable death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*). This refers to the subtle, superior fruit of maturation (*vipāka*) induced by uncontaminated karma with conceptual differentiation, which is assisted by the power of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Because the lifespan and body are transformed through the power of compassion and vows, they lack fixed limits; therefore, it is called "transformation."
The uncontaminated concentration and aspiration provide the necessary support for a wondrous efficacy that is difficult to fathom; thus it is called "inconceivable.
It is also termed the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*), because it is accomplished according to one's mental aspirations.
As stated in the sutras: "Just as with grasping as a condition, tainted karma as a cause continues into a future existence, whereby one is born into the three realms of existence;

so too, with the ground of the habituation of ignorance as a condition, untainted karma as a cause gives rise to the three kinds of mind-made bodies for arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who have attained mastery."

It is also called the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), because it is transformed from its original state by the power of untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), just like a magical creation.

As a treatise states: "If the Śrāvaka who has attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) has eternally exhausted future existence (*punarbhava*), how can he realize unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*)?"
One realizes unsurpassed enlightenment by relying on the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), not the retribution body (*vipākakāya*); therefore, this does not contradict reason.

If the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) assisted untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) to bring about birth and death, then those of the two vehicles with fixed natures would not eternally enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, just as ordinary beings are constrained by afflictions (*kleśa*).
How can the Truth of the Path truly cause suffering?
Who says it truly causes it? If not so, how then?

The aspiration of untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) supports tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*), causing the resulting fruit to continue in succession for a long time and to progressively increase in excellence; this is metaphorically termed "inducing" (*ākṣepa*).
When such induction occurs, it is not capable of inducing [the result] alone, but rather does so by relying on the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as a supporting condition.
However, the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) does not obstruct liberation, because it lacks the functional capacity to initiate karma or to nourish rebirth.
What need would there be for it to serve as a condition for experiencing the suffering of saṃsāra?
Its purpose is to realize one's own awakening and to bring benefit and happiness to others.

This refers to those of indeterminate lineage—pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—as well as bodhisattvas who have attained mastery through their great vows; because they have already permanently severed or suppressed the afflictive obstructions (kleśāvaraṇa), they no longer have the possibility of receiving further bodies of future birth-and-death (bhava-saṃskāra-kāya).

Fearing that the long-term cultivation of the bodhisattva path might be interrupted, he then employed the power of aspiration associated with untainted, supreme meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*)—according to the method of prolonging life—to sustain the causes of his present existence, ensuring that his fruit would not cease for a long duration.
By repeatedly receiving such support from their fixed vows, they eventually attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Yet, why would they require the assistance of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?

Since they have not yet fully realized signless great compassion and do not grasp at bodhi or sentient beings as being substantially real, there is no basis for them to give rise to intense compassionate vows.
Furthermore, the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) obstructs great enlightenment; therefore, in order to permanently eliminate it, one retains the body and remains for a long time.

Moreover, the cognitive obscuration serves as the basis for that which is with outflows (sāsrava); if this obscuration were absent, those [outflows] would certainly not exist. Thus, it provides great assistance in the maintenance of the body.

If the retained body is supported by mundane meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) and vows, it is subsumed under the *paricchinna-kāya* (segmental body), as it is an object of knowledge for the two vehicles and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

If it is supported by supramundane meditative concentration and vows (*anāsrava-samādhi-praṇidhāna*), it is subsumed under the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (transformative body), as it is not within their cognitive range.

From this it should be understood that the nature of the death-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa*) is comprised within the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*), while with respect to uncontaminated karma (*anāsravakarma*), it is a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
As for the fact that certain authoritative teachings describe it as being uncontaminated and transcending the three realms, this is stated in accordance with its auxiliary causes.
The "habitual tendencies of various karmas" mentioned in the verse refer to the seeds of the two types of karma previously described.
The "habitual tendencies of the two graspings" refer to the seeds of the two obstacles previously described, because both involve clinging.
The meaning of the remaining text, including the word "both" (*ubhaya*), is as explained previously.

Although the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*) lacks the [coarse] segmentation of the former, and although the distinct maturations (*vipāka*) of the preceding and succeeding moments exhaust themselves and arise anew respectively, it nevertheless involves repeated assistance that causes modification and transition from one state to another; thus, there is also the sense that what preceded has exhausted while something else arises again.
Although the present continuity of birth and death also exists, the seeds are necessarily present; thus, the verse speaks of them specifically.
Alternatively, it is to demonstrate that both the true causes and effects of maturation are inseparable from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that the present is not mentioned.
The manifest ripening cause does not immediately yield its fruit, because the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are intermittent and are not themselves ripening.

Since the cycle of birth and death throughout the past, present, and future does not depend on external conditions but arises from internal consciousness, one should know that the continuity of pure phenomena (*śukladharma*) is likewise so.

This refers to the untainted seeds that have been attached to the fundamental consciousness since beginningless time; through repeated perfuming by the evolving consciousnesses and so forth, they gradually increase in excellence until, at the ultimate stage of attaining Buddhahood, one transforms and abandons the originally defiled seeds of consciousness and transforms and acquires the newly arisen pure seed-consciousness, which sustains all seeds of merit.
By the power of their original vows, they give rise to various sublime functions that continue uninterruptedly throughout the limits of the future.
From this, one should know that there is only internal consciousness.
If there is only consciousness, for what reason did the World-Honored One, in various sūtras, speak of the three natures?
One should know that the three natures are likewise not separate from consciousness. Why is this?
The verse says:
20. Through various forms of conceptualization, one conceptualizes diverse things;
this nature of being conceptually constructed (parikalpita-svabhāva) does not exist at all.
21. The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises from conditions through conceptualization;
the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is that which is eternally devoid of the former nature.
22. Therefore, this [perfected nature] and the dependent nature are neither different nor not different.
"Just as with the nature of impermanence and so forth, it is not the case that one does not see this [nature] in that [object].
The commentary states:
It is called "universal imagination" (*parikalpa*) because it universally and exhaustively conceptualizes.
The categories are numerous and are thus described as "this" or "that.

That is to say, by means of pervasive conceptualization and false discrimination (*parikalpita-vikalpa*), one universally imagines various objects of conceptualization through those very same false discriminations; namely, the self-nature and specific distinctions of the falsely grasped aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, whether they be phenomena (*dharma*) or a self (*ātman*).
This falsely grasped nature and its distinctions are collectively termed the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Such a nature is entirely non-existent, for it cannot be found when investigated through either reasoning or scriptural authority.

Alternatively, the first phrase reveals the consciousness that performs the pervasive imagination (*parikalpaka-vijñāna*), the second phrase indicates the objects that are the basis of pervasive imagination (*parikalpya-viṣaya*), and the latter half of the verse then asserts that the self-nature of both the person (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*)—which are the objects of pervasive imagination—is non-existent, because it has already been extensively demonstrated that they cannot be apprehended.
First, what is the nature of that which is capable of universal imagination (*parikalpa*)?

One interpretation holds that the eight consciousnesses and their associated mental factors (*caitta*), when comprised within the outflowing (*sāsrava*) category, are all capable of universal imagination. This is because they have false discrimination as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because they all manifest as resembling the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*), and because it is taught that the *ālayavijñāna* takes as its objective support (*ālambana*) the seeds of false attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

There is an interpretation that the sixth and seventh mental complexes (*citta-varga*) which grasp at a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*) are the universal constructors (*parikalpa*). This is because it is taught that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of universal construction; because "mind" (*manas*) and "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) are both termed "mental consciousness"; because conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) is capable of universal construction; because those who grasp at a self and phenomena must possess wisdom (*prajñā*); because the two types of grasping necessarily coexist with ignorance (*avidyā*); because it is not taught that ignorance possesses a virtuous nature; because delusion (*moha*) and non-delusion (*amoha*) are not mutually exclusive; because no grasping is seen to lead toward the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*); because grasping at existence and grasping at non-existence do not arise simultaneously; because there has never been a case where grasping is not a perfuming agent (*vāsana*); and because all outflowing minds (*sāsrava-citta*) fail to realize reality. Thus, all these are termed false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*).

Although they appear as if characterized by the grasped and the grasper, they are not all subsumed under the category of the imaginatively constructing consciousness (*parikalpa*), lest even uncontaminated minds (*anāsrava-citta*) possess grasping, and lest the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of a Tathāgata also involve grasping.

The Sūtras state that the Buddha’s wisdom manifests various images, such as bodies and lands, like a mirror and so forth; therefore, if it lacked the function of taking objects as conditions (*ālambana*), it would not be wisdom and the like.

Although it is said that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) takes the seeds of the parikalpita-svabhāva as its conditions, the word "only" (*mātra*) is not used; thus, this is not a conclusive proof.
According to this principle, the capacity for pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) exists only within the sixth and seventh mental categories (*citta-varga*).

Although there are two such categories of consciousness, there are various forms of pervasive conceptualization—differing as two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, and so forth; therefore, it is said to be "this or that" (*tatra-tatra*).
Next, what is the nature of that which is universally conceptualized?

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that it is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mind and other factors involved in universal conceptualization.
How could the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) not be its object?
Because the ultimate is not the objective referent (*ālambana*) of false attachment.
It is also said to be the "universally conceptualized" (*parikalpita*) by way of indirect designation.
Although the thoroughly imagined nature is the object of that [cognition], it is not an objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya); therefore, it is not that which is thoroughly imagined.
What are the characteristics of the thoroughly imagined nature?
How does this differ from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?

According to one interpretation, the minds and mental factors of the three realms, due to false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) accumulated since beginningless time, each possess a single essence yet appear as two: namely, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), which correspond to the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*).
These two aspects exist subjectively but lack objective reality.
This characteristic is termed the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). The substance upon which these two depend is actually produced from conditions;
this nature is not non-existent and is called the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it is produced by conditions through false discrimination.
How is this known to be so?

Various sacred teachings state that false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), while the grasping of duality is termed the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

According to one interpretation, all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), by virtue of the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), manifest as two parts; because they arise from conditions, these too are the dependent nature.
Based upon this [dependent nature], the pervasive imagination falsely clings to it as being definitely real, existent or non-existent, identical or different, both or neither, and so forth;

these two alone are termed the "thoroughly imagined" (parikalpita-svabhāva). For all the holy teachings state that "only the measure," "only the two," and "only the manifold" are all named the "other-dependent" (paratantra-svabhāva).

Furthermore, since the treatises state that the four factors such as "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and the eleven consciousnesses, etc., are all subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*),
it would otherwise follow that the two aspects of the category of untainted subsequently attained wisdom (*anāsrava-prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) should be termed the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
If you grant that noble wisdom does not take those [imagined objects] as its objective condition, then the category of wisdom that takes them as its object should not be the Truth of the Path;
if you do not grant this, one should know that the same applies to contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*).

Furthermore, if these two parts were of the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), they would not function as objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), like a rabbit’s horns and so forth, because the essence of the thoroughly imagined is non-existent.
Furthermore, the two parts [of consciousness] would not be perfumed to form seeds, and subsequently, when the subsequent consciousnesses arise, they should lack these two parts.

Moreover, since all habitual tendencies (vāsanā) are subsumed under the objective division (nimittabhāga), how could it be that there is no dharma capable of acting as a causal condition (hetupratyaya)?

If the internal image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) produced by conditions were not of the nature of the dependent (*paratantra*), then the same would logically apply to the substance that serves as the basis for these two, as there is no difference in their causes.

By this principle, the substance of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) produced by various conditions—whether they consist of the image-part and seeing-part, and whether they are contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—are all of the nature of the dependent, because they arise in dependence upon other conditions.

Regarding the verse’s statement that "that which is produced from conditions is conceptualization," one should understand that this refers for the time being to the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) of the defiled portion; this is because the dependent nature of the pure portion is also the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
Alternatively, all mental states and mental factors—whether defiled or pure—are termed "conceptualization" because they are capable of cognitive apprehension (ālambana).
Thus, all dependent natures (paratantra-svabhāva), whether defiled or pure, are subsumed within this category of the dependent nature.

The perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is the true reality of all phenomena as revealed by the two kinds of emptiness; it is called "perfected" to manifest that its pervasive and eternal essence is not false or erroneous, thereby distinguishing it from self-characteristics, common characteristics, space, the self (ātman), and so forth.

Untainted (anāsrava) conditioned phenomena that are free from inversion and possess ultimate, pervasive excellence also receive this name; however, in the present verse, it refers to the former and not the latter.

This [emptiness] consists in the true suchness (tathatā) revealed by the two absences of self, which is eternally devoid of the previously mentioned thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) upon that other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
The phrase "spoken of as that" indicates that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are neither identical nor separate.
The phrase "permanently remote" indicates that the nature of the grasped and the grasper, which are falsely apprehended, is eternally non-existent in principle.

The preceding discussion on "meaning" (*artha*) clarifies that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not empty; the discussion on "nature" (*svabhāva*) clarifies that the two kinds of emptiness are not the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is by nature free from both existence and non-existence.

For the reasons stated above, this perfected nature is neither different nor non-different from that dependent nature. If they were different, True Suchness would not be the actual nature of the latter; if they were non-different, this nature would have to be impermanent.

If both [the prior and subsequent cognitions] were to take as their objects only that which is neither pure nor impure, then there would be no distinction between the functions of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*).
How, then, could these two natures be neither different nor identical?
It is just like the nature of impermanence, selflessness, and so forth.

If the nature of impermanence and so forth were different from the phenomena such as conditioned forces (*saṃskāra*), those phenomena would not be impermanent and so on; if they were not different, then this [nature] could not be their universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
By means of this analogy, it is shown that this perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and that dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are neither identical nor different.
The principle of phenomena and their true nature must necessarily be so, for they exist in mutual dependence as the ultimate and the conventional.
