Second is the concentration of the King who Accumulates Merit (*puṇyasaṃbhārarāja-samādhi*), because this sovereign accumulates boundless merit, possessing a power like that of a king which is without equal;
third is the concentration of the Virtuous Guardian (*satpuruṣarakṣa-samādhi*), because this can guard the virtuous and wholesome dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms;
fourth is the concentration of the Heroic Practice (*vikrāntagāmin-samādhi*), because it is the practice of the great heroic beings, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
These four objects of focus function as antidotes and are capable of inducing their respective activities, as explained in other passages.
There are three types of training in wisdom (*prajñā-śikṣā*):

first, non-conceptual wisdom of application (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-prajñā*); second, fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-prajñā*); and third, subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-nirvikalpa-prajñā*).
The bases, causes, conditions, objects, and modes of activity of these three natures are as explained in other passages.
Regarding these three types of wisdom, in the first two stages, all three exist as seeds, while in the present state, only the wisdom of application exists.

In the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), there are two manifest [forms] and three seeds; this is because there is no preparatory effort (*prayoga*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

In the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), prior to the seventh ground, both seeds and manifestations are common to all three types; from the eighth ground onward, there are two manifest [forms] and three seeds, because the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*) is contrary to preparatory effort.
All progress toward [the goal] is accomplished by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), because it arises spontaneously within untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā*).

In the state of ultimate perfection (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*), both the manifest and the seeds are of two kinds, because both the manifest and the seeds of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) have already been abandoned.

If categorized by their essential nature (*svabhāva*), ethical discipline (*śīla*) includes only ethical discipline; meditative concentration (*samādhi*) includes the dhyānas; and wisdom (*prajñā*) includes the latter five perfections.
If the accompanying factors (*sahāya*) are included as well, they all possess mutual inclusion.
If categorized according to their function, the precepts subsume the first three because they constitute the provisions, the essential nature, and the retinue;
meditative concentration subsumes dhyāna;
and wisdom subsumes the final five.
The three types of diligence are subsumed because they universally exert the three [trainings].
If categorized according to their manifest inclusion, ethical discipline subsumes the first four, because the first three are as previously explained and because of its protective nature;
meditative concentration subsumes dhyāna.
Wisdom subsumes the latter five.
Regarding these ten stages, all five [categories of] stages are present; however, their characteristics are most manifest during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Nevertheless, in the first two stages, for a bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment, the seeds belong to both types, while the manifest [dharmas] are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).

For a Bodhisattva who attains enlightenment gradually, both seeds and manifestations pertain to both types [of outflow and non-outflow], because they have already attained the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā*) regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Within the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), seeds pertain to both types, while manifestations are exclusively untainted.

Regarding the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*): prior to the seventh ground, both seeds and manifest activities (*vṛtti*) are common to both the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-out-flowing (*anāsrava*).
From the eighth ground onward, seeds are common to both types, while manifest activities are exclusively non-out-flowing.
In the state of ultimate fruition (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*), both the manifest and the seeds are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
These ten [perfections] have three names during the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*):

first, they are called "distant *pāramitās*," referring to the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*); at that time, the power of giving and the other perfections is still weak, being suppressed by the afflictions (*kleśa*) and unable to suppress them; consequently, the afflictions continue to manifest without one’s awareness.

The second is called the "near-perfection" (*upapāramitā*), referring to the second incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). At that time, the power of giving and the other perfections gradually increases; it is not that the afflictions (*kleśa*) subdue [the practitioner], but rather that the practitioner is able to subdue them. Consequently, the afflictions only manifest through intentional effort.

There are three great *pāramitās*, namely during the third incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). At that time, the power of generosity and the other perfections increases further, enabling them to ultimately subdue all afflictions (*kleśa*). Consequently, these afflictions never again manifest; yet, because there still remain subtle manifest and seeds of the knowable (*jñeya*) as well as seeds of the afflictions, [this stage] is not yet ultimate.
These ten categories of meaning have infinite distinctions; fearing that excessive detail would weary the reader, I shall briefly indicate their essential framework.
Although all ten are actually cultivated throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they are each cultivated in accordance with their predominant characteristics in each respective stage.
Although the practices of the ten stages have immeasurable gateways, they are all subsumed within the ten perfections (*pāramitās*).

Regarding the ten heavy obstacles: first is the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*), which refers to that which arises from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) among the two obstacles; it is established as the nature of an ordinary being based upon those seeds.
When the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the two vehicles manifests, one severs only one type [of affliction] and is said to "attain the nature of an ārya.
When the path of seeing of a bodhisattva manifests, one severs both types and is said to "attain the nature of an ārya."

When the two types of true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) manifest, the seeds of those two obstacles are necessarily no longer possessed, just as light and darkness certainly do not arise together, and just as the rising and falling of the two ends of a scale occur simultaneously.
It is necessarily so according to the principle that mutually exclusive phenomena cannot coexist; therefore, there is no fault of both natures being established simultaneously.

Since the seeds of affliction have already ceased at the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), what need is there to further give rise to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)?
Because the intention regarding the period for abandoning afflictions and realizing cessation differs, and because one must abandon the *dauṣṭhulya* (unwieldiness) of that category,

the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises to abandon this [unwieldiness] even though the seeds of affliction no longer exist during the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), and thereby one realizes the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of that category.

Although the arising of the Path of Seeing also severs the karmic results of the evil destinies and so forth, for the time being we speak only of the afflictions that give rise to them, as these are the root.
For this reason, it is said that in the first stage (*bhūmi*) one abandons two delusions (*moha*) along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):
first, the delusion of clinging to a self and phenomena, which is precisely the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) within this context.
Second is the delusion regarding the afflictions of the miserable destinies (*durgati*), which refers to the various karmas and fruits of those destinies.
One should understand that the category of delusions is here collectively termed "delusion" (*moha*); subsequent explanations should be understood according to this principle.
Alternatively, that [text] may simply state that two types of ignorance—the dull and the sharp—arise together as hindrances, and the term "coarse heaviness" (*dausthulya*) indicates those two kinds.

Or, it may refer to the unfitness (*akarmanyatā*) produced by those two; just as when entering the two meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), it is said that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is abandoned, and although the abandoned faculty of suffering is neither present nor a seed, it is still termed "coarse heaviness," so too should this be understood.
The subsequent mention of "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) should be explained by analogy with this.

Although that which is abandoned in the first stage (*bhūmi*) actually pertains to both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) is intended here to refer to the cognitive (*jñeya*) obstacle; for it is said that the ten types of ignorance (*avidyā*) are non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*). Thus, ignorance is precisely the delusion (*moha*) belonging to the category of the ten obstacles.
The two vehicles are also able to sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*); however, as these are common to them, they are not what is being discussed here.

Furthermore, regarding the ten non-defiled types of ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*), they are spoken of solely in reference to that which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Although within this stage one also suppresses the afflictions and abandons their coarse residues (*dauṣṭhulya*), this is not the primary intent; nor does one abandon the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Therefore, these are not mentioned here.

In reality, even during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the first stage, one also abandons a portion of the innate objects of knowledge (*jñeya*); however, for now, only that which is abandoned at the very beginning is discussed. One should understand that the abandonment occurring in the subsequent nine stages follows the same principle.

Since one has already dwelt for a long time within the stages of fulfillment (*paripūrṇabhūmi*), it stands to reason that one should proceed to abandon the obstacles that ought to be abandoned; otherwise, there would be no distinction between the paths of the three periods.

Therefore, it is said that once a Bodhisattva has attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they subsequently cultivate only the path that eternally extinguishes the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) throughout the ten stages. They retain the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) to assist their vows for rebirth, unlike the followers of the two vehicles who hasten toward parinirvāṇa. Thus, they do not abandon the afflictions during the stage of cultivation, but rather abandon them all at once only when they are about to attain Buddhahood.

The second is the obstacle of wrong conduct (*mithyāpratipatti-āvaraṇa*), which refers to a portion of the innate aspect (*sahaja*) of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the three types of karma resulting from the transgressions it gives rise to.
This obstacle hinders the extremely pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the second stage; upon entering the second stage, one is able to sever it forever.
Based on this, it is said that in the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*) one abandons two delusions (*moha*) along with their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):
first, the delusion of subtle transgressions, which is a portion of the innate [delusion] within this context;

and second, the delusion regarding the various courses of karma, which refers to the three types of action resulting from those transgressions, or specifically the delusion of initiating action without understanding its nature.

The third is the obscuration of dullness (*mṛdv-indriyatva-āvaraṇa*), which refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that causes one to forget what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated. This obscuration hinders the superior meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs of the third stage, as well as the three types of sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) they produce; upon entering the third stage, it can be permanently severed.
Consequently, it is said that on the third stage one abandons two delusions and their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):

first, the delusion of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-moha*), which is that which obstructs superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) within this stage. Because it was formerly frequently associated with sensual desire, it is called the "delusion of sensual desire"; now that superior concentration and the wisdom born of cultivation have been attained, since that [delusion] has been permanently severed, sensual desire is suppressed along with it, for it has operated in dependence upon it from beginningless time.

Second, the delusion regarding the perfection of the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retention, which is that which obstructs the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) regarding the *dhāraṇī*.

The fourth is the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle afflictions. This refers to a portion of the innate aspect within the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), comprised of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth that coexist with the sixth consciousness. It is called "subtle" because it is of the lowest grade, because it does not function through deliberate attention, and because it persists as a remote accompaniment to active manifestations.
These obstruct the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) of the fourth stage; upon entering the fourth stage, they can be permanently severed.
Because they previously mostly arose as being of the same substance as the spontaneously arising view of self within the sixth consciousness, they are designated by the name "affliction" (kleśa).

Now, since the untainted factors conducive to enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhipakṣadharma*) have been attained within the fourth stage, they are forever extinguished; thus, this view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth also never again arise.

In the first, second, and third stages, the practice of giving, morality, and cultivation is similar to that of the mundane world; it is only upon attaining the factors conducive to enlightenment in the fourth stage that one is termed "supramundane" (*lokottara*), and is therefore able to permanently destroy the two types of view of self and so forth.
How do we know that this [ignorance] is associated with the sixth consciousness?

It is because the grasping of self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth associated with the seventh consciousness is of a nature that contradicts the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*); therefore, it never functions again from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, whereas it can still manifest from the seventh stage downward, as it serves as the support for other afflictions. Since this [ignorance] is coarse while that [seventh-consciousness-associated ignorance] is subtle, their subduing occurs at different times; thus, this [ignorance] is associated only with the sixth consciousness.

The mention of "view of a self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth also includes the beginningless cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as well as attachment to meditative concentration (*samādhi-tṛṣṇā*) and attachment to the Dharma (*dharma-tṛṣṇā*).

These attachments to concentration and the Dharma still increase throughout the first three stages; they can only be permanently severed upon entering the fourth stage, because the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are particularly antagonistic to them.
For this reason, it is said that on the fourth stage one abandons two delusions along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):
first, the delusion of attachment to meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), which corresponds here to that associated with craving for concentration;
second, the delusion of attachment to phenomena (*dharma*), which corresponds here to that associated with craving for the teachings.
Because the two delusions subsumed under the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are abandoned, the two types of craving associated with afflictions (*kleśa*) also cease to function forever.

Fifth is the obstacle to parinirvāṇa in the Lesser Vehicle; this refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obstacles that causes one to loathe cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and take pleasure in nirvāṇa, being similar to the Lesser Vehicles' aversion to suffering and longing for cessation. This obstacle hinders the path of non-differentiation in the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), and upon entering the fifth stage, it can be permanently severed.
Based on this, it is said that in the fifth stage one abandons two delusions along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):
first, the delusion of exclusively directing mental attention away from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), which refers here to those who are weary of birth-and-death;
second, the delusion of exclusively directing mental attention toward nirvāṇa, which refers here to those who delight in nirvāṇa.

The sixth is the obstacle of the manifestation of coarse characteristics, which refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) consisting of the manifestation of coarse characteristics that grasp at defilement and purity. This obstacle hinders the path free from defilement and purity in the sixth stage; upon entering the sixth stage, it can be permanently severed.
For this reason, it is said that on the sixth stage one abandons two delusions and their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):

first, the delusion regarding the flow of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as they evolve, which is precisely the grasping at a defiled agent here, because the evolving flow of conditioned phenomena is subsumed under the defiled portion;

second, the delusion regarding the frequent manifestation of signs, which is precisely the grasping at a pure agent here, because by apprehending pure signs, the contemplation of signs frequently manifests, such that one is unable to abide for long in signless contemplation (*animitta-samādhi*).

The seventh is the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle characteristics; this refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) consisting of the manifestation of subtle characteristics that grasp at arising and ceasing. This obstructs the sublime path of signlessness (*animitta-mārga*) of the seventh ground, and upon entering the seventh ground, it can be permanently severed.
For this reason, it is said that on the seventh stage one abandons two delusions along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):
first, the delusion of the manifestation of subtle signs, which refers here to the grasping at arising, because one still perceives the subtle signs of arising within the process of saṃsāra;

second, the delusion of purely attending to the pursuit of signlessness, which refers here to the grasping at cessation, because one still perceives the subtle signs of cessation within the process of returning to extinction. Thus, while one purely applies attention to the pursuit of signlessness, one is as yet unable to give rise to superior practice regarding emptiness.

The obstacle to the application of effort regarding the eight signless states refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that prevents the signless contemplation from arising spontaneously.

In the first five stages, there is much contemplation with signs and little signless contemplation; in the sixth stage, there is little contemplation with signs and much signless contemplation; and in the seventh stage, there is exclusively signless contemplation, which, though constantly continuous, still involves application of effort.
Because there is still effortful application (*prayoga*) within the signless state, one is not yet able to manifest signs and lands spontaneously.

Such effortful application obstructs the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*) in the eighth stage; therefore, upon entering the eighth stage, it is permanently severed. Because it is permanently severed, one attains two masteries.

For this reason, it is said that on the eighth stage one abandons two delusions along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*): first, the delusion of exerting effort regarding the signless (*animitta*);
second, the delusion of non-mastery over signs, because it prevents mastery over signs, and because this [delusion] also subsumes a portion of the signs of the [buddha-]lands.
From the eighth bhūmi upward, because the purely untainted path arises spontaneously, the afflictions of the three realms never manifest again.
However, subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seventh consciousness may still arise, as the fruit of the wisdom realizing selflessness does not contradict them.

The ninth is the obstacle of being disinclined toward altruistic activity; this refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that causes one to lack the desire to diligently engage in deeds for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, instead delighting in cultivating one's own self-interest. This obstruction hinders the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) of the ninth stage, and upon entering the ninth stage, it is permanently severed.
For this reason, it is said that on the ninth stage one abandons two delusions along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*):

first, the delusion regarding mastery over the dhāraṇīs of wisdom and eloquence concerning the immeasurable teachings, immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables. Regarding "mastery over the dhāraṇīs of the immeasurable teachings," this refers to the unimpeded understanding of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); it is mastery over the retention (*dhāraṇī*) of what is expressed, because within a single meaning, all meanings are manifested.

Mastery over the *dhāraṇī* of immeasurable names, phrases, and syllables refers to the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); it is mastery over the retention of the expressive designations, because within a single name, phrase, or syllable, all names, phrases, and syllables are manifested.

Regarding "mastery over the dhāraṇī of subsequent wisdom and eloquence," this refers to the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); it is mastery over the retention (*dhāraṇī*) of successive explanations and interpretations of words and sounds, because one manifests all sounds within a single sound.

Second is the delusion regarding mastery of eloquence (*pratibhāna-vaśitā*). Mastery of eloquence refers to unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), because one skillfully preaches by thoroughly understanding the appropriate capacities [of listeners].
This delusion can obstruct these four kinds of mastery; all such obstacles are subsumed within this ninth hindrance.

Tenth is the obstacle consisting in the lack of mastery over all phenomena; that is to say, a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which prevents one from attaining mastery over all phenomena. This obstacle obstructs the great cloud of dharma-knowledge and the activities arising from what it contains in the tenth stage; upon entering the tenth stage, it can be permanently severed.
Based on this, the Tenth Ground is said to eliminate two types of ignorance along with their coarse residues (*dausthulya*):
first, the ignorance regarding great supernormal powers, which refers to the activity obstructed herein;
second, the ignorance regarding the penetration of subtle secrets, which refers to the obstruction of the great cloud of Dharma-knowledge and that which it contains.

Although on this stage one has attained mastery over phenomena, there remain residual obstructions that prevent it from being called "ultimate," namely: innate subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the seeds of spontaneously arising afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, all these [afflictions] are suddenly severed and one enters the stage of a Tathāgata.
For this reason, it is said that on the Buddha-stage two types of ignorance and their corresponding coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*) are abandoned:

first, the ignorance consisting of extremely subtle attachment toward all objects of knowledge, which is precisely the "subtle cognitive obscuration" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) mentioned here; [the second is the ignorance regarding the non-differentiation of the dharmadhātu].
The second is the extremely subtle obstruction of delusion regarding resistance; this refers to all the seeds of the spontaneously arising afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within this context.

Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that at the time of attaining bodhi, one suddenly abandons both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions, becoming an arhat and a Tathāgata, thereby realizing great nirvāṇa and great bodhi.
*Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only), Scroll Nine; *Cheng weishi lun*, Scroll Ten.
Composed by Dharmapāla and other Bodhisattvas.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
These eleven hindrances are subsumed within the two hindrances.

Among the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the seeds to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) are first severed at the initial stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) on the Ground of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); their active manifestations have already been suppressed prior to that ground.
The seeds to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are all severed instantaneously at the moment the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests.

While those obstacles manifest gradually prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) onward they can be entirely suppressed so that they never again arise. Just as an Arhat, by the power of intentional resolve, may allow them to temporarily manifest during the first seven stages without it being a fault, from the eighth stage upward they never arise at all.

Among the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), those seeds to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) are first severed at the initial moment of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) on the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); their active manifestations had already been suppressed prior to that stage.

As for the seeds to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are gradually eliminated throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), being finally and completely exhausted only when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests.

Those obstacles, which arise manifestly, are gradually suppressed prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), and are finally and permanently suppressed at the tenth stage; from the eighth stage upward, those associated with the six consciousnesses no longer manifest, because the mind of untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā-citta*) and its resultant continuity can oppose them.
The seventh [consciousness] may still manifest even when [the others] are conjoined, but it is only at the stage where the fruit of the wisdom of dharma-emptiness arises that it is suppressed.

As for the first five evolving consciousnesses, even if they have not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), their afflictions do not manifest because they are suppressed by the outflow-free state.

Although the seeds of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are not severed at all during the ten stages of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), their corresponding coarse heavinesses (*dauṣṭhulya*) are also gradually severed; for this reason, it is said that each of the two hindrances and their respective coarse heavinesses possesses the sense of being severed across three distinct stages.
Although the heavy obstructions (*dausthulya*) are severed in all stages, they are made manifest in three specific positions; therefore, these alone are specifically mentioned.
Regarding the severance of the seeds of the two obstacles, how is it—gradually or suddenly?

As for the seeds of the afflictive obstacles associated with the seventh consciousness, when those of the three vehicles are about to attain the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), they are suddenly severed across the three realms within a single moment.

Regarding the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), at the moment of attaining Buddhahood, they are all severed instantaneously within a single kṣaṇa; this is because they arise spontaneously from within and lack the distinction of coarse or subtle. As for the seeds of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) associated with the remaining six consciousnesses:
those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) are all severed instantaneously within the True Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) during the stage of seeing for the three vehicles.

Those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are severed according to their respective categories: for one class of practitioners of the two vehicles, they are severed gradually, category by category, through the nine grades across each of the nine stages of the three realms; for another class of practitioners of the two vehicles, the nine stages of the three realms are combined into a single aggregate and severed through the nine grades. For Bodhisattvas, however, these must be severed instantaneously across the three realms within a single kṣaṇa upon the arising of the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*).

Regarding the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): those to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) are all suddenly severed at the first moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*). Those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are severed gradually during the subsequent path of cultivation across the ten stages, until they are finally exhausted in a single moment when one actually gives rise to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*). This is because there are many distinct categories of these obstructions, arising from their various objects—both internal and external—and their diverse degrees of coarseness and subtlety.

When those of the two vehicles, whose faculties are dull, gradually eliminate obstacles, they must each separately give rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Their paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*) may be either distinct or collective. However, for Bodhisattvas with sharp faculties, during the stage of gradually eliminating obstacles, it is not necessary to separately give rise to the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation, because they are able to effect elimination and realization moment by moment.
The four [factors], beginning with the preparatory application (*prayoga*), may all be present at every moment when viewed in relation to what precedes and follows.

Regarding the ten kinds of *tathatā* (suchness): first is the all-pervading *tathatā*, which means that this suchness is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and there is not a single dharma that does not abide within it.
Second is the *tathatā* of supremacy, meaning that this *tathatā*, possessing boundless virtues, is the most supreme among all phenomena (*dharma*).
Third is the *tathatā* of the supreme outflow, meaning that the teachings flowing forth from this *tathatā* are far more supreme than other teachings.
Fourth is the *tathatā* of non-appropriation; this means that this *tathatā* has no point of attachment, as it is not the basis for appropriation by the grasping of a self (*ātman*) and so forth.
Fifth is the *tathatā* of undifferentiated category; this means that this *tathatā* has no distinction in its category, unlike the eye and other faculties which have different categories.
Sixth is the *tathatā* of being neither defiled nor pure; this means that the intrinsic nature of this *tathatā* is inherently undefiled, and it cannot be said that it becomes pure only later.
Seventh is the *tathatā* of the non-differentiation of phenomena; this means that although this *tathatā* is established in various ways through numerous teachings, it remains without distinction.

The eighth is the *tathatā* free from increase and decrease; this means that this *tathatā* is devoid of the grasping at increase and decrease, because it does not undergo increase or decrease in accordance with purity or defilement.

This same [tathatā] is also called the *tathatā* that is the basis for mastery over marks and lands, meaning that once this *tathatā* has been realized, one possesses mastery over both manifesting marks and manifesting lands.
The *tathatā* that is the basis for mastery over the nine knowledges; that is to say, once this *tathatā* has been realized, one attains mastery over the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

The *tathatā* that is the basis for mastery over karma and so forth; that is to say, once this *tathatā* has been realized, one attains universal mastery over all supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), activities, dhāraṇīs, and doors of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Although the nature of *tathatā* is in reality without differentiation, ten types are provisionally established according to its preeminent qualities.

Although all [qualities] have already been reached within the first stage (*bhūmi*), the practice of realization is not yet perfected; therefore, subsequent stages are established in order to bring it to fulfillment.

In this way, within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the bodhisattva courageously practices the ten superior conducts, eliminates the ten heavy obstructions, and realizes the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*), thereby being able to realize the two types of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
There are briefly six distinct stages of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*):

First, the transformation through the weakening of power and the strengthening of capacity. This refers to the first two stages. Because one practices resolute faith (*adhimukti*) as well as shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), the power of the defiled seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) is weakened, while the functional capacity of the pure seeds within that same consciousness is strengthened. Although one has not yet severed the seeds of the obstacles to realize the transformation of the basis in actuality, one gradually suppresses their active manifestation; thus, this is also termed a "transformation."

Second is the transformation of thorough penetration, which refers to the stage of penetration; through the power of the path of seeing, one thoroughly penetrates suchness, eliminates the heavy obscurations of the two hindrances produced by conceptualization, and realizes a portion of the true transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

Third is the transformation through cultivation, which refers to the stage of cultivation; because one repeatedly cultivates the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one gradually eliminates the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the two innate obstacles and progressively realizes the true transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the "transformation through penetration" (*prativedha-parāvṛtti*) occurs in the first six stages, wherein the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-bhāvanā*) manifests as a mixture of the ultimate and the conventional, causing the real and the unreal to appear and disappear respectively. It further states that the "transformation through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-parāvṛtti*) occurs in the final four stages, wherein the contemplation of signlessness manifests continuously for long periods; through this courageous cultivation, the remaining heavy residues (*dausthulya*) are severed, such that the unreal mostly no longer appears.

The fourth is the transformation of the perfection of the fruits, which refers to the stage of culmination. Having cultivated and accumulated boundless difficult practices over three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, at the moment the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, one eternally severs all innate coarse heavinesses (*dausthulya*). One suddenly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood, the perfect transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), which brings benefit and happiness to an inexhaustible degree until the end of the future.

The five inferior transformations refer to the stage of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), which exclusively seek self-benefit, loathe suffering, and aspire to quiescence; they are able only to penetrate the suchness of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-tathatā*), sever the seeds of afflictions, and realize true analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Because they lack superior capability, they are termed "inferior transformation."

The sixth is the "vast transformation," which refers to the stage of the Mahāyāna. For the sake of benefiting others, one aspires toward great enlightenment; one feels neither longing for nor aversion toward saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; one possesses the capacity to thoroughly penetrate the true suchness of the two kinds of emptiness; one simultaneously severs the seeds of both the cognitive and afflictive obstructions; and one suddenly realizes unsurpassed bodhi and nirvāṇa. Because it possesses this superior capability, it is called the "vast transformation."
The intention here is to speak of the vast transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), because it is attained by abandoning the two types of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
Briefly stated, there are four distinct meanings of transformation of the basis:
first, the path that effects the transformation (*parivartaka-mārga*).
This further consists of two types:

first, the path of suppression (*vibhava-mārga*), which means suppressing the power of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstacles so as to prevent them from giving rise to the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) of those two obstacles.

This applies to all three types of wisdom—the preparatory (*prayoga*), the fundamental (*maula*), and the subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)—whether they are with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), and whether they suppress them gradually or instantaneously according to their respective capacities.
Second is the path capable of abandonment, which refers to that which can eternally sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstructions.

This path is certainly not a contaminated preparatory stage (*prayoga*), because a contaminated state is induced by the habitual grasping at signs and thus has not yet eliminated such signs; furthermore, a preparatory stage is induced by the pursuit of what is to be realized and thus has not yet accomplished it.

There is an interpretation that fundamental non-conceptual wisdom directly realizes the ultimate truth revealed by the two kinds of emptiness; because it is devoid of objective appearances, it can sever the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
Subsequently attained wisdom is not so, and therefore it is not the path of abandonment.

There is another interpretation: although the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom does not directly realize the truth of the two kinds of emptiness and lacks the power to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding that truth, because it realizes without error the clearly manifest characteristics of both the established and the unestablished, it is also able to permanently sever the latent tendencies regarding phenomena.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there exists both a supramundane path of abandonment and a mundane-supramundane path of abandonment; there is no purely mundane path capable of permanently destroying the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), because [the mundane path] consists of what was previously practiced and because it is induced by the grasping of signs (*nimittagrāha*).

By this principle, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that delude one regarding reality—which are to be abandoned through insight as well as those to be abandoned through cultivation—can be correctly severed only by fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), because it directly realizes reality.

The remaining latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned through cultivation and which are deluded regarding phenomena can be correctly severed by both the fundamental and the subsequently attained [wisdoms].
Regarding the two bases of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), there are again two types:
First is the basis for maintaining seeds, which refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

Because it can maintain the seeds of both defiled and pure phenomena, it serves as the common support for both defiled and pure phenomena; through the holy path, it is transformed so that one abandons the defiled and attains the pure.
Although other aspects of the paratantra-svabhāva are also bases, they cannot sustain seeds; therefore, they are not mentioned here.
Second, the basis of delusion and awakening refers to true suchness (tathatā).

Because this [storehouse consciousness] can serve as the fundamental basis for both delusion and awakening, all defiled and pure phenomena arise in dependence upon it; furthermore, the Noble Path functions to cause the abandonment of the defiled and the attainment of the pure.
Although other factors also serve as bases for the phenomena of delusion and awakening, they are not the fundamental basis; therefore, they are not mentioned here.
Third, that which is relinquished through transformation;
this further has two aspects:
first, relinquishment through abandonment, which refers to the seeds of the two obstacles.

When the true path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) manifests, the obstacle and its antidote are in opposition; the former is thereby severed and extinguished, never to be realized again, which is termed "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*).

Because those seeds are severed, the false attachment to a self and phenomena no longer manifests; furthermore, the self and phenomena so grasped do not confront deluded cognition, which is also termed "abandonment. For this reason, it is called the abandonment of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Second, that which is abandoned refers to the remaining seeds of outflows (*sāsrava*) and inferior untainted (*anāsrava*) seeds.

When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, it induces the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that is supremely luminous and pure; since those [seeds] are not its support, they are all permanently abandoned.

Once those seeds have been relinquished, the presently existing tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and inferior untainted phenomena (*hīna-anāsrava-dharma*) will never arise again; since they will never arise, this is also called "relinquishment. For this reason, it is termed the relinquishment of the inferior phenomena of birth and death.

There is another interpretation: at the time when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests, the seeds of all remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena as well as the inferior uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena have already been abandoned, because they are abandoned simultaneously with the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).

There is another interpretation: at that time, [the bodhisattva] has not yet abandoned those [afflictions], because it would not be contradictory to the path of non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*); because a bodhisattva should not be devoid of the phenomena of birth and death; because in this stage there should be no consciousness to be perfumed (*vāsya*); because one abiding in the path of non-interruption should already be called a Buddha; and because the subsequent path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) would then be rendered useless.

From this it should be understood that other impure states (*sāsrava*) and the like are abandoned only when the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) arises, because the eighth pure consciousness (*viśuddhavijñāna*) is not the support for them.
Fourth, that which is attained through transformation.
This, in turn, has two aspects:
first, that which is manifested through realization, namely Great Nirvāṇa.

Although this is by nature primordially pure, it is obscured by adventitious hindrances and thus remains unmanifest; when the true Path of the Aryas arises and eliminates those hindrances, its characteristics become manifest, and this is termed "attaining Nirvāṇa."
This is established based on *tathatā* (suchness) as being free from obstructions; therefore, its essence is the pure *dharmadhātu*. Briefly, there are four distinct meanings of *nirvāṇa*:

First is the *nirvāṇa of the originally self-pure nature*. This refers to the principle of *tathatā*, the true nature of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*). Although it is subject to adventitious defilements, its fundamental nature is pure. It possesses immeasurable and subtle merits, is without birth or cessation, and is as serene as empty space. It is equally shared by all sentient beings and is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena. It is free from all marks and all conceptualization; it transcends the paths of thought and the tracks of language. It is realized only within the personal experience of true noble ones (*ārya*). Because its nature is fundamentally quiescent, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

Second is *nirvāṇa with remainder*, which refers to true suchness (*tathatā*) emerging from the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Although there remains a subtle suffering and its basis has not yet been extinguished, because the obscurations have been eternally stilled, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

Third is nirvana without remainder, which refers to the emergence from the suffering of birth and death within true suchness (*tathatā*). Since the afflictions have been exhausted and the remaining substratum has also ceased, all sufferings are forever stilled; therefore, it is called nirvana.

The fourth is non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*): it refers to suchness (*tathatā*) emerging from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), constantly supported by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and prajñā. Because of this, one does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, benefiting and bringing joy to sentient beings until the end of the future; being active yet eternally quiescent, it is therefore called nirvana.

All sentient beings possess the first [nirvāṇa]; those of the two vehicles who have attained the state beyond training may possess the first three; only our World-Honored One can be said to possess all four.
How, then, could the Sugata still have a remainder of support (*sopadhiśeṣa*)?
Although there is no actual basis, it appears as if there were;
or, when the basis for suffering is exhausted, it is called "without remainder," whereas when the basis for non-suffering remains, it is called "with remainder.
Therefore, the Blessed One may be said to possess all four [nirvāṇas].
If Śrāvakas and others possess the nirvana without remainder, how is it that in some places it is said they do not have it, while in other places it is said they lack nirvana altogether?
Is it possible that even the nirvana with remainder does not exist for them?

However, while the bodies and cognitions of śrāvakas and others still exist, there remains cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); because the basis of suffering has not been exhausted, the meaning of parinirvāṇa is obscured, and thus it is said that they have no nirvāṇa.

It is not that they truly lack the *sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*, which is the truth revealed by the exhaustion of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*). At that time, they have not yet realized *nirupadhiśeṣa-parinirvāṇa*; therefore, it is also said that they lack *nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*.
It is not that at a later time, after their bodies and cognitions have ceased, they lack the exhaustion of the basis of suffering as *nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*.
As for the statement that the two vehicles have no nirvāṇa, this is based on the absence of a dwelling place and does not rely on the preceding three [stages].
Furthermore, the statement that they lack the nirvāṇa without remainder is made in reference to those of the indeterminate nature among the two vehicles.

As soon as he realizes *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, he resolutely turns his mind toward seeking unsurpassed enlightenment; by the power of his concentration and vows, he maintains his physical body and remains for a long time, unlike those of a certain class who enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

This refers to those of the two vehicles who deeply delight in perfect quiescence; having attained the contemplation of the emptiness of persons and directly realized true suchness, they eternally extinguish the afflictive hindrances that induce rebirth and reach exhaustion. Thus, based on the ultimate truth, they manifest *nirvāṇa with remainder*.

Because the afflictions that could induce rebirth have been exhausted, there is no further basis for the maturation of future existence to arise. At the stage when the support of present suffering spontaneously ceases, other conditioned phenomena—lacking such a support—are simultaneously and instantaneously relinquished along with that support of suffering; this reveals *nirvāṇa without remainder* based upon ultimate truth.
At that time, although the bodies and wisdoms of the two vehicles do not exist, they may be said to exist by virtue of their realization.
In this stage, there is only pure *tathatā*, which is free from characteristics, profound, quiescent, and blissful; based on this, it is said that they are no different from a Buddha.
However, because they lack the activity of awakening for the benefit and happiness of others, it is further said that they differ from a Buddha.
Since the various cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) do not induce rebirth, how is it that by abandoning them one attains the "non-abiding" [nirvāṇa]?

They are able to obscure the true suchness of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmatathatā*), preventing the arising of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and prajñā, which would otherwise continue to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future. Therefore, when these obstructions are abandoned, the principle of the emptiness of phenomena is revealed; this principle is itself non-abiding nirvāṇa, because it causes one to abide in neither of the two extremes.
If the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) also obstruct nirvāṇa, why is it that by abandoning them one does not attain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*)?
For analytical cessation is the separation from bonds, and those [obstructions] are not bonds.
This being so, how could one attain nirvāṇa by abandoning them?
Not all forms of nirvāṇa are subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); otherwise, the naturally pure (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) would not be considered nirvāṇa.
That which binds sentient beings and causes them to dwell in saṃsāra—when this is severed, one is said to have attained the unconditioned state of analytical cessation.

The various cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) do not induce birth and death; unlike the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are not capable of binding sentient beings. Therefore, when these are severed, one does not attain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Nevertheless, because they are severed, the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmāśūnyatā*) is revealed. This principle, characterized by quiescence, is called nirvāṇa; yet this nirvāṇa does not have analytical cessation as its intrinsic nature.

Therefore, among the four types of parinirvāṇa and the various unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), the first and the last are *tathatā* (suchness), while the middle two are subsumed under *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through analytical discernment).

If cessation through analytical discernment is attained solely by severing the fetters (*bandhana*), then within these four, under which category are the two—namely, the "immovable" (*āniñjya*) and so forth—subsumed?
It is subsumed under non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because it is said to be a temporary separation.
Unconditioned analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is exclusively ultimate cessation, whereas there are cases of non-analytical cessation that are not permanent cessation.
Alternatively, even that which lacks a place of abiding is subsumed under analytical cessation, because it is attained through the power of true analysis by ceasing the obstructions.

There are two types of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): first, that obtained by severing bonds, which refers to the attainment resulting from the abandonment of afflictions that induce rebirth;
second, that obtained by removing obstructions, which refers to the realization attained through the elimination of hindrances.

Therefore, among the four types of parinirvāṇa and the various unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), the first is suchness (*tathatā*), while the latter three are all analytical cessations (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

As for the two [types of cessation], "immovable" and so forth, those that are temporary suppressions are subsumed under non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), whereas those that are ultimate cessations are subsumed under analytical cessation.
Since the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) also obstruct nirvāṇa, why are they said to be obstacles only to bodhi?
And when it is said that the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) only obstruct nirvāṇa, does that mean they cannot also act as obstacles to bodhi?
One should understand that the holy teachings speak according to predominant functions; in reality, however, both [the paths] are capable of penetrating and removing obstacles to both fruits.
Among the four types of nirvāṇa thus described, only the latter three are termed "attained through manifestation," while the two "attained through production" refer to Great Bodhi.
Although these possess the seeds capable of producing [the result] from the very beginning, they do not arise because they are obstructed by the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).

By the power of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), those obstructions are severed; thus, [the result] arises from the seeds, which is termed "attaining enlightenment" (*bodhiprāpti*). Once arisen, it continues in succession until the end of the future.

This refers to the mental states associated with the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-samprayukta-citta-varga*). What are these four? First is the mental state associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

This mental state is free from all conceptual discrimination; its objects and modes of activity are subtle and difficult to discern. It does not forget nor is it deluded regarding any objective phenomena; its nature and characteristics are pure and free from all defilements. It serves as the support for the seeds and manifestations of purely virtuous qualities, capable of manifesting and generating the reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdoms. It proceeds without interval or interruption until the end of the future, like a great perfect mirror manifesting all manner of forms and images.

The second is the mental state associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*). This refers to the mental state that contemplates all phenomena and all sentient beings—both oneself and others—as entirely equal; it is constantly accompanied by great compassion and other such qualities. It manifests various distinctions of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) and its lands according to the inclinations of sentient beings. It is the unique support for the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), is established upon non-abiding nirvāṇa, and continues as a single flavor throughout the limits of the future.

Third is the mental state associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). This refers to that mental state which functions without obstruction while skillfully observing the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena; it encompasses the observation of immeasurable doors of dhāraṇī and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as well as the precious jewels of the virtues they produce; it is able to manifest infinite varieties of functional activity within great assemblies, attaining mastery over them all; and it rains down the great Dharma rain to sever all doubts, causing all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness.

Fourth is the mental state associated with the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). This refers to the mental state that, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, universally manifests various transformations of the three karmas throughout the ten directions, thereby fulfilling the tasks to be performed through the power of its original vows.

Although each of these four classes of consciousness associated with the four wisdoms necessarily comprises twenty-two dharmas—both seeds and manifest forms, as well as the transforming subject and the transformed object—these are designated by the name "wisdom" because the function of wisdom is predominant. Therefore, these four classes collectively encompass all conditioned merits of the Buddha-ground without exception.
This transformation of the categories associated with the eight, seven, six, and five consciousnesses that are tainted (*sāsrava*) is attained in their respective order.

Although wisdom (*jñāna*) is not itself a consciousness, it transforms in dependence upon consciousness; because consciousness is primary, it is said that one "attains [the result] by transforming consciousness."

Furthermore, in the state with outflows (*sāsrava*), wisdom is weak while consciousness is strong; in the state without outflows (*anāsrava*), wisdom is strong while consciousness is weak. To encourage sentient beings to rely on wisdom and abandon consciousness, it is said that by transforming the eight consciousnesses, these four wisdoms are attained.

Regarding the mental complex associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), one interpretation holds that it first arises at the moment when the Bodhisattva’s diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) is present, because the seeds of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and the extremely subtle seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are abandoned simultaneously.
If the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom had not yet arisen at that time, there would be no consciousness capable of sustaining the pure seeds.

According to one interpretation, this wisdom first arises at the moment of the Path of Liberation (vimukti-mārga) when one first attains Buddhahood; for at the time the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) is present, the seeds of the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna) have not yet been suddenly abandoned, as they do not conflict with the Path of Non-interruption (ānantarya-mārga).
It does not obstruct tainted (*sāsrava*) or inferior untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas; rather, it is definitively incompatible with the fruit of Buddhahood.

Since the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) lacks a consciousness that can be perfumed (*vāsya*), and since untainted qualities would already have reached their full development [if such a consciousness existed], one would necessarily have attained Buddhahood [prior to this stage].

Because of this, this mental state (*citta-varga*) continues uninterruptedly from the initial attainment of Buddhahood until the end of the future, as it maintains the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) so that they are not lost.

The mental state associated with the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) first arises at the stage when the Bodhisattva’s Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) initially manifests, precisely because it opposes the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).

Because the grasping [to self] has not yet been severed during the subsequent ten stages (*bhūmi*), there may be interruptions in states such as those involving outflows (*sāsrava*); however, from the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha-bhūmi*) onward, it continues in succession with the pure eighth consciousness until the end of the future.

The mental complex associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) first arises during the stage of vision (*darśana-mārga*) of the two vehicles within the category of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Thereafter, it continues successively until the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*), or until the end of the bodhisattva’s stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), or up to the higher stages; it may manifest whenever it is not contaminated (*sāsrava*) or when one is in a state of non-consciousness (*acittaka*). The mental complex associated with the wisdom of the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) first arises during the stage of vision of the bodhisattvas; thereupon, it proceeds successively up to the higher stages, manifesting whenever it is not contaminated, is the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons, or occurs during a state of non-consciousness.

Regarding the mental state associated with the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), there are two interpretations. One view holds that because it is induced by the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) during the Bodhisattva’s stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), it can first arise [at that stage].

The other view maintains that it only first arises upon becoming a Buddha. This is because, within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the eyes and other faculties transformed from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) are not uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). It is logically inconsistent for uncontaminated consciousness to be produced by contaminated, non-common, necessarily concomitant, and co-objective sense organs. Furthermore, these two differ in their clarity regarding the object; therefore, this mental state requires the attainment of Buddhahood and reliance upon uncontaminated faculties before it can manifest.
Yet these are frequently interrupted because they arise through intentional mental application (*manasikāra*).

Although these four types of nature are all inherently present, they must be activated by perfuming (*vāsanā*) before they can manifest. They gradually increase during the stage of the cause and reach perfection at the stage of Buddhahood; neither increasing nor decreasing, they persist until the end of the future.
It arises solely from seeds and does not perfume them to form new seeds, lest the virtues of a preceding Buddha be superior to those of a subsequent Buddha.

Regarding the mental complex associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), one interpretation holds that it takes only suchness (*tathatā*) as its object; it is non-conceptual wisdom rather than subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) and its objective referent (*ālambana*) are unknowable.

There is an interpretation that this category takes all phenomena as its object; for the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is not deluded regarding any object, and the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that the mirror of the Tathāgata’s wisdom manifests the manifold images of the sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses.

Furthermore, because this [wisdom] definitely takes as its objects the untainted seeds as well as various images such as the body and the environment, its activity is subtle and is said to be "unknowable.

Just as the ālayavijñāna also takes the conventional as its object, this wisdom is non-conceptual when taking True Suchness (tathatā) as its object; however, when taking other objects, it is subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna). Its essence is one, yet it is divided into two according to its functions.
Because one realizes the conventional through the realization of the ultimate, it is called "subsequently attained.
The other two categories [of wisdom] should be understood accordingly.

Regarding the mental state associated with the Wisdom of Equality, there is one interpretation that it takes only the pure eighth consciousness as its object, just as the defiled seventh consciousness takes the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as its object.
One interpretation holds that it takes only *tathatā* (suchness) as its object, because it takes the equality of all phenomena as its object.

Another interpretation holds that it universally takes both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) as its objects; for the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that the wisdom of equality realizes ten kinds of equality, and the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that it takes all sentient beings as equal—regardless of self or other—and manifests infinite Buddha-images in accordance with the superior inclinations of others.
Therefore, this category [of mental states] universally takes both the ultimate and conventional as its objects; that it is subsumed under the two wisdoms is not contrary to principle.

The category of mind associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation takes the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena as its objects without obstruction, and is thus subsumed under the two wisdoms.

Regarding the mental complex associated with the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), one interpretation holds that it takes only the five kinds of present objects as its domain, because the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states that each of the Tathāgata’s five sense faculties functions with respect to all five objects.

There is another interpretation: this category [of wisdom] is also capable of universally cognizing all phenomena across the three periods of time without contradicting correct principle. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Was to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) initiates the various transformative activities of the three types of karma, discerns the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings, and perceives the meanings of the past, future, and present.
If it were not a universal object-condition (*sarvatraga*), it would lack this capacity;
however, according to the power of the mental inclination (*āśaya*) within this category of consciousness (*cittapakṣa*), it may take one, two, or many dharmas as its object.
Furthermore, when it is said that the five faculties operate with respect to the five objects, this does not imply that they operate *only* in that manner; therefore, there is no contradiction.

Because they arise following mental attention (*manasikāra*) and produce transformative karma by taking the characteristics of objects as their conditions, they are subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Although these four categories of mind are all universally capable of taking all phenomena as their objects, their functions differ.
That is to say, the category of mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) manifests the marks of the self-enjoyment body and its pure land while sustaining uncontaminated seeds;
the category of equality wisdom (samatājñāna) manifests the marks of the other-enjoyment body and its pure land;
and the category of accomplishing-activity wisdom (kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna) is able to manifest the transformation body and its land.

The category of the wisdom of observation examines the capacities and faults of both oneself and others; it rains down the great rain of Dharma to shatter the web of doubts and bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
There are many such diverse categories of distinctions.

These four categories of mind are termed "attained through production," and this "attainment through production" is collectively named *bodhi*. Together with the aforementioned *nirvāṇa*, they are termed "attained through transformation.

Although the meaning of "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) generally comprises four types, here we take only the two types of "attainment through transformation," because the verse speaks of "realizing the attainment of the transformation of the basis."
This stage of cultivation is said to be "capable of realization," because it has not yet realized [the fruit] and is therefore subsumed under the causal stage.
What are the characteristics of the subsequent stage of culmination?
The verse says:
30. This is the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu), inconceivable, virtuous, and eternal;
it is the body of liberation, blissful, and is called the Dharma by the Great Muni.
The Commentary states:
One should know that the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) attained during the preceding stage of cultivation is precisely the characteristic of the ultimate stage.
This means that these two aforementioned fruits of transformation of the basis are subsumed within the ultimate untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu).
All outflows (*āsrava*) are eternally exhausted, and no further outflows increase therein; its nature is pure, perfect, and luminous, and is therefore called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
"Realm" (*dhātu*) carries the meaning of a "repository"; for within this, it contains and encompasses boundless, rare, and great merits.
Alternatively, it is because of its causal significance, as it is able to produce the benefits and happiness of the five vehicles, both mundane and supramundane.

While the pure dharma-realm can be categorized as exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), how can the mental states and their attributes of the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-citta-varga*) be considered exclusively untainted?
Because they are subsumed within the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), they are exclusively comprised of the untainted (*anāsrava*).

That is to say, the Buddha’s virtues, as well as his body and environment, are all produced from the nature of the untainted; for the seeds of tainted phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) have been permanently abandoned.

Although he manifests the activities of a body subject to birth and death, as well as afflictions (*kleśa*), which appear to belong to the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*), they are in reality subsumed under the truth of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga-satya*).

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises state that fifteen of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are exclusively tainted; how then could the Tathāgata lack the five faculties, the five consciousnesses, and the five external objects?

There is another interpretation: the merit, body, and lands of the Tathāgata are profoundly deep and subtle, being neither existent nor non-existent; they transcend all conceptual discrimination and sever all frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Since they are not subsumed within the categories of the *dhātus* or *āyatanas*, this teaching does not contradict the aforementioned principle.

There is an interpretation that because the five faculties and five objects of the Tathāgata are produced by sublime meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are subsumed under the category of form within the dharma-dhātu; however, although the Buddha’s five consciousnesses rely on these [faculties] for their manifestation, they are not subsumed under the five objects because they differ in terms of coarseness and subtlety.

The five consciousnesses of the Tathāgata are not the five consciousness-elements (*pañca-vijñāna-dhātu*), because the Sūtras state that the Buddha-mind is always in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whereas the Śāstras state that the nature of the five consciousnesses is distracted (*vikṣipta*).
With which consciousness is the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) associated?
The sixth [wisdom] is associated with the arising of transformative activity (*nirmāṇa*).
How does it differ from the nature of the wisdom of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*)?

The latter observes the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, whereas this [sixth wisdom] only gives rise to transformative activity; thus, there is a distinction between them.
These two categories of wisdom should not arise simultaneously, because two cognitions of the same class do not arise together.
To allow that they do not arise together is not contrary to reason;
however, since they are of the same substance with distinct functions, their simultaneous occurrence is also not a fault.

Alternatively, when associated with the seventh pure consciousness (*viśuddha-saptama-vijñāna*), taking the eye and other faculties as its support and forms and other objects as its objective conditions, this constitutes the specific function of the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
That is to say, when the pure seventh consciousness manifests the marks of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and its lands for others, it is subsumed under the category of the Wisdom of Equality;
when it manifests transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), it is subsumed under the category of the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).
Is it not the case that this category subsumes the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the five consciousnesses?

It is not so; for the substance of the acquisition resulting from the transformation is not identical to those [consciousnesses], just as when one speaks of "attaining nirvāṇa" through the transformation of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), nirvāṇa cannot be subsumed under birth-and-death. Therefore, one should not raise an objection regarding this point.

There is another interpretation: the merit, body, and lands of the Tathāgata are, as appropriate, subsumed within the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu); these three categories all encompass both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

When the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises state that fifteen elements and so forth are exclusively contaminated, they are speaking based on the coarse and superficial objects of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and not referring to everything.
This means that among the eighteen elements (dhātus) accomplished by others, only the final three are subsumed under the untainted (anāsrava).
Although those accomplished by a Buddha are entirely untainted, they are not subsumed within the cognitive objects (viṣaya) known by the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

However, when other passages state that the Buddha’s qualities and so forth are not the *dhātus* and so on, it is because they differ from the characteristics of the *dhātus* as known by the inferior wisdom of the two vehicles;
this must necessarily be the case according to principle.

Why is this so? Because it is taught that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*); because it is taught that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are subsumed within the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*); and because the existence of nineteen elements and so forth is refuted by the Noble Ones.

If [the Tathāgata] were free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), he would not be the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth; nor should it be said that he is the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), the virtuous, the permanent, blissful, the body of liberation (*vimukti-kāya*), and so on.

Furthermore, it is stated in various places that one transforms the impermanent aggregates (*skandha*) to obtain the permanent aggregates; the same applies to the realms (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*). How then can it be said that the Tathāgata is not the aggregates, bases, and realms?
Therefore, the statement that they are "not" [existent] is a teaching of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the nature of the five consciousnesses is distracted, this refers to their establishment by other [conditions]; it does not mean they are established by the Buddha. Thus, within the Buddha’s body, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and so forth are all fully present and are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).

This fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is also inconceivable, because it transcends the path of discursive thought and verbal expression; because it is subtle, profound, and personally realized within; because it cannot be illustrated by any worldly analogies; because its nature is that of wholesome, pure phenomena (*śukla-dharma*); because the pure *dharmadhātu* is utterly secure, being free from arising and ceasing; because the wondrous functions of the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*) are boundless and supremely skillful; and because both [the basis and the fruit] possess characteristics that are beneficial and contrary to the unwholesome. For these reasons, both are described as "wholesome" (*kuśala*).

The treatises state that the eight bases, such as the locus (*sthāna*) and so forth, are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Yet, does the Tathāgata not possess the five faculties and three objects?
Regarding this, there are three explanations, which are explained in detail as previously stated.

All phenomena pertaining to the bodies and lands of all Tathāgatas are subsumed under Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*); therefore, they are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*). This is because the Noble Ones teach that Cessation and the Path are exclusively of a wholesome nature, and because they teach that the Buddha-lands and so forth are not [subsumed under] Suffering (*duḥkha*) or Origination (*samudaya*).

The appearances of tainted, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena transformed by the Buddha’s consciousness are all produced from untainted, wholesome seeds and are thus subsumed under the category of untainted wholesomeness.
Furthermore, these are eternal, for they have no end.
