The pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is without arising or cessation; because its nature is immutable, it is said to be eternal.
Because the basis for the mental states of the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna-cittavarga*) is eternal and because they are never interrupted or exhausted, they are also said to be eternal;

yet this is not an eternity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nitya*), for they arise from causes, and it is categorically taught that whatever arises must return to cessation, as neither form nor mind is seen to be anything other than impermanent.

Nevertheless, because the sentient beings transformed by the power of the original vows are inexhaustible, these four categories of wisdom continue without interruption or end until the limits of the future.
Furthermore, they are blissful, as they are free from any oppression or affliction.
The pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is called "blissful" because all its manifold characteristics are quiescent.
The mental states of the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna-cittavarga*) are called "blissful" because they are eternally free from affliction and harm.

Since the intrinsic nature of these two is entirely devoid of oppression and distress, and they are capable of bringing bliss to all sentient beings, both types of transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) are termed "blissful."

The two vehicles attain the fruit of the twofold transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) merely by eternally and completely abandoning the fetters of the afflictive hindrances (kleśāvaraṇa); as they lack any superior qualities, it is therefore called only the "body of liberation" (vimukti-kāya).
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One has realized the unsurpassed dharma of tranquil silence; therefore, he is named the Great Muni.
The two fruits attained by this Honored Muni forever transcend the two obstacles and are also termed the Dharmakāya.

Because it is adorned with immeasurable, boundless, and great meritorious qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the term "body" (*kāya*) is used here in the sense of a collection of entities and their bases;

therefore, this Dharma-body has these five factors as its nature. It is not the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) alone that is called the Dharma-body, for both results of the two types of transformation (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) are subsumed within it.
Thus, the Dharma-body has three distinct aspects:

first, the Svabhāvakāya (Self-nature Body), which refers to the true and pure Dharma-realm of all Tathāgatas. It is the equal basis for the Saṃbhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya; it is free from characteristics, quiescent, and transcends all conceptual proliferation. It possesses boundless, true, and eternal merits, and is the equal, ultimate nature of all phenomena.
This very intrinsic nature is also called the *dharmakāya*, because it is the basis upon which the dharmas of great merit depend.
Second is the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), which is of two kinds:

first, the self-enjoyment [body], which refers to the boundless, true merits arising from the immeasurable accumulations of merit and wisdom cultivated by all Tathāgatas over three incalculable eons; as well as their extremely perfect, pure, constant, and pervasive form-bodies, which remain in a state of serene continuity until the end of the future, perpetually enjoying for themselves the vast joy of the Dharma.

Second is the enjoyment for others (*para-sambhogika*), which refers to the manifestation by all Tathāgatas—through their wisdom of equality—of a subtle and pure body of merit. Dwellings in purely pure lands, they manifest great supernormal powers and turn the wheel of the true Dharma for the assembly of bodhisattvas abiding on the ten stages, resolving the net of doubts of the multitude and causing them to enjoy the bliss of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
The combination of these two types is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body).

Third is the *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Body), which refers to the immeasurable transformation bodies manifested by the Tathāgatas through their *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom) according to the various classes of beings. Dwelling in both pure and impure lands, they manifest supernatural powers and preach the Dharma for the sake of bodhisattvas who have not yet reached the [bodhisattva] grounds, as well as for those of the two vehicles and ordinary worldlings, appearing in accordance with their respective capacities to cause each of them to obtain all manner of beneficial and blissful matters.

Regarding the inclusion of the three bodies (*trikāya*) within the five natures of phenomena (*pañcadharmasvabhāva*), one interpretation holds that the first two [natures] subsume the *svābhāvikakāya*. This is because the sūtras state that suchness (*tathatā*) is the *dharmakāya*, and the treatises state that by transforming the *ālayavijñāna* one attains the *svābhāvikakāya*; for it is through the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—specifically the category of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom—that this body is realized.

The middle two wisdoms comprise the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*): it is said that the Wisdom of Equality manifests as the Buddha-body for all bodhisattvas within the purely pure lands; it is said that the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation preaches the Dharma within great assemblies to sever doubts and manifest sovereign mastery; and it is said that by transforming the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), one attains the Enjoyment Body.

The final category of wisdom subsumes the Nirmāṇakāya (Transformation Body), because it is taught that the Kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna (Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks) manifests immeasurable and inconceivable transformations throughout the lands of the ten directions.
Furthermore, since the excellence of wisdom fully encompasses the three bodies, one should know that all three bodies possess actual wisdom.

There is an interpretation that the first [of the three bodies] subsumes the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-nature body). This is because it is taught that the self-nature body is by nature eternal; because it is taught that the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* is without arising or ceasing; because it is taught that it is attained through the cause of realization and not through the cause of birth; and furthermore, because it is taught that the *dharmakāya* is shared by all Buddhas, pervades all phenomena, and—like space—is without marks, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and neither form nor mind.

However, when it is said that one attains [the dharmakāya] by transforming the ālayavijñāna, it means that by transforming and extinguishing the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of the two obstacles within the eighth consciousness, the dharmakāya is manifested.
Among the distinctions of wisdom, the dharmakāya is described as their basis, because it is their true nature.
Although the *svabhāva-dharmakāya* possesses truly real and boundless qualities, because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it cannot be described as a substance such as form or mind.

Among the qualities of the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), the truly real qualities within the category of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) are subsumed under the eternal and pervasive *rūpakāya*, which comprises the *svasaṃbhogakāya*. The Buddha-bodies manifested within the category of the equality wisdom (*samatājñāna*) comprise the *parasambhogakāya*. The various bodily forms manifested according to the species [of beings] within the category of the all-accomplishing wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) comprise the *nirmāṇakāya*.
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is said to be the Enjoyment Buddha because one attains enjoyment by transforming the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

Although one also attains enjoyment by transforming the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), it is not mentioned briefly here regarding the attainment of enjoyment, as its transformation is taught specifically to manifest the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*).

Furthermore, it is taught that the *dharmakāya* is without birth or cessation, is attained solely through realization, and is neither form nor mind; yet the category of the *ādarśajñāna* (great perfect mirror wisdom) is the opposite of this. If it were not the *saṃbhogakāya*, to which body would it belong?

Furthermore, because the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) subsumes the Buddha’s unique, conditioned, and real virtues, the actual form and mind of the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) are all subsumed within the enjoyment body.

Moreover, since both the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are manifested as skillful means for the sake of transforming others, it cannot be said that their essence consists of actual wisdom.

Although it is said that the wisdom of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is subsumed under the excellence of wisdom, because it appears as if it were wisdom or is produced by wisdom, it is metaphorically designated by the name "wisdom" while its actual substance is not wisdom. It is merely stated that the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) and the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) can manifest the three activities of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body; it is not said that these two bodies are themselves the two wisdoms. Therefore, these two wisdoms are subsumed under the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).

However, although the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the body of communal enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*) lack actual mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), they possess manifested mind and mental factors; for the spiritual power of the Unsurpassed Awakened One is inconceivable, enabling him to manifest phenomena that lack physical form.
If it were not so, how could the Tathāgata manifest greed, anger, and the like,
given that he has long since severed them?
Furthermore, how could śrāvakas, animals, and others know the mind of the Tathāgata?

Because even Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment cannot know the Tathāgata’s true mind, this sūtra states that the Tathāgata transforms immeasurable classes of beings so that they all possess minds;

it further states that the Tathāgata’s *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom) manifests as the three karmas through transformation; and it states that these transformations possess a dependent mind, because the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) appears from the dependent true mind.
Although it is said that transformations lack faculties, mind, and so forth, this is stated in reference to other [transformations] and does not refer to those of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, because the transformed material faculties and the mental states and mental factors lack the functional utility of faculties and so on, they are not said to exist.
Thus, although these three bodies are all fully endowed with boundless merits, each possesses its own distinct characteristics.

That is to say, the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-nature body) consists solely of the true, eternal, blissful, self, and pure; it is free from all defilements, serves as the basis for all virtues, and is characterized by unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) merit, devoid of the differentiated marks and functions of form, mind, and so forth.
The self-enjoyment body possesses immeasurable kinds of genuine qualities, such as sublime form and mind;

whereas the other-enjoyment and transformation bodies possess only the qualities of infinite, semblance-like form and mind that serve to benefit and bring happiness to others through their transformative manifestations.
Furthermore, the svabhāvakāya is primarily comprised of self-benefit, because it is quiescent, blissful, and devoid of activity.
It also concurrently benefits others, acting as a dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) that enables all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness.
Furthermore, because they serve as the basis for the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), they are comprised of both benefits.
The self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) belongs exclusively to self-benefit.
If the other-enjoyment body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body belong exclusively to the benefit of others, it is because they manifest for the sake of others.

Furthermore, the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-nature body) relies upon the *dharmatā-bhūmi* (dharma-nature land). Although there is no distinction in essence between this body and its land, they differ in terms of their attributes and characteristics belonging to the Buddha-dharma.

Both this Buddha-body and its land are not subsumed under the category of form (*rūpa*); although their dimensions cannot be described as small or large, their extent is boundless according to their phenomenal manifestations, just as empty space pervades all places.

The body of self-enjoyment likewise relies upon its own land; that is to say, the pure consciousness associated with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), through the maturation of causes and conditions for a purely immaculate Buddha-land cultivated for one's own benefit in the past, continuously transforms from the moment of initial enlightenment until the end of the future into a purely immaculate Buddha-land, which is all-pervasive, boundless, and adorned with various jewels. The body of self-enjoyment constantly dwells in reliance upon this.

Just as the pure land is immeasurable, so too are the dimensions of its inhabitants; each of their faculties and marks of excellence is boundless, for they are produced by the guidance of infinite roots of goodness.

Since merit and wisdom are not material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), although it cannot be said that they have a specific form or magnitude, they may nonetheless be described as pervading all places, based on what they realize and the bodies upon which they rely.

The Enjoyment Body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*) also relies upon its own land. This means that through the power of the wisdom of equality and great compassion, and by virtue of the maturation of causes and conditions for a pure Buddha-land cultivated in the past for the benefit of others, it transforms into a pure land according to what is appropriate for Bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Whether small or large, inferior or superior, it changes and evolves over time; the Enjoyment Body dwells in reliance upon this, and the dimensions of the body that relies upon it likewise have no fixed limit.

If the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) relies upon a transformation land (*nirmāṇabhūmi*), this refers to the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) through the power of great compassion. Due to the maturation of causes and conditions for pure and impure Buddha-lands cultivated for the benefit of others in the past, it manifests as a Buddha-land according to what is appropriate for sentient beings who have not yet ascended the stages (*bhūmi*). Whether pure or impure, small or large, it changes and transforms over time; the Buddha’s transformation body dwells in reliance upon it, and the dimensions of that supporting body are likewise without fixed limit.
Because the self-nature body (*svābhāvikakāya*) and its realm are realized identically by all Tathāgatas, they are without distinction in essence.

Although the bodies of self-enjoyment (*sambhogakāya*) and their supporting realms differ according to the individual transformations of each Buddha, they are all infinite and do not obstruct one another.

Regarding the remaining two [types of] bodies and lands, they are either common or uncommon depending on the sentient beings to be converted by the Tathāgatas. When the beings to be converted are common, at the same place and the same time, the various Buddhas each transform themselves into bodies and lands that are similar in shape without obstructing one another; these interpenetrate one another as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), causing the consciousnesses of those to be converted to manifest [these forms]. That is to say, within a single land, there is a single Buddha-body manifesting supernatural powers and preaching the Dharma for their benefit.

Regarding those that are unique, they are manifested by a single Buddha alone; for since beginningless time, the lineages of all sentient beings have been naturally and mutually interconnected—some many belonging to one, or one belonging to many—and thus the beings to be converted may be either common or unique.
It is not so; for it would be truly useless for many Buddhas to remain in the world for a long time, each performing arduous labors, since a single Buddha is able to benefit all sentient beings.

These various bodies and lands—whether pure or impure—which are manifested upon the untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*), share the same nature as the manifesting consciousness: they are both wholesome and untainted. Being produced by purely wholesome and untainted causes and conditions, they are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), and are therefore neither suffering (*duḥkha*) nor its origin (*samudaya*).

The characteristics of consciousness regarding the aggregates and so forth do not necessarily all coincide, because they are produced through the combined drawing-forth of causes and conditions from three factors.

That which is manifested upon a contaminated consciousness is, like the transforming consciousness itself, entirely contaminated; it arises solely from contaminated causes and conditions, and is therefore subsumed under suffering and its origin, rather than under cessation and the path.

The characteristics of wholesome consciousnesses and so forth are not necessarily identical, because they are produced through the combined drawing-forth of causes and conditions from the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
One should understand that the same applies to the similarities and differences among the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth;
otherwise, there would be no fifty-two [mental factors] and so on.

However, the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and so forth manifest based upon consciousness; they are not as substantially real within the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*) as the nature of consciousness itself.

Otherwise, the principle of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) would necessarily fail to be established, because one would be admitting that both consciousness and its internal objects are equally substantially existent.

Alternatively, the aspects, the seeing [consciousness], and so forth arise from conditions; all are dependently originated and their reality or unreality is like that of consciousness itself. The term "only" (vijñaptimātra) excludes external objects but does not negate internal objects; otherwise, even true suchness (tathatā) would have to be unreal.
Since internal objects and consciousness are both not unreal, why speak only of "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) and not of objects?
Consciousness exists solely internally, whereas objects extend to the external; for fear of confusing the two with external things, one speaks only of "consciousness-only."

Some foolish people are deludedly attached to external objects; they give rise to afflictions and karma, sinking into the cycle of birth and death, yet fail to understand that one must contemplate the mind and strive for liberation.

Out of compassion for them, I speak of "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra), so that they may contemplate their own minds and attain liberation from birth and death; it does not mean that internal objects are entirely non-existent like external ones.
Alternatively, the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) and so forth all have consciousness as their nature, arising as various manifestations through the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Since suchness (*tathatā*) is also the actual nature of consciousness, there is no separate dharma apart from the nature of consciousness.
In this context, the term "consciousness" (vijñāna) also refers to mental factors (caitta), because the mind and its factors are necessarily associated.

Since the three parts of this treatise establish the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra), it is therefore called the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only).
This treatise is also called "Purifying Consciousness-Only" (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), because it reveals the principle of consciousness-only with extreme clarity and purity.

The title of this root text is "Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only" (*Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratā*), because the principle of consciousness-only is fully and perfectly revealed by these thirty verses, neither more nor less.

Having analyzed the meaning of the nature and characteristics of Consciousness-Only according to the sacred teachings and correct reasoning, I dedicate the merit thus obtained to all living beings; may we together swiftly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment.

The Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only, Scroll Ten; Postscript to the Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only, composed by Shen Xuanming of Wuxing. To begin with, the ocean of enlightenment is limpid and profound, encompassing the myriad currents while fathoming the ultimate source;
the divine pivot reveals the subtle, pervading all phenomena while coalescing into the supreme truth.

He brightens the sun of wisdom to mirror the six realms of darkness, and releases the clouds of compassion to purify the eight quarters of the world; he expounds the single voice for universal liberation, and gallops afar on the three vehicles.
He embodied the half-vessel of Ājñātakauṇḍinya, ferrying those still bound by existence through the Deer Park;
he illuminated the full-capacity of Subhūti, unraveling the emptiness of emptiness on Vulture Peak.
Though he transcended the dust of both eternalism and nihilism, how could he have discarded the raft of existence and emptiness?
It manifests the spiritual lineage of the Unsurpassed and concentrates the Middle Way within this teaching.
Yet, when the Golden River’s radiance faded, the pure source was divided and could no longer be traced;
as the jade tablets scattered their blossoms, the turbid winds of later times were fanned into a competitive surge.
Thus, twenty-eight heterodox views bewildered the swan-like sages within the Five Indias, while sixteen teachers threw the ox-like masses into chaos under the four rulers.

Among those who lead toward sainthood, Vasubandhu was truly the one; he was an Arhat of this Bhadrakalpa who concealed his innate wisdom to guide beings through transformation. His radiance soared and his brilliance nurtured, giving birth to a manifestation that illuminated the world with its spiritual essence.

Yao constantly illuminated the eight aggregates and refined the primal sentiments through the six *pādas*; he excelled in discussing the "mushrooms" (sublime truths) within the *Abhidharmakośa* and established the remaining schools of the "existence" doctrine. He gathered the profound waves of the Mahāyāna and investigated the ultimate principles of emptiness; as his transformation rose toward the zenith, he shone upon the ultimate limit, and this eulogy unifies him with the profound stillness of the One.
The *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is the final work of Vasubandhu, wherein he returned to his fundamental source.
Its principles conceal a profound ocean, floating the realms of perception upon the River of Glory;
its meanings rise like billowing smoke and wind, adorning the rainbow-like verses within the Mysterious Garden.

The words encompass the myriad phenomena, and the characters contain a thousand expositions; their wondrous purport is transcendentally sublime, and their profound radiance is as brilliant as the stars. The subtle threads remain unexpressed as the spirit merges with the realm of the ineffable; solitary luminosity withdraws its reflections, and secret thoughts flow from hidden sources.

Subsequently, there arose ten great Bodhisattvas, such as Dharmapāla and Sthiramati, who concealed the profound pearl within the Eight Treasuries and erected a lofty structure around the Fourfold Enclosure. They dwelt in the illumination of the two causes and took refuge in the purity of the three contemplations; ascending to the radiance of the Ten Stages, they moistened the forest of the worthy with the waters of clarified wisdom.
Neighboring the threshold of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment, they brightened the moon of practice to dispel the heavy night.

Gentle yet fragrant and powerful, he followed in the illustrious footsteps of the former sages; his words gushed forth like a spring and his precious insights flew like the wind. Having all examined the root verses, he composed this commentary, titled the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, or alternatively, the *Viśuddhavijñaptimātratā-śāstra*.
The dual grasping outside the empty mind causes one to stagnate in the deluded paths of existence;
the single mind within conscious awareness leads one to cling to the false attachment of returning to emptiness.
When this mind and its objects are obscured, it is for this reason that one sinks long in the sea of suffering.
Realizing that all things are empty and non-existent, he ascended high upon the shore of awakening.
The ninety heterodox paths were swept away like a tempest dispersing starry banners;
the eighteen Hinayana schools were halted like a carriage with its axle-pin stuck, unable to support the dragon-drawn chariot.

He exhausted the mysteries of the spirit and embodied its subtlety; he reached the depths of the obscure and probed the mechanisms of the divine. His essence pierced through the Ten Branches and his insight comprehended the Nine Divisions. Looking back upon the Ten Wings, he spread his immortal feathers; bowing toward the Nine Schools, he deepened the jade waves. He exhausted the rare and subtle ultimate principles and elucidated the profound scriptures of the Dharma King. Both name and designation were transcended, and both the trap and the image were forgotten. He caused the brilliant sun to shine upon the Western Regions and concealed the rainbow light within Zhendan (China). Saving all beings and propagating the Way, he loftily returned to the virtue of the Patriarchal Source.

Now, as for the Great Upādhyāya, the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang: his person embodies sagacity and abandons the unreal; he treads upon benevolence and soars upon wisdom. He realized the stillness of the nine gates of dhyāna on Mount Rong, and the eighty thousand profound streams surged forth into the vast ocean. He layered golden walls that shone like the moon and towered above jade palaces that rose like drifting clouds; he surpassed the fragrant purity of the clear orchid and nurtured the flowering grace of the dragon’s wings.

Lamenting that the subtle words have hidden their luster and sighing that the great principles have lost their radiance, I have thus uttered this vow and undertaken this distant journey. I swim in the waters of the Auspicious River, climb the low branches of the Jewel Tree, travel in spiritual rapture along the carved railings, and pace with ease upon the Snowy Peaks; ascending the purple steps to realize the Way, I gaze upon the profound shadows to solemnize my causal roots.
Gathering the profound and observing the extraordinary, he set the Azure Dragon in motion for two cycles;
sealing the sandalwood and carving the *sūtras*, he turned the White Horse back through the Three Qin lands.

Our Great Tang celebrates the manifestation of the Golden Wheel and receives auspicious signs from the pivot of the heavens; it has suddenly come to dwell in glory over the great chiliocosm and soars like a celestial bird through the six eloquences. Its divine transformation permeates the hidden depths as the Nine Immortals present their treasures; its profound principles are widely expounded as the hundred spirits take up their offices. With the jade pendant suspended in solemnity, the Emperor’s presence is deeply honored, as his dreams repeatedly commune with the radiance of the heavens.
Unfurling the silk cords and manifesting the blossoms of brilliance, the radiant and soaring texts provide profound assistance.

Thereupon, an imperial decree was issued to promulgate the translation, commanding Yu Zhining, Duke of Yan and Senior Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs, Xu Jingzong, Duke of Gaoyang and Director of the Chancellery, and others to refine and polish the language; while the śramaṇa Shi Shentai and others were to verify the meaning, and the śramaṇa Shi Jingmai and others to examine the phrasing.
Beginning from the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era and ending at the close of the Xianqing era, sixty sections were compiled and one thousand scrolls produced.

These works surpass those of Mount Penglai and the Kunlun ranges, causing the Dharma-treasure to flourish once more and opening the way for the masses of the deluded. Both the eulogies of virtue and the prefaces to the scriptures were composed by imperial brush; such a flourishing of the profound wind has never been heard of before.

In the fourth year of the Xianqing era, when the dragon rested in harmony with the auspicious signs and the season of profound yin arrived, with the intercalary month falling in the Yang period, I compiled these ten types of Buddhist scriptures totaling four thousand five hundred stanzas; categorizing and classifying them according to their respective origins, I have unified them into a single work consisting of ten fascicles.

As the months reached their cycle and the compilation was finally completed, the glosses and explanations were meticulously summarized and the differences between the indigenous and foreign traditions were thoroughly investigated. Its rhythms startled the *shao* melodies and its literary brilliance adorned the celestial vault; the White Phoenix displayed its rarity and the Purple Microcosm manifested its auspiciousness. Thus, works that differ in wording but are identical in meaning became as if produced by a single master; this demonstrates that the principles of the ancient sages and the worthies of today are one and the same.

The Tripiṭaka master Daoci was of a distinguished and noble lineage, a scion of a refined and illustrious clan. In his prime, he tasted the flavor of the Way; on splendid days, he investigated the mysteries. His scholarly achievements were as lofty as those of Linruo, and his discernment as clear as a mirror amidst the clouds. His dignified demeanor was as pure as polished jade, surpassing the profound clarity of Daosui;
his elegant style was as fragrant as orchids, eclipsing the soaring eloquence of Fatai.
The immortal strains of the sūtras resonate through the eight Brahma-sounds, while the cranes of the celestial realm dance as auspicious omens;
the elegant patterns are unfolded across the nine chapters, casting the reflections of phoenixes upon the paulownia trees in brilliant splendor.
As the light ascends, the translation companions look down upon the hidden sagacity, merging with its radiant glow.
Ascending the ranks of those who uphold the wondrous meaning, he surveys the expansive teachings with lofty vision.
He captures the first light of the morning sun upon the jade-like landscape, illuminating the profound scholars;
he unfurls transcendent brushstrokes that span the heavens, soaring beyond both the mundane and the sacred.

Having personally received the fourfold eloquence and being encouraged in speech by the threefold illumination, he opened up new vistas like windows and doors and guided others across the fords and streams; his artistic skill relied upon the white silk, and his penetration of principles was entrusted to the spirit. He synthesized the essential outlines, distinguished their categories and grades, and further compiled commentaries on the meanings to transmit them to future students.
I hope this teaching may spread across the vast lands of the Yellow River, surpassing the "Turtle Diagram" of the *Shuowen*;
and that its auspiciousness may float through the Purple Palace, eclipsing the "Connected Pearls" of the "Qilin" inscriptions.
Thus, exhausting my humble and meager efforts, I shall set forth its fundamental principles.
